MFMod North Macedonia: Model Manual

A guided map of the World Bank MFMod / MFMSA model for North Macedonia (C:\WBG\MKD9), built from master.prg, readdat.prg, equations.prg, solve.prg, the optional climate, BCA and transport modules, and the two data workbooks (MKDrawOctober2026.xlsx, ExogVarsOctober2026.xlsx). Every equation shown is the actual code in your files. Click any to jump to it on the dependency map.

1980–2025History in the workfile
2026First forecast year
2012–2100Solve period
2012–2050Excel front-end display
AnnualFrequency

1. How the model is built

Everything is driven by master.prg. It sets the global dates and switches, then calls the other programs in this order:

master.prgdates, switches, data path
→
readdat.prgimport Excel, build derived series
→
equations.prgestimate equations, add identities
→
climateeqs / bca / transportonly if switch = 1
→
solve.prgadd factors, extend exogenous vars, solve
→
convergence_check.prgcharts of % changes
→
interface.prgstrings for the Excel front end

After the build, readexovars.prg opens the solution workfile, imports your forecast assumptions from ExogVarsOctober2026.xlsx (sheets Labor, Fiscal, Cmdy, TradeP, NomFXidx, RealFXidx, Prices, Financing), solves scenario 3 ("Lab") with those variables overridden, and copies the _3 values into the baseline from 2023 on.

Behavioural equations

Estimated by OLS (equation _X.LS …). Coefficients written as numbers are imposed (calibrated); only C(n) terms are estimated. Most are error-correction models (ECM).

Identities

Accounting rules added with MKD.APPEND @IDENTITY, e.g. GDP = C + G + I + X − M. They always hold exactly.

Exogenous variables

Inputs the model does not explain, such as foreign demand, commodity prices, tax rates, population and TFP. You set them; the model reacts.
Switches in master.prg: !climate=0, !BCA=0 (border carbon adjustment), !TRNS=0 (transport) and !SR=0 (slower energy transition). With these settings the core macro model described on this page is what runs. The optional modules are summarised in section 17.

What an ECM equation means

Almost every behavioural equation has the same two-part shape. If you understand one, you understand them all:

Δln Yt = −λ · [ ln Yt−1 − ln Y*t−1 ] + β · Δln Xt + constant + dummies

Long run (error correction)

Y* is where Y "should" be according to theory, e.g. consumption equal to real disposable income. If Y was above Y* last year, growth slows. λ is the speed of adjustment: λ = 0.2 closes about 20% of the gap each year.

Short run (dynamics)

How Y responds immediately when its drivers change this year. β is the short-run elasticity: β = 0.5 means 1% faster income growth adds 0.5 pp to growth this year.

EViews notation: DLOG(X) = Δln X ≈ growth rate; X(-1) = last year; @PC(X) = % change; @DURING("2009") = dummy that equals 1 only in 2009; @LOGIT(C(1)) forces a coefficient between 0 and 1; DUMH = 1 in history and 0 in the forecast.

🧪 Test it in EViews · Model overview dashboard

What it checks: The model's block structure and the main baseline indicators from 2010 to 2035.

What you should see: Growth converging to potential (≈ 2.4%), the gap closing to 0, inflation near 2%, and stable fiscal and external ratios. The forecast period is shaded.

Paste into a new EViews program (File → New → Program) in the MKD workfile and press Run. Results open as a dashboard and a spool (all tables and graphs). Objects start with OV_; remove them with delete OV_*.

' ==============================================================================
'  MFMod MKD  |  TEST OV: Model overview
'  Purpose : Main macro aggregates of the baseline: growth, gap, inflation, labour, fiscal, external
'  Needs   : Baseline solved (actual series = baseline, *_0 series exist).
'  Output  : spool OV_SPOOL (tables + graphs) and dashboard OV_DASH
'  Clean up: delete OV_*
' ==============================================================================
%hs = "2010"      ' first year shown
%fs = "2026"      ' first forecast year (shaded area)
%fe = "2035"      ' last year shown
spool OV_SPOOL
smpl @all

' ---- Model structure -------------------------------------------------------
freeze(OV_BLOCK) MKD.block
OV_SPOOL.append OV_BLOCK

' ---- Indicators ------------------------------------------------------------
series OV_GDPG = @pc(MKDNYGDPMKTPKN)
OV_GDPG.displayname Real GDP growth, %
series OV_POTG = @pc(MKDNYGDPPOTLKN)
OV_POTG.displayname Potential GDP growth, %
series OV_GAP = MKDNYGDPGAP_
OV_GAP.displayname Output gap, % of potential
series OV_INF = @pc(MKDFPCPITOTLXN)
OV_INF.displayname CPI inflation, %
series OV_UNR = MKDLMUNRTOTLCN
OV_UNR.displayname Unemployment rate, %
series OV_BAL = MKDGGBALOVRLCN/MKDNYGDPMKTPCN*100
OV_BAL.displayname Fiscal balance, % GDP
series OV_DEBT = MKDGGDBTTOTLCN/MKDNYGDPMKTPCN*100
OV_DEBT.displayname Public debt, % GDP
series OV_CA = MKDBNCABFUNDCD/MKDNYGDPMKTPCD*100
OV_CA.displayname Current account, % GDP

' ---- Graphs ----------------------------------------------------------------
smpl {%hs} {%fe}
group OV_G1 OV_GDPG OV_POTG
freeze(OV_GR1) OV_G1.line
OV_GR1.addtext(t) "Real and potential GDP growth, %"
OV_GR1.draw(shade, bottom) {%fs} {%fe}
OV_GR1.draw(line, left) 0
OV_SPOOL.append OV_GR1
smpl {%hs} {%fe}
group OV_G2 OV_GAP
freeze(OV_GR2) OV_G2.line
OV_GR2.addtext(t) "Output gap, % of potential"
OV_GR2.draw(shade, bottom) {%fs} {%fe}
OV_GR2.draw(line, left) 0
OV_SPOOL.append OV_GR2
smpl {%hs} {%fe}
group OV_G3 OV_INF OV_UNR
freeze(OV_GR3) OV_G3.line(m)
OV_GR3.addtext(t) "Inflation and unemployment, %"
OV_GR3.draw(shade, bottom) {%fs} {%fe}
OV_SPOOL.append OV_GR3
smpl {%hs} {%fe}
group OV_G4 OV_BAL OV_CA
freeze(OV_GR4) OV_G4.line
OV_GR4.addtext(t) "Fiscal balance and current account, % of GDP"
OV_GR4.draw(shade, bottom) {%fs} {%fe}
OV_GR4.draw(line, left) 0
OV_SPOOL.append OV_GR4
smpl {%hs} {%fe}
group OV_G5 OV_DEBT
freeze(OV_GR5) OV_G5.line
OV_GR5.addtext(t) "Public debt, % of GDP"
OV_GR5.draw(shade, bottom) {%fs} {%fe}
OV_SPOOL.append OV_GR5

' ---- Table (every 5 years) -------------------------------------------------
smpl @all if @year>=2015 and @year<=2035 and @mod(@year,5)=0
group OV_T1 OV_GDPG OV_POTG OV_GAP OV_INF OV_UNR OV_BAL OV_DEBT OV_CA
freeze(OV_TB1) OV_T1.sheet
OV_SPOOL.append OV_TB1

graph OV_DASH.merge OV_GR1 OV_GR2 OV_GR3 OV_GR4 OV_GR5
OV_DASH.align(2,1,1)
OV_DASH.addtext(t) "MFMod MKD | Test OV"
smpl @all
show OV_DASH
show OV_SPOOL

Step-by-step walkthrough: what happens when you run master.prg

Follow the build in the order EViews executes it. Each step shows what the code does and why. Open the step's code to see the exact lines from your files.

Phase A · master.prg: set up the run
  1. Clean start and working folderCloses every open workfile, turns on the message log, and makes the folder where master.prg lives the current directory, so all include .\programs\… paths work.
    code
    close @all
logmode l
%path = @runpath
cd %path
  2. Define the global dates (strings used everywhere)
    %beg_dat = 1980first year of the workfile
    %end_dat = 2025last year of history; equations are estimated up to here and the forecast starts the next year
    %fcst_start = 2026first forecast year
    %solve_start = 2012, %solve_end = 2100the model is solved from 2012 so add factors cover 2012–2025, then forecast to 2100 (a long horizon to check convergence)
    %display_start/end = 2012/2050what the Excel front end shows

    To roll the model forward one year, change %end_dat (and the data file) first. Every sample in readdat, equations and solve keys off it.

  3. Name the country and model; set switches%cty = "MKD" is the prefix for all series and %model = "MKD" is the EViews model object. !check_id (test that identities add up), !check_insmpfit (in-sample fit test) and the module switches !climate, !BCA, !TRNS, !SR are all 0. %solve_method = "g" selects Gauss-Seidel.
  4. Point to the data file%data = %path + "data\MKDrawOctober2026.xlsx".
    readdat.prg repeats the same header and re-sets %data to the absolute path C:\WBG\MKD9\Backend\Data\MKDrawOctober2026-XL2.xlsx. The XL2 file is the one actually imported.
  5. Call the building blocks in orderinclude readdat.prg → include equations.prg → (climate / BCA / transport if switched on) → include solve.prg → include convergence_check.prg → include interface.prg. The wfsave lines at the end are commented out, so you save the solution workfile by hand (or through the front end).
Phase B · readdat.prg: build the database
  1. Create an empty annual workfile and an empty modelwfcreate a 1980 2100 makes yearly observations 1980–2100; model MKD creates the model object that equations and identities will be added to.
  2. Import the Excel sheetsFive import commands read MAIN (A2:AC210), Y (population), CMDY (commodities), external_Q2 (partners) and Extra (A2:AC46). The 3rd column of each row (the mnemonic) becomes the series name, and #N/A becomes NA. The header rows that also get imported as junk series are deleted next (delete ser* …).
  3. Compute deflatorsA loop sets XN = CN / KN for GDP, C, G, I, inventories, X, M, GDP fc, agriculture, services, energy and electricity. Public and private investment get the total investment deflator, and their real values are recomputed from it.
  4. Helper seriesDUMH = 1 (history dummy, set to 0 later in solve.prg) and MKDINFLEXPT = 1.35.
  5. Close the national accountsInventories = total GFCF − public − private; statistical discrepancy = GDP − (C+G+I+X−M); domestic demand GDE; GDP per capita; terms of trade. On the production side, industry = GDP fc − agriculture − services and net taxes = GDP mp − GDP fc.
  6. Wages and the labour shareNYYWBTOTLCN_ = 0.59; the average wage is converted from monthly to annual (×12); wage bill = wage × employment.
  7. Effective tax ratesPIT/wage bill, CIT/(GDP×0.41), VAT/(C+G), excise/C, customs/M, all ×100. These become the exogenous tax-rate inputs.
  8. Labour market and NAIRULabour force = participation × working-age population; unemployment is recomputed from employment. The series are extended after 2025 (u → 7.2 with persistence 0.9; participation → 57 with persistence 0.7), then HP-filtered (λ = 100) to get the NAIRU LMUNRSTRLCN and structural participation LMPRTSTRLCN. Structural employment LMEMPSTRLCN follows from these.

    The scalars sigmaL, zeta, markupW, replaceRatio and denom2 are left over from a theoretical NAIRU formula that is commented out; the target is simply 7.2.

  9. Capital stockδ = 5%. A trial capital series is accumulated from the first investment year; its K/Y ratio 15 years later sets the initial stock. The real capital stock is then K = K(−1)(1−δ) + I − inventories.
  10. TFPRaw TFP = GDP / (L*0.59·K−10.41), extended at +1.6% a year after 2025 and HP-filtered → MKDNYGDPTFP.
  11. Potential, gap, marginal cost, cost of capitalPotential GDP, output gap and PSTAR are calculated. The rental rate is set as R = 0.41·GDPCN/K−1, and the risk premium is backed out so that the user-cost identity holds exactly in history: 
    MKDNEKRTPREMFR = 100*MKDNEKRTTOTLXN*(1-MKDGGREVCITTXN/100)/MKDNEGDIFTOTXN - (MKDFMLBLPOLYXN + MKDDEPR*100 - MKDINFLEXPT)
  12. Fiscal aggregatesTax totals, "other revenue" as the residual to total revenue, transfers, current spending, implicit interest rates on external and domestic debt, the external share of debt, the debt valuation residual GGDBTVALTCN, balances (% of GDP), and structural/cyclical balances.
  13. BOP aggregatesG&S = merchandise + services; "other" primary and secondary income as residuals; net balances; current account; other investment; overall BOP; reserves change. NA exports, imports and GDP are converted to EUR (/MKDPANEUATLS).
  14. External indicators2010-based FX and price indices, the 12 trade weights (normalised), the export market XMKT, REER, NEER, and the commodity-weighted export and import price indices PXKEY and PMKEY.
  15. R&D stock and trendR&D capital (5% depreciation, distributed lags) and T_LR = @trend. readdat ends here: "moving onto equations".
Phase C · equations.prg: estimate and assemble

Two kinds of commands appear, and the difference matters:

equation _NAME.LS …

Creates an equation object and estimates it right away by OLS over the sample set by the smpl line just above it. It is not yet in the model; solve.prg merges every equation object later.

MKD.APPEND @IDENTITY …

Writes an accounting identity directly into the model. Nothing is estimated.
  1. Private consumption (smpl 2007–2025) → card
  2. Domestic interest rate (to 2019) → card
  3. Private investment (2000–2025), then the rental-cost identity → card, card
  4. Public investment (CN, KN), private investment CN identity, government consumption CN (to 2019) → card
  5. Exports (to 2025) and imports (2004–2025) → X, M
  6. GDP fc deflator: Phillips curve (2006–2025) → card
  7. Wage equation (to 2025) → card
  8. Consumption deflator (2003–2025) → card
  9. Public/private investment deflators (1995–2019), total investment deflator identity, government consumption deflator → card
  10. Export deflator (to 2023) and import deflator (to 2025) → PX, PM
  11. Sector value added and sector deflators (agri, industry; to 2019) → card
  12. Labour: employment (to 2025), unemployment tracking, NAIRU → EMP, NAIRU
  13. Fiscal: debt split (external/domestic), debt accumulation, valuation share; then the if !current = 1 branch selects the spending-share rules (capital, wages, G&S, subsidies, SRA, social transfers, pensions) plus the transfer identities; then the revenue equations (tax rate × base, or % of GDP) → section 11
  14. BOP: remittances, other income as % of GDP; BOP G&S follow NA trade; merchandise shares; CPI; capital and financial account shares; exchange rate tied to EUR/USD → section 8
  15. Discrepancy and net taxes as constant shares of GDP (2000–2025)
  16. Policy rate rule (2000–2024) → card
  17. The big identity block: real and nominal GDP, GFCF total, GDE, potential, gap, capital, PSTAR, deflators, EUR conversions, all BOP balances, FX cross rates, REER/NEER, XMKT, PXKEY/PMKEY, fiscal balances, revenue and expenditure totals, interest = rate × lagged debt, financing, structural balances, services VA residual, GDP fc, labour force, structural employment.
  18. Last pieces: participation equation (2000–2025), unemployment identity, wage bill identity, R&D stock and R&D spending share.
Phase D · solve.prg: turn it into a forecast
  1. Merge every equation object in the workfile into model MKD (@wlookup("*","equation")).
  2. Find quasi-identities: equations ending in DUMH are listed so that their add factors can be zeroed later.
  3. Solve history 2012–2025 with add factors so the model reproduces the data exactly.
  4. Extend all exogenous series to 2100 with the ρ = 0.5 rule; set DUMH = 0 and freeze T_LR.
  5. Decay add factors by 15% per year, and set quasi-identity add factors to 0.
  6. Solve 2012–2100, copy the _0 results into the base series, and drop the discrepancy and net-tax equations.
  7. Then convergence charts, front-end strings, and, run separately, readexovars.prg to load your ExogVars assumptions and re-solve.
🧪 Test it in EViews · Check every stage of the build

What it checks: Data coverage of key series, which ones have an equation, and whether the solved baseline reproduces history.

What you should see: First years ≈ 2000, last years = 2050 (forecast filled); 'yes' for behavioural variables; baseline minus data = 0 in history (PASS).

Paste into a new EViews program (File → New → Program) in the MKD workfile and press Run. Results open as a dashboard and a spool (all tables and graphs). Objects start with WK_; remove them with delete WK_*.

' ==============================================================================
'  MFMod MKD  |  TEST WK: Step-by-step build check
'  Purpose : Checks each stage of master.prg: data loaded, equations created, model solved, history reproduced
'  Needs   : Baseline solved (actual series = baseline, *_0 series exist).
'  Output  : spool WK_SPOOL (tables + graphs) and dashboard WK_DASH
'  Clean up: delete WK_*
' ==============================================================================
%hs = "2010"      ' first year shown
%fs = "2026"      ' first forecast year (shaded area)
%fe = "2035"      ' last year shown
spool WK_SPOOL
smpl @all

' ---- Stage 1-2: data coverage and equations --------------------------------
%list = "MKDNYGDPMKTPKN MKDNECONPRVTKN MKDNEGDIFPRVKN MKDNEEXPGNFSKN MKDNEIMPGNFSKN MKDNEWRTTOTLCN MKDLMEMPTOTLCN MKDNECONPRVTXN MKDGGREVTOTLCN MKDGGEXPTOTLCN MKDBNCABFUNDCD MKDNYGDPTFP MKDXMKT MKDFMLBLPOLYXN"
table(16,5) WK_DATA
WK_DATA(1,1) = "Series"
WK_DATA(1,2) = "First"
WK_DATA(1,3) = "Last"
WK_DATA(1,4) = "Obs"
WK_DATA(1,5) = "Has equation"
!r = 1
for %v {%list}
  !r = !r + 1
  WK_DATA(!r,1) = %v
  WK_DATA(!r,2) = @otod(@ifirst({%v}))
  WK_DATA(!r,3) = @otod(@ilast({%v}))
  WK_DATA(!r,4) = @obs({%v})
  if @isobject("_" + %v) then
    WK_DATA(!r,5) = "yes"
  else
    WK_DATA(!r,5) = "-"
  endif
next
WK_DATA.setwidth(1) 20
WK_SPOOL.append WK_DATA

' ---- Stage 3-4: solved baseline vs data ------------------------------------
series WK_ACT = MKDNYGDPMKTPKN
WK_ACT.displayname Real GDP, data/actual
series WK_BAS = MKDNYGDPMKTPKN_0
WK_BAS.displayname Real GDP, baseline solution
series WK_ERR = (MKDNYGDPMKTPKN_0/MKDNYGDPMKTPKN-1)*100
WK_ERR.displayname Baseline minus data, %
smpl {%hs} {%fe}
group WK_G1 WK_ACT WK_BAS
freeze(WK_GR1) WK_G1.line
WK_GR1.addtext(t) "Real GDP: data vs solved baseline"
WK_GR1.draw(shade, bottom) {%fs} {%fe}
WK_SPOOL.append WK_GR1
smpl {%hs} {%fe}
group WK_G2 WK_ERR
freeze(WK_GR2) WK_G2.line
WK_GR2.addtext(t) "Baseline minus data, % (should be 0 in history)"
WK_GR2.draw(shade, bottom) {%fs} {%fe}
WK_GR2.draw(line, left) 0
WK_SPOOL.append WK_GR2

' ---- Automatic checks (PASS if max |error| below threshold) ----------------
table(3,4) WK_CHK
WK_CHK(1,1) = "Check"
WK_CHK(1,2) = "Max |error|"
WK_CHK(1,3) = "Threshold"
WK_CHK(1,4) = "Result"
smpl 2005 2025
series WK_E2 = (MKDNYGDPMKTPKN_0/MKDNYGDPMKTPKN-1)*100
!m = @max(@abs(WK_E2))
WK_CHK(2,1) = "Baseline reproduces history (real GDP, %)"
WK_CHK(2,2) = !m
WK_CHK(2,3) = 0.01
if !m < 0.01 then
  WK_CHK(2,4) = "PASS"
else
  WK_CHK(2,4) = "CHECK"
endif
smpl 2005 2025
series WK_E3 = (MKDFPCPITOTLXN_0/MKDFPCPITOTLXN-1)*100
!m = @max(@abs(WK_E3))
WK_CHK(3,1) = "Baseline reproduces history (CPI, %)"
WK_CHK(3,2) = !m
WK_CHK(3,3) = 0.01
if !m < 0.01 then
  WK_CHK(3,4) = "PASS"
else
  WK_CHK(3,4) = "CHECK"
endif
WK_CHK.setwidth(1) 46
WK_SPOOL.append WK_CHK
smpl @all

graph WK_DASH.merge WK_GR1 WK_GR2
WK_DASH.align(2,1,1)
WK_DASH.addtext(t) "MFMod MKD | Test WK"
smpl @all
show WK_DASH
show WK_SPOOL

⚙ Supply side step by step: capital, labour, TFP, potential GDP, output gap

How the model calculates what the economy can produce (potential GDP) and how far actual GDP is from it (the output gap), first for history (2000–2025) and then for the forecast (2026+). The numbers are North Macedonia's, recomputed from MKDrawOctober2026.xlsx with the same steps as readdat.prg; the TFP result matches MKDNYGDPTFP in your ExogVars file. Your workfile is always the reference: use the EViews code tab to see the exact values.

Think of the economy as a factory. To know how much it can produce, you need three things:

Capital Kmachines, buildings, roads
+
Labour L*workers at "normal" unemployment
+
TFPhow efficiently K and L are used
→
Potential GDPTFP · L*0.59 · Kt−10.41
→
Output gapactual GDP vs potential

0.59 is the labour share (how much of GDP goes to workers); 0.41 = 1 − 0.59 is the capital share. Capital is taken from the end of last year (Kt−1), the machines already installed.

PieceCodeHistory (2000–2025)Forecast (2026+)
CapitalMKDNEGDIKSTKKNBuilt from investment data, starting from an estimated initial stockSame formula, with investment from the model's equations
Labour L*MKDLMEMPSTRLCNPopulation × smoothed participation × (1 − smoothed unemployment)Population and participation from the Labor sheet; NAIRU moves slowly toward 7.2%
TFPMKDNYGDPTFPWhat is left of GDP after K and L (Solow residual), then smoothedYour assumption from the Labor sheet (+1.27% in 2026 rising to +1.42% a year)
Potential GDPMKDNYGDPPOTLKNTFP · L*0.59 · Kt−10.41Same formula (an identity in the model)
Output gapMKDNYGDPGAP_(actual GDP ÷ potential − 1) × 100Same; actual GDP now comes from the demand equations

1 · Capital stock

Capital works like a bank account: each year 5% wears out and new investment is added.

Capitalt = Capitalt−1 × 0.95 + Investmentt − Inventoriest

Problem: nobody measured the capital that already existed in 2000. Trick (readdat.prg):

StepWhatMKD number
APretend capital was 0 in 2000 and add investment each yearreaches 1,506,856 in 2015
BBy 2015 the missing old capital has mostly worn out, so take capital ÷ GDP in 20151,506,856 ÷ 676,401 = 2.23
CInitial capital 2000 = 2.23 × GDP 2000 (447,143)996,126
DStart from 996,126 and apply the formula above every year2,458,937 in 2025

2 · Labour: structural employment L*

Potential GDP does not use actual employment (which moves with the business cycle) but structural employment: how many people would work if unemployment were at its "normal" level (the NAIRU).

StepWhatFormula / code
1People aged 15+MKDSPPOPWORK (millions)
2Share who want to work = participation rateMKDLMPRTTOTLCN
3Unemployment rate, recalculated from employmentu = (1 − employment ÷ labour force) × 100
4Extend the series to 2100 (u → 7.2% with persistence 0.9; participation → 57% with persistence 0.7) so the filter has no end-point problemreaddat.prg
5Smooth both with the HP filter (λ = 100): the trend of unemployment is the NAIRU, the trend of participation is structural participationMKDLMUNRSTRLCN, MKDLMPRTSTRLCN
6Structural employmentL* = (1 − NAIRU/100) × (structural part./100) × population

Employment and population are in millions of persons (0.705 = 705,000). Unemployment fell from about 34% to 11.5%, and the NAIRU follows it smoothly from 34.6% to 12.0%. That is why L* grew even though the population shrank.

3 · TFP (total factor productivity)

TFP is what is left after accounting for capital and labour: the part of GDP explained by technology, efficiency and organisation. It cannot be observed, so it is backed out from the production function (the Solow residual):

TFP rawt = GDPt ÷ ( L*t0.59 × Kt−10.41 )

The raw series jumps with the business cycle (for example in 2020), so it is extended after 2025 at +1.6% a year and smoothed with the HP filter (λ = 100). The smooth line is MKDNYGDPTFP.

SourceFormulaContribution
TFPgrowth of TFP≈ 0.5

Potential GDP≈ 2.5

Potential is not the maximum GDP. It is the GDP the economy can sustain with unemployment at the NAIRU and stable inflation.

5 · Output gap

Output gapt = ( Actual GDPt ÷ Potential GDPt − 1 ) × 100

Positive gap: the economy produces more than it can sustain, so prices and wages rise faster. Negative gap: idle capacity, so inflation slows and unemployment is above the NAIRU.

YearActual GDPPotential GDPGap %What it means
2010599,390589,5171.7slightly overheated
2019753,764738,8272.0economy above potential: +2.0%
2020723,671754,199-4.0COVID: far below potential (−4.0%)
2021761,561771,193-1.2recovering
2023803,362810,306-0.9small negative gap
2025863,140864,431-0.1almost closed (−0.1%)

Where the gap acts in the model: the Phillips curve (+0.2 × gap in the GDP deflator), employment (+0.1 × change in gap), and wages (through unemployment − NAIRU). Higher prices cut real income and raise the cost of capital, which pulls GDP back to potential.

Long-run rule of thumb: when capital grows as fast as potential, potential growth ≈ TFP growth ÷ 0.59 + L* growth. With TFP at 1.42% and L* flat after 2035, potential grows about 2.4% a year. That is the 2.41 in the last column of your ExogVars Labor sheet.

EViews code: see everything with SHOW

Open your MKDSoln workfile, go to File → New → Program, paste one block, press Run. The MKD…CHK series should equal the model's own series (difference ≈ 0).

A. Capital stock and initial capital 

' ===== INITIAL CAPITAL and CAPITAL STOCK (run as a program) =====
smpl @all
' A: pretend capital = 0 in 2000, accumulate investment
smpl 2000 2000
series MKDKTRIAL = MKDNEGDIFTOTKN
smpl 2001 @last
MKDKTRIAL = MKDKTRIAL(-1)*(1-0.05) + MKDNEGDIFTOTKN
' B: ratio capital/GDP in 2015
smpl @all
series MKDKRATIO = @elem(MKDKTRIAL,"2015") / @elem(MKDNYGDPMKTPKN,"2015")
' C: initial capital in 2000 = ratio x GDP 2000
series MKDKINIT = MKDKRATIO * @elem(MKDNYGDPMKTPKN,"2000")
' D: rebuild the capital stock
smpl 2000 2000
series MKDKCHECK = MKDKINIT
smpl 2001 @last
MKDKCHECK = MKDKCHECK(-1)*(1-0.05) + MKDNEGDIFTOTKN - MKDNEGDISTKBKN

smpl 2000 2031
show MKDNEGDIFTOTKN MKDNEGDISTKBKN MKDNYGDPMKTPKN MKDKTRIAL MKDKTRIAL/MKDNYGDPMKTPKN MKDKRATIO MKDKINIT MKDNEGDIKSTKKN MKDKCHECK MKDNEGDIKSTKKN-MKDKCHECK MKDNEGDIKSTKKN/MKDNYGDPMKTPKN
smpl @all
' delete MKDKTRIAL MKDKRATIO MKDKINIT MKDKCHECK

B. Labour, TFP, potential GDP, output gap: history and forecast 

' ===== LABOUR, TFP, POTENTIAL GDP, OUTPUT GAP (run as a program) =====
smpl @all
' 1) Structural employment L*
series MKDLSTRCHK = (1-MKDLMUNRSTRLCN/100)*(MKDLMPRTSTRLCN/100*MKDSPPOPWORK)
' 2) TFP raw = Solow residual (history only)
series MKDTFPRAW = MKDNYGDPMKTPKN/(MKDLMEMPSTRLCN^MKDNYYWBTOTLCN_*MKDNEGDIKSTKKN(-1)^(1-MKDNYYWBTOTLCN_))
' 3) Potential GDP and output gap
series MKDPOTCHK = MKDNYGDPTFP*MKDLMEMPSTRLCN^MKDNYYWBTOTLCN_*MKDNEGDIKSTKKN(-1)^(1-MKDNYYWBTOTLCN_)
series MKDGAPCHK = (MKDNYGDPMKTPKN/MKDPOTCHK-1)*100
' 4) Potential growth split into TFP, labour and capital (percentage points)
series MKDCONTTFP = 100*dlog(MKDNYGDPTFP)
series MKDCONTLAB = 100*MKDNYYWBTOTLCN_*dlog(MKDLMEMPSTRLCN)
series MKDCONTCAP = 100*(1-MKDNYYWBTOTLCN_)*dlog(MKDNEGDIKSTKKN(-1))

' ---- HISTORY ----
smpl 2000 2025
show MKDSPPOPWORK MKDLMPRTTOTLCN MKDLMPRTSTRLCN MKDLMUNRTOTLCN MKDLMUNRSTRLCN MKDLMEMPTOTLCN MKDLMEMPSTRLCN MKDLSTRCHK
show MKDNYGDPMKTPKN MKDLMEMPSTRLCN MKDNEGDIKSTKKN(-1) MKDTFPRAW MKDNYGDPTFP
show MKDNYGDPPOTLKN MKDPOTCHK MKDNYGDPMKTPKN MKDNYGDPGAP_ MKDGAPCHK

' ---- FORECAST ----
smpl 2026 2050
show MKDNYGDPTFP @pc(MKDNYGDPTFP) MKDSPPOPWORK MKDLMPRTSTRLCN MKDLMUNRSTRLCN MKDLMEMPSTRLCN MKDNEGDIFTOTKN MKDNEGDIKSTKKN
show MKDNYGDPPOTLKN @pc(MKDNYGDPPOTLKN) MKDCONTTFP MKDCONTLAB MKDCONTCAP MKDNYGDPMKTPKN @pc(MKDNYGDPMKTPKN) MKDNYGDPGAP_
smpl @all
' delete MKDLSTRCHK MKDTFPRAW MKDPOTCHK MKDGAPCHK MKDCONTTFP MKDCONTLAB MKDCONTCAP
🧪 Test it in EViews · Supply side in graphs

What it checks: Potential GDP, output gap, raw vs filtered TFP, employment vs L*, unemployment vs NAIRU, capital/output and the contributions of TFP, labour and capital, with automatic identity checks.

What you should see: GDP oscillating around potential in history and converging in the forecast; filtered TFP smooth through the noisy raw residual; contributions bars summing to potential growth; both checks PASS. (If bar(s) is rejected by your EViews version, change it to bar.)

Paste into a new EViews program (File → New → Program) in the MKD workfile and press Run. Results open as a dashboard and a spool (all tables and graphs). Objects start with SU_; remove them with delete SU_*.

' ==============================================================================
'  MFMod MKD  |  TEST SU: Supply side
'  Purpose : Capital, labour, TFP, potential GDP and the output gap; history vs forecast
'  Needs   : Baseline solved (actual series = baseline, *_0 series exist).
'  Output  : spool SU_SPOOL (tables + graphs) and dashboard SU_DASH
'  Clean up: delete SU_*
' ==============================================================================
%hs = "2000"      ' first year shown
%fs = "2026"      ' first forecast year (shaded area)
%fe = "2040"      ' last year shown
spool SU_SPOOL
smpl @all
series SU_Y = MKDNYGDPMKTPKN
SU_Y.displayname Real GDP
series SU_YP = MKDNYGDPPOTLKN
SU_YP.displayname Potential GDP
series SU_GAP = MKDNYGDPGAP_
SU_GAP.displayname Output gap, %
series SU_YPC = MKDNYGDPTFP*MKDLMEMPSTRLCN^MKDNYYWBTOTLCN_*MKDNEGDIKSTKKN(-1)^(1-MKDNYYWBTOTLCN_)
SU_YPC.displayname Potential GDP recomputed
series SU_TFPR = @pc(MKDNYGDPMKTPKN/(MKDLMEMPSTRLCN^MKDNYYWBTOTLCN_*MKDNEGDIKSTKKN(-1)^(1-MKDNYYWBTOTLCN_)))
SU_TFPR.displayname Raw Solow residual growth, %
series SU_TFPG = @pc(MKDNYGDPTFP)
SU_TFPG.displayname Filtered TFP growth, %
series SU_L = MKDLMEMPTOTLCN
SU_L.displayname Employment
series SU_LS = MKDLMEMPSTRLCN
SU_LS.displayname Structural employment L*
series SU_U = MKDLMUNRTOTLCN
SU_U.displayname Unemployment rate, %
series SU_NAIRU = MKDLMUNRSTRLCN
SU_NAIRU.displayname NAIRU, %
series SU_KY = MKDNEGDIKSTKKN/MKDNYGDPMKTPKN
SU_KY.displayname Capital / output ratio
series SU_IY = MKDNEGDIFTOTKN/MKDNYGDPMKTPKN*100
SU_IY.displayname Investment / GDP, % (real)
series SU_CTFP = 100*dlog(MKDNYGDPTFP)
SU_CTFP.displayname TFP contribution, pp
series SU_CLAB = 100*MKDNYYWBTOTLCN_*dlog(MKDLMEMPSTRLCN)
SU_CLAB.displayname Labour contribution, pp
series SU_CCAP = 100*(1-MKDNYYWBTOTLCN_)*dlog(MKDNEGDIKSTKKN(-1))
SU_CCAP.displayname Capital contribution, pp

' ---- Graphs ----------------------------------------------------------------
smpl {%hs} {%fe}
group SU_G1 SU_Y SU_YP
freeze(SU_GR1) SU_G1.line
SU_GR1.addtext(t) "Real GDP vs potential GDP"
SU_GR1.draw(shade, bottom) {%fs} {%fe}
SU_SPOOL.append SU_GR1
smpl {%hs} {%fe}
group SU_G2 SU_GAP
freeze(SU_GR2) SU_G2.line
SU_GR2.addtext(t) "Output gap, % of potential"
SU_GR2.draw(shade, bottom) {%fs} {%fe}
SU_GR2.draw(line, left) 0
SU_SPOOL.append SU_GR2
smpl {%hs} {%fe}
group SU_G3 SU_TFPR SU_TFPG
freeze(SU_GR3) SU_G3.line
SU_GR3.addtext(t) "TFP growth: raw Solow residual vs filtered, %"
SU_GR3.draw(shade, bottom) {%fs} {%fe}
SU_GR3.draw(line, left) 0
SU_SPOOL.append SU_GR3
smpl {%hs} {%fe}
group SU_G4 SU_L SU_LS
freeze(SU_GR4) SU_G4.line
SU_GR4.addtext(t) "Employment vs structural employment"
SU_GR4.draw(shade, bottom) {%fs} {%fe}
SU_SPOOL.append SU_GR4
smpl {%hs} {%fe}
group SU_G5 SU_U SU_NAIRU
freeze(SU_GR5) SU_G5.line
SU_GR5.addtext(t) "Unemployment rate vs NAIRU, %"
SU_GR5.draw(shade, bottom) {%fs} {%fe}
SU_SPOOL.append SU_GR5
smpl {%hs} {%fe}
group SU_G6 SU_KY SU_IY
freeze(SU_GR6) SU_G6.line(m)
SU_GR6.addtext(t) "Capital/output ratio and investment/GDP"
SU_GR6.draw(shade, bottom) {%fs} {%fe}
SU_SPOOL.append SU_GR6
smpl {%hs} {%fe}
group SU_G7 SU_CTFP SU_CLAB SU_CCAP
freeze(SU_GR7) SU_G7.bar(s)
SU_GR7.addtext(t) "Contributions to potential growth, pp"
SU_GR7.draw(shade, bottom) {%fs} {%fe}
SU_GR7.draw(line, left) 0
SU_SPOOL.append SU_GR7

' ---- Automatic checks (PASS if max |error| below threshold) ----------------
table(3,4) SU_CHK
SU_CHK(1,1) = "Check"
SU_CHK(1,2) = "Max |error|"
SU_CHK(1,3) = "Threshold"
SU_CHK(1,4) = "Result"
smpl 2001 2040
series SU_E2 = (SU_YPC/MKDNYGDPPOTLKN-1)*100
!m = @max(@abs(SU_E2))
SU_CHK(2,1) = "Potential GDP identity (recomputed vs model, %)"
SU_CHK(2,2) = !m
SU_CHK(2,3) = 0.01
if !m < 0.01 then
  SU_CHK(2,4) = "PASS"
else
  SU_CHK(2,4) = "CHECK"
endif
smpl 2001 2040
series SU_E3 = (MKDNEGDIKSTKKN-(MKDNEGDIKSTKKN(-1)*(1-MKDDEPR)+MKDNEGDIFTOTKN-MKDNEGDISTKBKN))/MKDNEGDIKSTKKN*100
!m = @max(@abs(SU_E3))
SU_CHK(3,1) = "Capital accumulation (K = K(-1)(1-d) + I - inventories)"
SU_CHK(3,2) = !m
SU_CHK(3,3) = 0.01
if !m < 0.01 then
  SU_CHK(3,4) = "PASS"
else
  SU_CHK(3,4) = "CHECK"
endif
SU_CHK.setwidth(1) 46
SU_SPOOL.append SU_CHK
smpl @all
smpl @all if @year>=2000 and @year<=2040 and @mod(@year,5)=0
group SU_T1 SU_Y SU_YP SU_GAP SU_TFPG SU_CTFP SU_CLAB SU_CCAP SU_U SU_NAIRU SU_KY
freeze(SU_TB1) SU_T1.sheet
SU_SPOOL.append SU_TB1

graph SU_DASH.merge SU_GR1 SU_GR2 SU_GR3 SU_GR4 SU_GR5 SU_GR6 SU_GR7
SU_DASH.align(2,1,1)
SU_DASH.addtext(t) "MFMod MKD | Test SU"
smpl @all
show SU_DASH
show SU_SPOOL

🧭 Modeller's notes: what to know beyond the code

What an experienced macro modeller would check first in this model: how shocks travel, what anchors the long run, what holds the model together, the economy's key numbers compared with the model's assumptions, how to run a scenario, a checklist before trusting a forecast, and a prioritised list of improvements. Everything is derived from your equations and data; where a number would need the solved model, the note says so.

The economy in numbers (2025, from MKDrawOctober2026.xlsx) vs the model

IndicatorValueWhy it matters for the model
Exports / GDP61%Very open economy (trade ≈ 133% of GDP). The import equation decides how much of any demand shock "leaks" abroad, which makes it the single most important equation for multipliers.
Imports / GDP72%
Private consumption / GDP65%The largest demand component: the consumption ECM drives most of the cycle.
Remittances / GDP8.9% (11.7% in 2015)Large part of household income; in the model it is a fixed % of GDP (no link to the EU cycle).
Wage bill / GDP (avg. gross wage × employment)51% (45% in 2015)The model uses a labour share of 0.59 in the production function, P*, the investment target and the CIT base. The measured share is lower, so check whether 0.59 is intended (e.g. it includes self-employed income).
Investment / GDP (real, incl. inventories)31% (22% without inventories)Inventories are about 28% of measured investment in 2025: very large and partly a statistical residual. They are subtracted from capital but included in the initial K/Y ratio.
Capital / GDP≈ 2.85Steady state K/Y = (I/Y)/(g+δ); with δ = 5% and g ≈ 2.4%, a K/Y of 2.85 needs an investment rate (excluding inventories) of about 21%.
Current account / GDP−4.4%Financed in the model by FDI/portfolio as % of GDP; reserves absorb the rest (no feedback).
Fiscal balance / GDP−3.8%With no debt rule, long-run debt ≈ deficit ÷ nominal growth (see "Long-run anchors").
Public debt / GDP55%
Interest / revenue5.6%Spending rule uses revenue minus last year's interest, so higher interest crowds out other spending one-for-one.
TFP growth: history 2015–2025 vs forecast assumption≈ 0.5% vs 1.27 → 1.42%The forecast almost triples TFP growth. It is the main driver of long-run potential (≈ 2.4%), so justify it explicitly (convergence, EU accession, FDI) or test 0.8–1.0% as a sensitivity.
Policy rate 20255.35%Model rule reacts to domestic inflation; the ECB rate is in the data (DEUFMLBLPOLYXN) but not used.

How shocks travel through the model

Arrows follow the actual equations. ↑ = rises, ↓ = falls. "SR" = first 1–2 years, "LR" = after the error-correction terms work.

1 · Higher government spending (e.g. +1% of GDP goods & services)

Important first: spending is a fixed share of revenue, so you must exclude (exogenize) MKDGGEXPGNFSCN to shock it; otherwise the rule pulls it back.

G (fiscal) ↑ → NA government consumption ↑ (quasi-identity) → GDP ↑ → imports barely move in year 1 (short run tied to potential, long run to domestic demand with lag) → large impact multiplier → output gap ↑ → GDP deflator ↑ (0.2 × gap), unemployment ↓ → wages ↑ → disposable income ↑ → consumption ↑ → revenue ↑ → other spending categories ↑ too (share-of-revenue rule): a pro-cyclical loop → deficit and debt ↑ → if debt > 60% of GDP, domestic interest rate ↑ (5 bp per pp) → interest ↑ → other spending ↓ next year.

Expect: an impact multiplier that is probably too high for an economy where imports are 72% of GDP; imports catch up over 2–4 years and the multiplier falls.

2 · VAT rate +1 pp

MKDGGREVGNFSXN ↑ → VAT revenue ↑ → spending ↑ the same year (share rule), so the balance improves much less than the revenue gain → consumer prices ↑ by the full Δln(1+VAT) immediately → real disposable income ↓ → consumption ↓ → GDP ↓ → policy rate ↑ (1.2 × inflation above expectations) → real-rate term in consumption ↓ further → wages follow lagged consumer prices (second-round effects).

Tip: to measure a consolidation, exclude the spending equations so the extra revenue is saved.

3 · Lower foreign demand (e.g. German imports −2%)

Partner imports ↓ → XMKT ↓ (Germany ≈ 61% of the weight) → exports ↓ (short-run elasticity C(5), long run 1:1) → GDP ↓ → gap ↓ → inflation ↓, employment ↓. Imports respond only through domestic demand, not through exports.

Expect: because much of MKD's exports (free zones: automotive parts, catalysts) are re-exported imports, the real GDP and current-account hit is smaller than the model shows. Consider adding exports to the import equation.

4 · Oil / energy price +20%

WLDFCRUDE_PETRO ↑ → PMKEY ↑ (oil weight 7.7) and PXKEY ↑ (weight 1.2) → import deflator ↑ (0.8 world prices) → consumer prices ↑ (0.3 on impact) → real income ↓ → consumption ↓ → terms of trade ↓ → relative import price ↑ → import volumes ↓ (−0.4 SR) → policy rate ↑. Nominal imports ↑ → current account worsens.

5 · Stronger US dollar (EUR/USD ↓)

DEUPANUSATLS ↑ → denar/USD ↑ by the same % (peg to the euro) → USD commodity prices in denars ↑ → import and export prices ↑ (like an oil shock, but on all commodities) → consumer prices ↑. The denar/EUR rate is unchanged, so EU trade is unaffected.

Watch: remittances in the consumption equation are converted with the USD rate, so a dollar move also changes household income in the model, which should not happen for euro remittances (see the roadmap).

6 · Policy rate +1 pp (exogenized)

MKDFMLBLPOLYXN ↑ → user cost of capital ↑ → private investment ↓ (−0.15 SR, long-run target ↓) → capital ↓ → potential GDP ↓ permanently (small) → consumption ↓ (−0.2 × change in real rate: temporary) → domestic debt rate ↑ → interest ↑ → other public spending ↓ (rule).

The model has no exchange-rate channel here (peg) and no credit or bank-lending block in the core version.

7 · TFP +1% (permanent)

MKDNYGDPTFP ↑ → potential GDP ↑ 1% → output gap ↓ (negative) → inflation ↓; marginal cost P* ↓ (P* ∝ 1/A1/α) → inflation ↓ further → wages ↑ (productivity) → private investment ↑ (higher potential) → capital ↑ → potential ↑ again (≈ +1/0.59 = +1.7% in the long run) → actual GDP rises gradually to the new potential. Short run: employment ↓ (productivity term in the employment equation).

8 · Remittances +1% of GDP

Remittance share ↑ → disposable income ↑ → consumption ↑ (C(3) on impact, 1:1 long run) → domestic demand ↑ → imports ↑ (gradually) → GDP ↑, current account improves by the remittances minus the extra imports.

🧪 Test it in EViews · Follow a demand shock through the model

What you should see: C and GDP jump in 2027, imports absorb part of it, employment and wages follow with a lag, CPI rises slightly, revenue rises (and is spent through the share rule), then everything fades back to baseline.

What pins down the long run (steady state)

VariableConverges toBecause
Real GDP growth≈ TFP growth/0.59 + labour growth ≈ 2.4%Potential GDP; the gap closes through prices and wages
Inflation (GDP deflator, consumption)INFLEXPTPhillips curve weights expectations; wages error-correct to prices; the Taylor rule pushes inflation to expectations
UnemploymentNAIRU → 7.2% (very slowly)Employment → structural employment; NAIRU equation with 0.98 persistence
Consumption / incomeconstantConsumption ECM with income elasticity 1
Imports / domestic demandconstant (given relative prices)Homogeneity in the import ECM
Exports / export marketconstant (given relative prices)Homogeneity; the trend T_LR is frozen
Capital / GDP(I/Y) ÷ (g + δ)Investment target ∝ potential ÷ real user cost
Revenue / GDPconstantFixed effective tax rates × bases that grow with GDP
Public debt / GDPd* ≈ deficit ÷ nominal growthNo debt rule; see the table below
Denar/EURfixed (≈ 61.5)Peg
REERdrifts if INFLEXPT ≠ partner inflationOnly reported; it does not feed back into trade

Where public debt ends up without a fiscal rule

Deficit (% GDP)Nominal growth 4.0%4.5%5.0%
2%50%44%40%
3%75%67%60%
4%100%89%80%

Nominal growth ≈ 2.4% real + inflation (INFLEXPT). With the 2025 deficit (−3.8%) persisting, debt would drift toward roughly 85–100% of GDP over several decades (depending on the inflation assumption). The spending-share rule keeps the deficit roughly proportional to revenue, so the deficit does not correct by itself.

What closes the model (and what does not)

Fiscal closure: open

Spending = share × (revenue − lagged interest). Nothing reacts to debt, apart from the small domestic-rate premium above 60%. Debt can drift. For long-run work, switch on the debt rule (!current = 0 branch in equations.prg) or exogenize the balance and let one instrument adjust.

External closure: reserves

Current account − financial flows = change in reserves. Under the peg this is correct accounting, but nothing reacts if reserves fall (no risk premium, no interest-rate response, no net-foreign-asset effect on consumption). Always check the reserves path in long scenarios.

Monetary closure: inflation anchor

INFLEXPT anchors prices; the Taylor-type rule moves the policy rate with inflation. Under a peg the theoretically consistent rule is "ECB rate + premium", so in the model a euro-area rate shock does not reach North Macedonia unless you shock the policy rate yourself.
🧪 Test it in EViews · What closes the model (fiscal)

What it checks: Each spending item as a share of (revenue − last year's interest), and the resulting balance and debt.

What you should see: Shares moving in history but constant in the forecast (the share rule); a debt ratio that may keep drifting because no debt target is active.

Paste into a new EViews program (File → New → Program) in the MKD workfile and press Run. Results open as a dashboard and a spool (all tables and graphs). Objects start with M4_; remove them with delete M4_*.

Running a scenario the right way

Tool (EViews model)What it doesUse it for
MKD.scenario(n,a=2,i="baseline",c) "name"New scenario copied from the baseline; results get suffix _2Every experiment
MKD.override X + edit X_2Uses your changed path for an exogenous variableTax rates, foreign demand, commodity prices, TFP, population
MKD.exclude YTurns an endogenous variable into an input (its equation is switched off)Fixing spending, the policy rate, employment…
Change the add factor Y_A_2 (override Y_A)Shifts an equation up or down while keeping its dynamicsJudgement: "consumption 1% stronger in 2027"
MKD.solve(s=d,d=d,o=g,i=a,c=1e-6)Deterministic, dynamic, Gauss-SeidelSolve both baseline and scenario on the same sample
' Example: VAT +1 pp from 2027, spending held at baseline (pure consolidation)
MKD.scenario(n,a=2,i="baseline",c) "vat+1"
MKD.scenario "vat+1"
smpl @all
series MKDGGREVGNFSXN_2 = MKDGGREVGNFSXN
smpl 2027 @last
MKDGGREVGNFSXN_2 = MKDGGREVGNFSXN + 1
smpl 2016 2050
MKD.override MKDGGREVGNFSXN
MKD.exclude MKDGGEXPGNFSCN MKDGGEXPWAGECN MKDGGEXPCAPTCN MKDGGEXPSUBSCN MKDGGEXPTSOCCN MKDGGEXPTPNSCN MKDGGEXPTOTSCN MKDGGEXPSRATCN
MKD.solve(s=d,d=d,o=g,i=a,c=1e-6,f=t,v=t,g=n)
smpl 2025 2035
show (MKDNYGDPMKTPKN_2/MKDNYGDPMKTPKN_0-1)*100 (MKDNECONPRVTXN_2/MKDNECONPRVTXN_0-1)*100 (MKDGGBALOVRLCN_2-MKDGGBALOVRLCN_0)/MKDNYGDPMKTPCN_0*100 MKDNYGDPGAP_2-MKDNYGDPGAP_0

Good practice: report results as deviations from baseline (%, or pp for rates and ratios); look at year 1, year 5 and the long run; shock one thing at a time; always say how the shock is financed (excluded spending, debt, other taxes); check that the gap closes and inflation returns to INFLEXPT.

Checklist before trusting a forecast

#CheckHow
1Identities add upSet !check_id = 1 in master.prg; the largest residual should be ≈ 0
2Add factors are small at the end of historyLook at *_A for 2023–2025; a big add factor means the equation does not explain recent data, and it will persist (decays only 15% a year)
3No missing exogenous dataAny NA in an exogenous input after 2025 stops or distorts the solve; check the ExogVars sheets cover 2026–2050
4The output gap closesconvergence_check.prg: the gap should cross zero and settle
5Inflation → INFLEXPT, unemployment → NAIRUPlot @pc(MKDNECONPRVTXN) vs MKDINFLEXPT
6Ratios stay sensibleC/GDP, M/GDP, I/GDP, K/GDP, revenue and spending/GDP, CA/GDP, debt/GDP, reserves
7Supply assumptions are defensibleTFP growth vs history (0.5% vs 1.4%), participation, NAIRU path, population (2021 census revision)
8Data series are consistente.g. the CPI series in the raw file drops from 109.4 (2023) to 103.5 (2024): check for a base or definition change
9Compare with other forecastsMoF fiscal strategy, NBRM, IMF WEO, European Commission

' ==============================================================================
'  MFMod MKD  |  TEST M6: Forecast checklist (automatic)
'  Purpose : Runs the checklist: identities, add factors, missing inputs, gap, inflation, unemployment, debt, CA

' ==============================================================================
%hs = "2010"      ' first year shown
%fs = "2026"      ' first forecast year (shaded area)
%fe = "2035"      ' last year shown
spool M6_SPOOL
smpl @all

' ---- Automatic checks (PASS if max |error| below threshold) ----------------
table(6,4) M6_CHK
M6_CHK(1,1) = "Check"
M6_CHK(1,2) = "Max |error|"
M6_CHK(1,3) = "Threshold"
M6_CHK(1,4) = "Result"
smpl 2005 2050
series M6_E2 = (MKDNYGDPMKTPKN-(MKDNECONPRVTKN+MKDNECONGOVTKN+MKDNEGDIFTOTKN+MKDNEEXPGNFSKN-MKDNEIMPGNFSKN+MKDNYGDPDISCKN))/MKDNYGDPMKTPKN*100
!m = @max(@abs(M6_E2))
M6_CHK(2,1) = "Real GDP expenditure identity, %"
M6_CHK(2,2) = !m
M6_CHK(2,3) = 0.01
if !m < 0.01 then
  M6_CHK(2,4) = "PASS"
else
  M6_CHK(2,4) = "CHECK"
endif
smpl 2005 2050
series M6_E3 = (MKDNECONPRVTCN/(MKDNECONPRVTKN*MKDNECONPRVTXN)-1)*100
!m = @max(@abs(M6_E3))
M6_CHK(3,1) = "Nominal C = real x deflator, %"
M6_CHK(3,2) = !m
M6_CHK(3,3) = 0.01
if !m < 0.01 then
  M6_CHK(3,4) = "PASS"
else
  M6_CHK(3,4) = "CHECK"
endif
smpl 2033 2035
series M6_E4 = MKDNYGDPGAP_
!m = @max(@abs(M6_E4))
M6_CHK(4,1) = "Output gap in 2033-2035, % (closes?)"
M6_CHK(4,2) = !m
M6_CHK(4,3) = 0.5
if !m < 0.5 then
  M6_CHK(4,4) = "PASS"
else
  M6_CHK(4,4) = "CHECK"
endif
smpl 2033 2035
series M6_E5 = @pc(MKDFPCPITOTLXN)-MKDINFLEXPT
!m = @max(@abs(M6_E5))

M6_CHK(5,3) = 0.5
if !m < 0.5 then
  M6_CHK(5,4) = "PASS"
else
  M6_CHK(5,4) = "CHECK"
endif
smpl 2033 2035

  M6_CHK(6,4) = "CHECK"
endif

' ---- Add factors at the end of history (should be small) -------------------
%af = "MKDNECONPRVTKN MKDNEGDIFPRVKN MKDNEEXPGNFSKN MKDNEIMPGNFSKN MKDNEWRTTOTLCN MKDLMEMPTOTLCN MKDNECONPRVTXN MKDNEEXPGNFSXN MKDNEIMPGNFSXN MKDNYGDPFCSTXN"

Improvement roadmap (my priorities)

PriorityChangeWhyEffort
1Convert remittances in the consumption equation with MKDPANEUATLS (EUR), not MKDPANUSATLS; same for BOP interest and gov. external financingBOP data are in EUR: today remittance income is about 10% too low and moves with EUR/USDSmall
2Imports: add export growth (import content) and use domestic demand, not potential, in the short runRealistic multipliers and current-account responses in a 72%-imports economyMedium (re-estimate)
3Fiscal closure: activate a debt-anchored rule (persistence + debt target) or a balance targetStable long-run debt; meaningful fiscal scenariosSmall (code exists)
4Policy rate under the peg: MKD rate = ECB rate (DEUFMLBLPOLYXN) + spread, optionally with a reserves termCorrect transmission of euro-area monetary policySmall
5Review the labour share (0.59 vs measured ≈ 0.5)Affects TFP, P*, the investment target and the CIT baseMedium
6Remittances linked to income in host countries (Germany, Switzerland, Italy…)EU cycle → household income channelSmall
7Initial capital: use the same investment definition (without inventories) in the trial stockConsistent K/Y and TFP levelSmall
8Structural NAIRU (formula already in readdat.prg)Tax and labour-market reforms affect potentialMedium
9Use REER (or relative prices vs partners) in export demandCompetitiveness from wage and price developments vs the EUMedium (re-estimate)

Steady state & long-run assumptions

The model has no single "steady state" written in one place. Its long run comes from three sources: exogenous assumptions (ExogVarsOctober2026.xlsx, values read from your file), fixed parameters (readdat.prg, equations.prg) and the long-run ratios built into the ECMs and ratio equations. Together they put the model on a balanced growth path up to 2050.

1 · Supply side: what sets long-run growth

AssumptionVariableValueSource
TFP growthMKDNYGDPTFP+1.36%/yr 2025–30, +1.42%/yr 2030–50 (history 2015–25: +0.52%)ExogVars · Labor
Labour share αMKDNYYWBTOTLCN_0.59 (capital 0.41)ExogVars / readdat
Depreciation δMKDDEPR5% a yearreaddat.prg
Working-age populationMKDSPPOPWORK≈ 1.53 million, flat to 2050UN medium variant
Total populationMKDSPPOPTOTL1.82 → 1.59 million (2025 → 2050)UN medium variant
Structural participationMKDLMPRTSTRLCN53.9% → 55.7% by 2035, then flatExogVars
NAIRU targetMKDLMUNRTARGT7.2%readdat / ExogVars
NAIRU speedequation2% of the gap a year (half-life ≈ 34 years)equations.prg
Long-run real GDP growth ≈ TFP growth ÷ α + growth of structural employment ≈ 1.42 ÷ 0.59 + ≈ 0 ≈ 2.4% a year (the ExogVars file shows 2.41). With total population falling, GDP per capita grows ≈ 2.9%.
Calculator: TFP growth %   α   structural employment growth %   population growth %

2 · Prices, interest rates and the external environment

AssumptionVariableLong-run value
Inflation expectations (anchor)MKDINFLEXPT1.35% (2025) → 2.0% from ≈ 2035
Euro-area inflationDEUNECONPRVTXN≈ 2% a year
EUR/USDDEUPANUSATLS0.887 EUR per USD, constant
Denar/EURpeg (MKDPANEUATLS)constant; denar/USD moves with EUR/USD
US interest rateUSAINTRXN4.4% (2026) → 3.5% from 2030
Spread on external debtMKDINTREDIFF0.38 pp → external rate ≈ 3.9%
Investment risk premiumMKDNEKRTPREMFR5.5 pp, constant
Policy rateTaylor rulelong run = neutral rate C(2) (estimated; open the equation), since inflation = expectations
Oil priceWLDFCRUDE_PETRO$99 in 2026 → ≈ $70 by 2030, then slow rise
German imports (main export market)DEUNEIMPGNFSKD+3.0%/yr 2025–30, only +0.9%/yr 2030–40

3 · Fiscal assumptions (effective rates, constant from 2025)

TaxVariableEffective rateBase
VATMKDGGREVGNFSXN9.68%C + G nominal
PITMKDGGREVPITTXN6.28%wage bill
CITMKDGGREVCITTXN4.78%GDP × (1 − α)
ExciseMKDGGREVEXCSXN4.77% (from 2035)private consumption
CustomsMKDGGREVCUSTXN1.85%imports

Effective rates = revenue ÷ base, not statutory rates (18% VAT, 10% PIT/CIT). Spending: every item is a fixed historical share of (revenue − last year's interest); the debt rule is off. SSC, grants and other revenue are fixed % of GDP. External share of public debt: 45.4%, constant.

4 · Long-run ratios built into the equations

Ratio held constant in the long runEquation type
Consumption / real disposable incomeECM, elasticity 1
Imports / domestic demand (adjusted for relative prices)ECM, elasticity 1
Exports / partner demand (market share)ECM, elasticity 1
Real wage / productivity (labour share)ECM
Capital / output (set by the user cost of capital)investment ECM
Employment / structural employmentECM
Sector and government deflators / consumer pricesECMs
Remittances, FDI, portfolio, other BOP flows / GDPratio equations (historical averages)
Spending items / net revenue; SSC, grants, other revenue / GDPratio equations
Add factors → 0decay × 0.85 a year (solve.prg)

All ECMs are listed in 🔁 ECMs & other models.

5 · What this implies on the steady-state path (≈ 2035–2050)

VariableApproximate steady-state behaviour
Real GDP, consumption, investment, imports≈ 2.4% a year
Productivity and real wages≈ 2.4% a year (structural employment flat)
Inflation≈ 2% (expectations and the euro anchor)
Nominal GDP≈ 4.4% a year
Output gap0
Unemploymentmoves very slowly toward 7.2% (NAIRU half-life ≈ 34 years)
Exports≈ growth of partner demand (≈ 1% after 2030), so slower than GDP

6 · Points to watch

#IssueWhy it matters
1TFP growth 1.4% ≈ 3 × the 2015–25 average (0.52%)Most of the long-run GDP growth rests on this one assumption: test it with scenario S29 (±0.5 pp).
2Export markets ≈ 0.9% after 2030 vs GDP ≈ 2.4%With market-share elasticity 1, exports/GDP falls; imports follow demand, so the current account deteriorates over time.
3Participation target: 57 in readdat.prg (HP extension) vs 55.7 in ExogVarsCheck which one the solved model uses (MKDLMPRTSTRLCN in the workfile).
4readdat.prg extends raw TFP at 1.6% before the HP filter; ExogVars gives ≈ 1.4%Make sure the ExogVars path is the one used in the forecast.
5Debt rule offLong-run debt/GDP is not targeted; it is whatever spending shares and revenue imply. Check that it stabilises.
6NAIRU half-life ≈ 34 yearsUnemployment does not reach 7.2% within the forecast horizon.

7 · EViews: show all assumptions and implied growth rates

' ===== Steady state & long-run assumptions: values and implied growth rates =====
' run after the baseline is solved (actual series = baseline)
smpl 2015 2050
group G_SUPPLY MKDNYGDPTFP MKDNYYWBTOTLCN_ MKDDEPR MKDSPPOPWORK MKDSPPOPTOTL MKDLMPRTSTRLCN MKDLMUNRTARGT MKDLMUNRSTRLCN
group G_PRICES MKDINFLEXPT DEUPANUSATLS MKDPANEUATLS USAINTRXN MKDINTREDIFF MKDINTREXN MKDNEKRTPREMFR MKDFMLBLPOLYXN WLDFCRUDE_PETRO
group G_FISCAL MKDGGREVGNFSXN MKDGGREVPITTXN MKDGGREVCITTXN MKDGGREVEXCSXN MKDGGREVCUSTXN MKDEXTLSHAREXN
' implied growth rates (% a year) and long-run ratios
group G_GROWTH @pc(MKDNYGDPTFP) @pc(MKDNYGDPPOTLKN) @pc(MKDNYGDPMKTPKN) @pc(MKDNYGDPMKTPKN/MKDSPPOPTOTL) @pc(MKDLMEMPSTRLCN) @pc(MKDNEWRTTOTLCN/MKDNECONPRVTXN) @pc(MKDNECONPRVTXN) @pc(MKDNYGDPMKTPCN) @pc(MKDXMKT) @pc(MKDNEEXPGNFSKN) @pc(MKDNEIMPGNFSKN)
group G_RATIOS MKDNYGDPGAP_ MKDLMUNRTOTLCN MKDNECONPRVTCN/MKDNYGDPMKTPCN*100 MKDNEGDIKSTKKN/MKDNYGDPMKTPKN MKDNEEXPGNFSCN/MKDNYGDPMKTPCN*100 MKDNEIMPGNFSCN/MKDNYGDPMKTPCN*100 MKDBNCABFUNDCD/MKDNYGDPMKTPCD*100 MKDGGBALOVRLCN/MKDNYGDPMKTPCN*100 MKDGGDBTTOTLCN/MKDNYGDPMKTPCN*100
show G_SUPPLY
show G_PRICES
show G_FISCAL
show G_GROWTH
show G_RATIOS
' long-run growth check: TFP growth / alpha + structural employment growth
series LRG_CHECK = (dlog(MKDNYGDPTFP)/MKDNYYWBTOTLCN_ + dlog(MKDLMEMPSTRLCN))*100
show LRG_CHECK @pc(MKDNYGDPPOTLKN)
smpl @all

Not run on your workfile. If a name does not exist (e.g. a series renamed in your version), EViews stops at that line: remove it from the group. LRG_CHECK should be close to potential-GDP growth once capital grows with output.

🧪 Test it in EViews · Steady state in graphs

What it checks: The steady-state growth rates, the long-run growth rule of thumb, inflation vs its anchor, population and the long-run ratios to 2050.

What you should see: Growth lines flattening near 2.4% (per capita ≈ 2.9%), potential growth meeting the rule of thumb, inflation converging to 2%, exports/GDP drifting down and the CA ratio moving accordingly.

Paste into a new EViews program (File → New → Program) in the MKD workfile and press Run. Results open as a dashboard and a spool (all tables and graphs). Objects start with M8_; remove them with delete M8_*.

' ==============================================================================
'  MFMod MKD  |  TEST M8: Steady state in graphs
'  Purpose : Growth rates, inflation, population and long-run ratios converging to the steady state
'  Needs   : Baseline solved (actual series = baseline, *_0 series exist).
'  Output  : spool M8_SPOOL (tables + graphs) and dashboard M8_DASH
'  Clean up: delete M8_*
' ==============================================================================
%hs = "2015"      ' first year shown
%fs = "2026"      ' first forecast year (shaded area)
%fe = "2050"      ' last year shown
spool M8_SPOOL
smpl @all
series M8_TFP = @pc(MKDNYGDPTFP)
M8_TFP.displayname TFP growth, %
series M8_POT = @pc(MKDNYGDPPOTLKN)
M8_POT.displayname Potential growth, %
series M8_GDP = @pc(MKDNYGDPMKTPKN)
M8_GDP.displayname Real GDP growth, %
series M8_GPC = @pc(MKDNYGDPMKTPKN/MKDSPPOPTOTL)
M8_GPC.displayname GDP per capita growth, %
series M8_LRG = (dlog(MKDNYGDPTFP)/MKDNYYWBTOTLCN_+dlog(MKDLMEMPSTRLCN))*100
M8_LRG.displayname Rule of thumb: TFP/alpha + L* growth, %
series M8_INF = @pc(MKDNECONPRVTXN)
M8_INF.displayname Consumption deflator inflation, %
series M8_EXP = MKDINFLEXPT
M8_EXP.displayname Inflation expectations, %
series M8_POPW = MKDSPPOPWORK
M8_POPW.displayname Working-age population
series M8_POPT = MKDSPPOPTOTL
M8_POPT.displayname Total population
series M8_PART = MKDLMPRTSTRLCN
M8_PART.displayname Structural participation, %
series M8_XY = MKDNEEXPGNFSCN/MKDNYGDPMKTPCN*100
M8_XY.displayname Exports, % GDP
series M8_MY = MKDNEIMPGNFSCN/MKDNYGDPMKTPCN*100
M8_MY.displayname Imports, % GDP
series M8_CA = MKDBNCABFUNDCD/MKDNYGDPMKTPCD*100
M8_CA.displayname Current account, % GDP
series M8_DEBT = MKDGGDBTTOTLCN/MKDNYGDPMKTPCN*100
M8_DEBT.displayname Debt, % GDP
smpl {%hs} {%fe}
group M8_G1 M8_TFP M8_POT M8_GDP M8_GPC
freeze(M8_GR1) M8_G1.line
M8_GR1.addtext(t) "Growth rates converge to the steady state, %"
M8_GR1.draw(shade, bottom) {%fs} {%fe}
M8_GR1.draw(line, left) 0
M8_SPOOL.append M8_GR1
smpl {%hs} {%fe}
group M8_G2 M8_POT M8_LRG
freeze(M8_GR2) M8_G2.line
M8_GR2.addtext(t) "Potential growth vs rule of thumb, %"
M8_GR2.draw(shade, bottom) {%fs} {%fe}
M8_SPOOL.append M8_GR2
smpl {%hs} {%fe}
group M8_G3 M8_INF M8_EXP
freeze(M8_GR3) M8_G3.line
M8_GR3.addtext(t) "Inflation vs expectations anchor, %"
M8_GR3.draw(shade, bottom) {%fs} {%fe}
M8_SPOOL.append M8_GR3
smpl {%hs} {%fe}
group M8_G4 M8_POPW M8_POPT M8_PART
freeze(M8_GR4) M8_G4.line(m)
M8_GR4.addtext(t) "Population and participation"
M8_GR4.draw(shade, bottom) {%fs} {%fe}
M8_SPOOL.append M8_GR4
smpl {%hs} {%fe}
group M8_G5 M8_XY M8_MY
freeze(M8_GR5) M8_G5.line
M8_GR5.addtext(t) "Exports and imports, % GDP"
M8_GR5.draw(shade, bottom) {%fs} {%fe}
M8_SPOOL.append M8_GR5
smpl {%hs} {%fe}
group M8_G6 M8_CA M8_DEBT
freeze(M8_GR6) M8_G6.line(m)
M8_GR6.addtext(t) "Current account and debt, % GDP"
M8_GR6.draw(shade, bottom) {%fs} {%fe}
M8_SPOOL.append M8_GR6
smpl @all if @year>=2015 and @year<=2050 and @mod(@year,5)=0
group M8_T1 M8_TFP M8_POT M8_GDP M8_GPC M8_INF M8_EXP M8_XY M8_MY M8_CA M8_DEBT

graph M8_DASH.merge M8_GR1 M8_GR2 M8_GR3 M8_GR4 M8_GR5 M8_GR6

show M8_DASH
show M8_SPOOL

🎯 How to shock the model: add factors, overrides, exclude

What actually happens when you "shock a variable by 1%". It depends on the type of variable (exogenous, behavioural, identity) and on the form of its equation (DLOG, LOG, level, ratio). This tab explains the four methods, the units of the add factor, and gives ready EViews programs.

1. First ask: what kind of variable is it?

Variable typeExampleHow you shock it by %Add factor?
Exogenous (world, policy, assumptions)EUR/USD DEUPANUSATLS, oil price, foreign demand, tax rates, TFP, populationOverride the series: X_3 = X_0*1.01No. You change the data itself (method D).
Behavioural endogenous (estimated equation)real private consumption MKDNECONPRVTKN (not …XN, which is the consumption deflator), investment, exports, imports, deflators, wagesThrough the add factor (methods A or B), or exogenise it (method C)A, B: yes · C: no
IdentityGDP = C + I + G + X − M; nominal = real × deflatorCannot be shocked. Shock one of its components.No add factor
Quasi-identity (ends in C(1)*DUMH)NA government consumption from fiscal dataShock the fiscal source variable, or exclude itAdd factor = 0 in the forecast

2. For a behavioural variable: three choices

MethodYou giveEViews computesEquation during shockUse when
A · Direct add factorthe add factor (the cause)the effect on Yactive"Households become more optimistic, what happens?" The size of the effect comes from the model.
B · Exact % via add factorthe target path of Y (the effect)the add factor that produces itactive (after computing the add factor)"C will be exactly 1% higher in 2027–2030, then the model decides how it returns."
C · Exogenisethe path of Ynothing for Y; only the rest of the modelswitched offOutside information (known investment project, fixed spending); no reaction of Y at all.

Key idea: an add factor is the equation's residual. In history it makes the equation fit the data; in the forecast it decays (× 0.85 a year). A scenario shock is added on top of the baseline add factor: Y_A_3 = Y_A + shock.

The add factor is in the units of the equation's left-hand side

Most MKD behavioural equations are written as DLOG(Y) = … + Y_A. DLOG(Y) = LOG(Y) − LOG(Y(-1)), so the add factor adds to LOG(Y), not to Y.

We want   Y_new = Y × 1.01
In logs   LOG(Y_new) = LOG(Y) + LOG(1.01)
So        add factor = LOG(1.01) = 0.00995
Shock wantedCorrect add factorIf you type the % directlyYou get
+1%LOG(1.01) = 0.009950.01+1.005%
+5%LOG(1.05) = 0.04880.05+5.13%
+10%LOG(1.10) = 0.09530.10+10.52%
−10%LOG(0.90) = −0.1054−0.10−9.52%

For small shocks (1–2%) p and LOG(1+p) are almost the same; for 5% and more use LOG(1+p).

Rule by equation form

Left side of the equationAdd factor units+p% shockTypical MKD variables
DLOG(Y) = …log pointsLOG(1+p) in the first year (fades afterwards)consumption, investment, exports, imports, deflators, wages, employment
LOG(Y) = …log pointsLOG(1+p) every year of the shocksome price and long-run relations
Y = … (level)units of Yp × Y_0some fiscal items
Y/X = … (ratio, share)units of the ratiop × (Y/X)_0taxes as % of base, spending shares
a rate (%)percentage pointsusually a pp shock, not %: +1 pp → 1 (or 0.01 if stored as a fraction)unemployment, policy rate, NAIRU

Not everything is in logs: when you change a series directly (exogenous variable, or the target path in method B/C), just multiply: X_3 = X_0*1.01. The log rule is only for the add factor of a log equation. Check the left side in the equation catalogue.

A · Direct add factor shock: you choose the cause

' ===== A: consumption add factor +1% in 2027 (model decides the rest) =====
MKD.scenario(n, a=4, i="baseline", c) "C add factor +1%"
MKD.scenario "C add factor +1%"
MKD.override MKDNECONPRVTKN_A
smpl @all
series MKDNECONPRVTKN_A_4 = MKDNECONPRVTKN_A        ' copy baseline add factor
smpl 2027 2027
MKDNECONPRVTKN_A_4 = MKDNECONPRVTKN_A + log(1.01)   ' +0.00995 on top
smpl 2026 @last
MKD.solve(s=d,d=d,o=g,i=a,c=1e-6)
smpl 2025 2035
show (MKDNECONPRVTKN_4/MKDNECONPRVTKN_0-1)*100 (MKDNYGDPMKTPKN_4/MKDNYGDPMKTPKN_0-1)*100 MKDNECONPRVTKN_A_4-MKDNECONPRVTKN_A
smpl @all

' ---- Graphs: scenario vs baseline (deviations) -----------------------------
spool SHA_SPOOL

LineWhat it does
scenario(n, a=4, …)New scenario copied from the baseline; all results go into series ending in _4. Baseline (_0) and data are not touched.
override MKDNECONPRVTKN_AThe scenario reads the add factor from MKDNECONPRVTKN_A_4, its own copy. Without this you would change the baseline add factor.
series …_A_4 = …_AThe copy starts equal to the baseline add factor in all years.
+ log(1.01) in 2027The shock: consumption growth +1 pp in 2027 (see "Add factor units").
solveSolves over the forecast range with the consumption equation active.

What you will see: in 2027 C is a bit more than +1% (higher C → GDP and income ↑ → C ↑ again: the multiplier). From 2028 the effect fades, because the error-correction term pulls C back to its long-run level.

For a temporary push this is the natural shock. To keep C at +1% for several years you would need a different add factor every year (it must cancel the ECM pull-back and the income feedback), which you cannot compute by hand. Use method B instead.

B · Exact % path via add factor: you choose the effect, EViews finds the cause

Here the line MKDNECONPRVTKN_3 = MKDNECONPRVTKN_0 * 1.01 does not shock the add factor. It sets the target. The add factor is the result of step 3.

' ===== B: C exactly +1% in 2027-2030 via add factor =====
' 0. new scenario, results in *_3
MKD.scenario(n, a=3, i="baseline", c) "C +1% via AF"
MKD.scenario "C +1% via AF"

' 1. exclude C, override BOTH C and its add factor (ONE line each!)
MKD.exclude  MKDNECONPRVTKN
MKD.override MKDNECONPRVTKN MKDNECONPRVTKN_A
smpl @all
series MKDNECONPRVTKN_3   = MKDNECONPRVTKN_0     ' baseline path
series MKDNECONPRVTKN_A_3 = MKDNECONPRVTKN_A     ' copy of baseline add factor
smpl 2027 2030
MKDNECONPRVTKN_3 = MKDNECONPRVTKN_0 * 1.01       ' TARGET +1%

' 2. solve with C fixed
smpl 2026 @last
MKD.solve(s=d,d=d,o=g,i=a,c=1e-6)

' 3. compute the add factor that reproduces this path (writes into _A_3)
smpl 2027 2030
MKD.addinit(v=n) MKDNECONPRVTKN

' 4. equation active again, solve
MKD.exclude
smpl 2026 @last
MKD.solve(s=d,d=d,o=g,i=a,c=1e-6)

' check
smpl 2025 2035
show (MKDNECONPRVTKN_3/MKDNECONPRVTKN_0-1)*100 MKDNECONPRVTKN_A MKDNECONPRVTKN_A_3 MKDNECONPRVTKN_A_3-MKDNECONPRVTKN_A
smpl @all

' ---- Graphs: scenario vs baseline (deviations) -----------------------------
spool SHB_SPOOL
smpl @all
series SHB_GDP = (MKDNYGDPMKTPKN_3/MKDNYGDPMKTPKN_0-1)*100

StepCodeWhat it doesWhy
0scenario(n, a=3, …)New scenario, results in _3Baseline and data stay untouched
1aexclude MKDNECONPRVTKNSwitches off the consumption equation; C becomes an inputWe force the path first
1boverride C C_AC read from _3; add factor read from _A_3Without override an excluded variable keeps its actual values, and addinit would overwrite the baseline add factor
1c–d…_3 = …_0, then ×1.01 in 2027–2030Baseline everywhere, +1% in the shock yearsThis is the target
2solveGDP, income, prices, imports, taxes… respond to the higher CNow every right-hand-side variable of the C equation has its shocked value
3addinit(v=n)For 2027–2030: the add factor that makes the C equation fit exactly (v=n = no residual)How much push the equation needs to deliver +1% by itself
4aexclude (empty)Clears the exclude list: the equation is active againFrom now on the equation decides C
4bsolve2027–2030: C = +1% again, now produced by the equation. From 2031 the add factor returns to baseline and the equation decides how C goes backThe difference from method C, where C would jump straight back in 2031
checkshow …% deviation and extra add factor2027–2030 must show 1.00

Reading the result: the extra add factor is largest in 2027 (≈ 0.01) and smaller but positive in 2028–2030. It holds C up against the ECM pull, net of the extra income the model creates by itself.

If the check is not 1.00 in 2027–2030: your EViews version evaluated addinit with the actual data instead of the _3 solution. Then compute the add factor by hand: run steps 0–2, and set MKDNECONPRVTKN_A_3 = MKDNECONPRVTKN_A + (target DLOG − fitted DLOG) for 2027–2030, with the fitted value evaluated on the _3 series.

C · Exogenise only: fixed path, no reaction of Y

' ===== C: consumption fixed at +1% in 2027-2030, equation switched off =====
MKD.scenario(n, a=5, i="baseline", c) "C +1% fixed"

MKD.exclude  MKDNECONPRVTKN
MKD.override MKDNECONPRVTKN
smpl @all

smpl 2027 2030
MKDNECONPRVTKN_5 = MKDNECONPRVTKN_0 * 1.01
smpl 2026 @last

Steps 0–2 of method B without steps 3–4. The consumption equation is off for the whole forecast: C equals your path in every year (baseline outside 2027–2030), so it cannot react to income, prices or interest rates. GDP, imports, taxes, the budget and the BOP still respond.

This is how you hold a policy variable fixed, e.g. spending in a VAT consolidation (see Modeller's notes → Running a scenario).

Shock rangeMeaning
smpl 2027 @lastPermanent: level +10% from 2027 onward
smpl 2027 2027Temporary: +10% in 2027 only, back to baseline in 2028

Peg: the denar/USD rate MKDPANUSATLS follows the German EUR/USD rate by an equation. To move the denar against the dollar, shock DEUPANUSATLS; overriding the MKD rate alone fights the peg equation. Tax rates (e.g. VAT MKDGGREVGNFSXN) are shocked in pp: +1, not ×1.01.

Common mistakes

MistakeResultFix
Shocking the add factor without override …_AYou change the baseline add factor; baseline and scenario both moveAlways override the add factor and edit the _A_n copy
Two override (or exclude) linesThe second line replaces the first listPut all variables in one command
Typing 0.10 for a 10% shock in a DLOG equation+10.5% instead of +10%Use log(1.10)
Using % for a rateUnemployment ×1.01 = +0.07 pp, not +1 ppShock rates in pp
Shocking an identity (e.g. GDP)Overwritten by the identityShock a component
Expenditure shock without excluding the fiscal ruleSpending is a share of revenue: the rule pulls it backExclude MKDGGEXPGNFSCN (and related) first
_0 series does not existError "not defined"Solve the baseline with alias _0 first, or use the series without suffix
Solving over @allModel tries to solve history, may failSolve over the forecast range, as in solve.prg

Report results as deviations from baseline: % for levels, pp for rates and ratios. Look at year 1, year 5 and the long run.

30 scenarios for North Macedonia, step by step

Each scenario is a complete EViews program: copy it, paste it into a new program in the MKD workfile (after the baseline is solved, so the _0 series exist) and press Run. Each one uses its own alias (_11 … _40), so they don't overwrite each other.

The output table (same in every scenario, columns in this order)
1 GDP real % · 2 private consumption % · 3 private investment % · 4 exports % · 5 imports % · 6 CPI % · 7 unemployment pp · 8 fiscal balance pp of GDP · 9 public debt pp of GDP · 10 current account pp of GDP · then the scenario's own extra columns. All are deviations from baseline.

Methods: D = change an exogenous series · A = shock an add factor · C = exclude (switch off) an equation and set the path · see the other tabs for the theory. "Spending fixed" means the 8 share-rule spending items are excluded at baseline, so the result is not mixed with the fiscal rule.

S01 Recession in Germany External D · exogenous

Why for North Macedonia: Germany is the main export market (about 61% of the foreign-demand index XMKT) and the base of the automotive-parts supply chains in the free zones.

Shock: German real imports −3% in 2027 and −1.5% in 2028, back to baseline from 2029 (temporary). Results in series ending _11.

Step by step, what happens:

  1. DEUNEIMPGNFSKD ↓ is an exogenous input, so you override the series (no add factor).
  2. MKDXMKT (identity, weighted partner imports) ↓ by about 0.61 × 3% ≈ 1.8%.
  3. Export equation (DLOG, ECM toward XMKT): exports ↓ with the short-run elasticity, then follow XMKT one-for-one.
  4. GDP ↓ (identity) → output gap ↓ → GDP deflator ↓ (0.2 × gap) → employment ↓, unemployment ↑.
  5. Wage bill ↓ → disposable income ↓ → consumption ↓ (second round).
  6. Imports ↓ only via domestic demand (no direct link to exports in this model).
  7. Revenue ↓ → under the share rule, spending ↓ too (pro-cyclical).

What to look at: Exports and GDP in 2027–2028, then how fast they return in 2029–2030; CA and fiscal balance.

Caution: Real-world exports from the free zones contain many imports, so the true GDP hit is smaller than the model shows (imports do not react to exports).

S02 Permanent EU slowdown External D · exogenous

Why for North Macedonia: About 80% of MKD exports go to the EU; a lasting weaker EU (energy prices, industrial decline) lowers export demand permanently.

Shock: Real imports of all EU partners in XMKT (BEL, DEU, ESP, GRC, HRV, ITA, HUN, ROU) −2% from 2027 (permanent). Results in series ending _12.

EViews program 

' ===== S02: Permanent EU slowdown =====
MKD.scenario(n, a=12, i="baseline", c) "S02"
MKD.scenario "S02"
%list = "BELNEIMPGNFSKD DEUNEIMPGNFSKD ESPNEIMPGNFSKD GRCNEIMPGNFSKD HRVNEIMPGNFSKD ITANEIMPGNFSKD HUNNEIMPGNFSKD ROUNEIMPGNFSKD"
MKD.override {%list}
for %v {%list}
  smpl @all
  series {%v}_12 = {%v}
  smpl 2027 @last
  {%v}_12 = {%v}*0.98
next
smpl 2026 @last
MKD.solve(s=d,d=d,o=g,i=a,c=1e-6)

' all tables and graphs: show S02_SPOOL
' clean up: delete S02_*

Step by step, what happens:

  1. Eight exogenous partner series are overridden in one override line (the loop only fills the series).
  2. XMKT ↓ by close to 2% (EU partners have most of the weight).
  3. Exports ↓ about 2% in the long run (ECM toward XMKT).
  4. GDP and employment ↓; the gap closes slowly because potential does not move (labour, capital and TFP are unchanged at first).
  5. Lower GDP → lower investment target (potential is linked to capital, so K ↓ slowly) → small permanent loss of potential.

What to look at: Long-run export level (should approach −2%), GDP in year 5, unemployment.

Caution: A permanent demand loss in this model is mostly a cyclical effect; it does not change potential much unless investment falls.

Step by step, what happens:

  1. Oil price ↑ → MKDPMKEY ↑ much more than MKDPXKEY (identities with fixed weights).
  2. Import deflator ↑ (DLOG eq. on PMKEY × denar/USD); export deflator ↑ less → terms of trade ↓.
  3. Consumption deflator ↑ (0.3 × import prices on impact) → CPI ↑.
  4. Real disposable income ↓ → real consumption ↓.
  5. Relative import price ↑ → import volumes ↓ (−0.4 short run), which cushions GDP.
  6. Nominal imports ↑ → current account worsens.
  7. Policy rate rule reacts to inflation → rate ↑ → investment ↓.

What to look at: CPI in 2027, real C, CA % GDP, policy rate.

Caution: No separate energy block: the effect works only through PMKEY. The 2022 energy-price shock is a useful check.

Step by step, what happens:

  1. Same chain as S04 (PMKEY → import deflator → consumption deflator), but temporary.
  2. Prices rise in 2027 and fall back in 2029; the price level stays higher for a while because the deflator equations have inertia.
  3. Real consumption ↓ while prices are high, then recovers.
  4. Policy rule: rate ↑ temporarily.

What to look at: The path of CPI growth: up in 2027, down (possibly negative) in 2029.

Caution: Electricity prices are regulated in MKD; the model has no regulated-price channel, so the pass-through may differ from the data.

Step by step, what happens:

  1. Wheat and maize enter both PMKEY and PXKEY (MKD also exports agricultural goods).
  2. Net effect on terms of trade is small; import and export deflators both ↑.
  3. CPI ↑ via the import deflator in the consumption deflator equation.
  4. Volumes react little.

What to look at: CPI effect: compare with S04 to see the relative weight.

Caution: The model's consumption deflator does not know the CPI basket weights; food inflation passes through only via the import-price index. A large-shock check against 2022 is useful.

S07 Fall in metal and steel prices External D · exogenous

Step by step, what happens:

  1. PXKEY ↓ strongly; PMKEY ↓ less (iron ore is also imported, weight 4.6) → terms of trade ↓.
  2. Export deflator ↓ → relative export price vs GDP deflator ↓ → export volumes ↑ a little (0.5 short-run elasticity on relative price).
  3. Nominal exports ↓ → CA worsens, nominal GDP ↓ → revenue ↓ → share-rule spending ↓.
  4. GDP deflator ↓ → lower inflation.

What to look at: Nominal vs real: real GDP may hardly move, while nominal GDP, revenue and the CA worsen.

Caution: In reality steel output also falls when prices fall (plant closures). The model has no sector-volume effect; add an export add factor (S11 method) if you expect that.

Why for North Macedonia: The denar is pegged to the euro, so the denar/USD rate moves with EUR/USD; commodities are priced in USD.

Step by step, what happens:

  1. Peg equation: @PC(MKDPANUSATLS) = @PC(DEUPANUSATLS) → denar/USD +10%; denar/EUR unchanged.
  2. All USD commodity prices × denar/USD ↑ → import and export deflators ↑ (like S04 + S07 at once).
  3. CPI ↑ → real income ↓ → consumption ↓.
  4. Model artefact: remittances in the consumption equation are multiplied by the USD rate, so household income ↑ by about 10% of remittances. This should not happen for euro remittances.

What to look at: MKDPANEUATLS should not move; check consumption — part of its response is the remittance artefact.

Caution: Shock the German rate, never MKDPANUSATLS alone (the peg equation would fight the override). Fix the remittance conversion (roadmap item 1) before using this scenario for policy.

Step by step, what happens:

  1. Identity MKDINTREXN = MKDINTREDIFF + USAINTRXN → effective external rate +2 pp.
  2. External interest ↑ gradually as the rate applies to the existing debt stock.
  3. Deficit ↑ → debt ↑ → domestic interest rate ↑ (debt premium: 5 × (debt/GDP − 0.6) in MKDINTRDXN).
  4. Share rule uses revenue minus last year's interest → higher interest crowds out other spending one-for-one → G ↓ → GDP ↓.

What to look at: Interest bill, balance and debt % GDP; the fall in other spending.

Caution: In the model, a higher spread does not hit private borrowing costs directly; in reality it would also raise bank lending rates.

S10 Remittances fall by 1% of GDP BOP & finance A · add factor (ratio)

Why for North Macedonia: Private transfers are about 9% of GDP; a recession in Germany, Switzerland or Italy would reduce them.

Shock: Add factor of the ratio equation MKDBXFSTREMTCD/MKDNYGDPMKTPCD = C(1): −0.01 from 2027. Results in series ending _20.

Step by step, what happens:

  1. Behavioural (ratio) equation → shock the add factor, in ratio units: −0.01 = −1% of GDP (not LOG).
  2. Remittances ↓ → household income term in the consumption ECM ↓ → consumption ↓ (short-run elasticity C(3), long run 1:1 with income).
  3. GDP ↓, imports ↓ via domestic demand.
  4. Current account ↓ (secondary income) → financed by reserves in the model.

What to look at: Remittances % GDP should show −1.0; then consumption and CA.

Caution: Because of the USD conversion in the consumption equation, the size of the income effect is distorted (≈ 10% too low).

S11 New FDI export plant in a free zone BOP & finance A · add factors (ratio + DLOG)

Why for North Macedonia: Free-zone FDI (automotive, electrical equipment) brought big export gains after 2010.

Shock: FDI +1% of GDP in 2027–2028 (ratio add factor +0.01) and exports +2% a year in 2027–2028 (DLOG add factor +LOG(1.02)). Results in series ending _21.

Step by step, what happens:

  1. Two add factors in one override line.
  2. FDI is only a financing item (ratio to GDP): in the model it raises the financial account and reserves, nothing else.
  3. The real effect comes from the export add factor: +2 pp growth in 2027 and 2028 → exports ≈ +4% level.
  4. From 2029 the export ECM pulls exports back toward XMKT → the gain fades (the model does not know the plant stays).
  5. GDP ↑ → employment ↑ → consumption ↑.

What to look at: Exports by year: rising until 2028, then fading.

Caution: To keep the export gain permanent, use method B (target path) for exports, or add investment (private investment add factor).

Step by step, what happens:

  1. Identity: user cost MKDNEKRTTOTLXN = investment deflator × (policy rate + premium + δ − expected inflation) / (1 − CIT).
  2. User cost ↑ → private investment ↓ (−0.15 short run, and a lower long-run target).
  3. Capital stock ↓ → potential GDP ↓ permanently.
  4. Demand ↓ in the short run (investment), supply ↓ in the long run (capital).

What to look at: Capital and potential GDP in 2030–2035: this is one of the few shocks with a permanent supply effect.

S13 NBRM raises the policy rate by 1 pp Monetary C · exclude (rule)

Why for North Macedonia: Under the euro peg, NBRM follows the ECB; a temporary rate rise to defend reserves is a realistic case.

Shock: Policy rate MKDFMLBLPOLYXN fixed at baseline +1 pp in 2027–2028 (rule switched off). Results in series ending _23.
