Step by step, what happens:

  1. The policy rate has a rule (reacts to inflation) → exclude it, then set the path (in pp).
  2. Excluded for the whole forecast: after 2028 it equals baseline (does not react).
  3. User cost ↑ → private investment ↓.
  4. Consumption: −0.2 × change in the real rate (temporary).
  5. Domestic debt rate MKDINTRDXN ↑ (C(2) × policy rate) → interest bill ↑.
  6. No exchange-rate channel (peg).

What to look at: Investment and GDP 2027–2029, interest bill.

Caution: The model has no credit or bank-lending channel, so effects are small.

S14 Inflation expectations de-anchor (+1 pp) Monetary D · exogenous

Why for North Macedonia: After the 2022–2023 inflation episode, expectations may stay above the euro-area level.

Shock: MKDINFLEXPT +1 pp from 2027. Results in series ending _24.

EViews program 

' ===== S14: Inflation expectations de-anchor (+1 pp) =====
MKD.scenario(n, a=24, i="baseline", c) "S14"
MKD.scenario "S14"
MKD.override MKDINFLEXPT
smpl @all
series MKDINFLEXPT_24 = MKDINFLEXPT
smpl 2027 @last
MKDINFLEXPT_24 = MKDINFLEXPT+1
smpl 2026 @last

Step by step, what happens:

  1. Expected inflation enters the GDP deflator equation (weight (1 − C(3)) × 0.5) → actual inflation ↑.
  2. Policy rule reacts to (inflation − expectations): rate barely moves, because both rise.
  3. User cost: (policy rate − expected inflation) ↓ → real cost of capital ↓ → investment ↑ (!).
  4. Higher prices → nominal revenue ↑ → share-rule spending ↑.

What to look at: Inflation path and investment.

Caution: The investment ↑ result shows a weakness: the nominal rate does not follow expectations under the peg in the model.

Step by step, what happens:

  1. The rate is exogenous → override it (+1 pp, not ×1.01).
  2. Spending follows revenue by the share rule → exclude all spending items and keep them at baseline, otherwise the extra revenue is spent.
  3. VAT revenue = rate × (C + G nominal) ↑.
  4. Consumption deflator: long-run term includes LOG(1+VAT/100) → prices ↑ by about 1/1.18 ≈ 0.85%.
  5. Real disposable income ↓ → real consumption ↓ → GDP ↓.
  6. Balance improves; debt/GDP ↓.

What to look at: Balance % GDP vs GDP loss: the ratio is the cost of consolidation.

  1. Revenue ↑ → spending ↑ the same year (share rule).
  2. Government demand ↑ partly offsets the consumption loss.
  3. Balance improves much less than in S15.

What to look at: Compare S15 and S16 side by side: the difference is the effect of the fiscal rule.

Caution: This is why every revenue scenario must say how it is financed or used.

Step by step, what happens:

  1. PIT revenue = rate × wage bill ↑.
  2. Consumption equation uses wage bill × (1 − PIT/100): disposable income ↓ about 1.1% of the wage bill.
  3. Consumption ↓ (short run C(3), long run 1:1) → GDP ↓.
  4. No labour-supply effect (NAIRU target fixed at 7.2).

What to look at: Balance improvement vs consumption loss; compare with S15 (VAT).

Caution: The structural NAIRU formula with PIT is commented out in readdat.prg; with it, PIT would also affect potential.

Step by step, what happens:

  1. CIT revenue = rate × profits (nominal GDP × (1 − labour share)) ↑.
  2. User cost of capital is divided by (1 − CIT/100) → ↑ → private investment ↓.
  3. Capital ↓ → potential GDP ↓ in the long run.
  4. Small short-run demand effect, larger long-run supply effect.

What to look at: Revenue gain vs potential-GDP loss after 5–10 years.

Caution: The CIT base uses labour share 0.59; if the true share is lower (≈ 0.5), revenue per pp is underestimated.

Step by step, what happens:

  1. Excise revenue = rate × nominal C ↑.
  2. No price effect: the excise rate is not in the consumption deflator equation (only VAT is).
  3. So consumption hardly falls; the balance improves almost one-for-one.

What to look at: Compare with S15: a VAT rise lowers C, an excise rise almost does not.

Caution: This is a gap in the model: in reality excises raise CPI. Add an add factor to the consumption deflator (+LOG(1+0.02×share)) to correct.

Step by step, what happens:

  1. Customs revenue = rate × nominal imports ↓.
  2. No price effect on imports in the model → only the deficit worsens.
  3. Debt ↑ → domestic interest rate ↑ (debt premium) slowly.

What to look at: Revenue loss and debt path.

Caution: In reality import prices would fall and real income rise; add an add factor to the import deflator to capture it.

Step by step, what happens:

  1. SSC are a ratio to GDP in the model (no rate) → add factor in ratio units: +0.005 = +0.5% of GDP.
  2. No effect on wages, prices or consumption: the model has no SSC in the consumption or wage equations.
  3. Only the balance and debt improve.

What to look at: Balance +0.5 pp; GDP practically unchanged.

Caution: Clearly unrealistic for real policy: SSC reduce net wages. Combine with a PIT-type shock (S17) to approximate the income effect.

Step by step, what happens:

  1. Capital spending has a share rule → exclude it and set the path in denars (level, not %).
  2. Quasi-identity: NA public investment grows like fiscal capex → real public investment ↑.
  3. Total investment ↑ → GDP ↑ (imports catch up only over 2–4 years → large impact multiplier).
  4. Capital stock K ↑ → potential GDP ↑ (Cobb-Douglas, capital share 0.41).
  5. Deficit ↑ about 1% of GDP → debt ↑.
  6. After 2030 capex returns to baseline; K stays higher and depreciates at 5% a year.

What to look at: Year-1 multiplier (ΔGDP / 1% of GDP), potential GDP in 2030–2035, debt.

Caution: The impact multiplier is probably too high (imports react to potential, not demand, in the short run). Big projects also have high import content (foreign contractors).

Step by step, what happens:

  1. Exclude the wage-bill share rule and set the level ×1.10.
  2. NA government consumption follows (GNFS + wages) → real G ↑ (quasi-identity).
  3. GDP ↑ → employment ↑ → private wage bill ↑ → consumption ↑.
  4. Deficit ↑ permanently → debt ↑.

What to look at: G and GDP; balance and debt over 10 years.

Caution: Public wages do not enter the household income term of the consumption equation directly (only the economy-wide wage bill does), so the consumption effect is indirect.

  3. Transfers are in household income in the consumption equation → consumption ↑.
  4. Deficit ↑, debt ↑.

What to look at: Consumption and balance; compare with S23 (wages) per denar spent.

S25 Energy subsidies +0.5% of GDP Fiscal spending C · exclude

Step by step, what happens:

  1. Subsidies enter transfers (other) → household income in the consumption equation ↑ → consumption ↑.
  2. No price effect: subsidies do not lower prices in the model.
  3. Deficit ↑ for two years, debt permanently higher.

What to look at: Combine with S05 (gas spike) to see how much the subsidy offsets the real-income loss.

Caution: Real energy subsidies lower regulated prices; add a negative add factor to the consumption deflator to reflect that.

Step by step, what happens:

  1. Grants are a ratio-to-GDP equation → add factor +0.01.
  2. Grants are part of total revenue → the share rule would spend them on everything, so exclude all spending items and raise only capex.
  3. Same real effects as S22, but the deficit hardly changes (financed by grants).
  4. Potential GDP ↑ via capital.

What to look at: GDP and potential like S22, balance close to zero: compare with S22.

S27 Emigration: working-age population −5% by 2030 Supply side D · exogenous

Why for North Macedonia: The 2021 census showed a large population loss from emigration; it is the main risk to potential growth.

Shock: MKDSPPOPWORK falls 1.25% per year 2027–2030 vs baseline, then stays −5%. Results in series ending _37.

Step by step, what happens:

  1. Identity: structural employment L* = (1 − NAIRU/100) × participation/100 × population ↓ 5%.
  2. Potential GDP = TFP × L*^0.59 × K(−1)^0.41 ↓ ≈ 0.59 × 5% ≈ 3% at first.
  3. Investment target is tied to potential → investment ↓ → K ↓ → potential falls further, toward −5% in the long run.
  4. Employment follows L* (ECM −0.3); wage equation: productivity ↑ per worker → real wage ↑.
  5. GDP per capita changes much less than GDP.

What to look at: Potential GDP, GDP and GDP per worker in 2030–2035.

Caution: Remittances may rise with emigration (not in the model: they are a fixed % of GDP).

S28 Higher labour participation (+3 pp by 2030) Supply side D · exogenous

Step by step, what happens:

  1. Structural participation is exogenous; actual participation follows it (MKDLMPRTTOTLCN equation).
  2. L* ↑ by about 3/57 ≈ 5% → potential ↑ (about 0.59 × 5% at first, more as K follows).
  3. More labour supply than jobs at first → unemployment rate ↑ temporarily → wages ↓ relative → employment catches up.

What to look at: Unemployment (temporary rise) and potential GDP.

Step by step, what happens:

  1. TFP is exogenous (extended outside the model) → override.
  2. Potential GDP ↑ directly (TFP is a multiplier) and further through capital (investment target ↑).
  3. Long-run growth ≈ TFP growth / 0.59 → +0.5 pp TFP ≈ +0.85 pp GDP growth.
  4. Output gap ↓ at first (potential rises before demand) → inflation ↓ temporarily.
  5. Wages: productivity ↑ → real wage ↑ → consumption ↑.

What to look at: Potential and GDP growth rates; the gap in the first years.

Caution: This is the most powerful assumption in the model; the baseline already assumes TFP growth about 3× its 2015–2025 average. Use this scenario also with a negative sign (−0.5 pp) as a risk scenario.

Step by step, what happens:

  1. The target is exogenous; NAIRU follows it very slowly: NAIRU = 0.98 × NAIRU(−1) + 0.02 × target.
  2. So NAIRU falls by only ≈ 2% of the gap per year: −0.04 pp in 2027, about −0.4 pp by 2035.
  3. L* ↑ → potential ↑ (small) → employment ↑.

What to look at: How slowly NAIRU moves. To test a faster reform, exclude MKDLMUNRSTRLCN and set its path directly.

Caution: The 0.98 persistence is imposed, not estimated; it makes labour reforms almost invisible within 10 years.

Before using results for policy: run the checklist in Modeller's notes; remember the known model issues (remittances in USD, imports not reacting to exports, share-rule fiscal closure, no credit channel). Scenarios S08, S19, S20, S21 and S25 show exactly where these matter.

🎓 Training course explained: the World Bank MFMSA workshop files

The nine workshop files (theory, model layout, names, accounting, add factors, Excel interface, front-end changes, model build, interest note), explained in plain language. Each one is compared with what your MKD code actually does. Click a slide to enlarge it.

The World Bank MFMSA training pack for North Macedonia, explained

These nine files are the material from the World Bank workshop. Together they explain what the model is (theory), how it is built (EViews back end) and how to use it (Excel front end). Read them in this order:

#FileWhat it teachesWho it is forRelated part of this manual
101_WhatIsMFMod.pdfPhilosophy and theory: why a macro-structural model, potential GDP, firms, prices, consumption, investmentEveryone (concepts)📘 Theory
204_ModelLayout_MKD.pptxThe map of the MKD model, block by block: potential output, expenditure, production, fiscal, BOP, labour, money, international linksEveryone, the most important file6–12, 13
305_ReadingMFMSA.pptxHow to read variable names (mnemonics) and EViews equationsBeginners2. Reading names
407_LinksBetweenSheets.pptxNational accounting: GDP three ways, BOP, fiscal accounts, central bank, how the accounts linkEveryone3. Data, 8. BOP
509_AddFactors.pptxWhat an add factor is and how to use it for judgement in a forecastForecasters15, 🎯 How to shock
602_InterfaceOptions.pptxThe Excel front end ("MFMod StandAlone" ribbon): folders, buttons, options, solve modesThe "driver" (user)–
711_MakingChangesFrontEnd.pptxHow to change the Excel sheets: columns B, C, E, F, drop-downs, the Reports pageAdvanced users–
812_ModelBuild_MKD.pptxThe back-end build process: data file, sequence of EViews programs, four update exercisesThe "technician"▶ Step-by-step
9INT.docxA note on how interest payments are calculated and how to target themFiscal analysts11. Fiscal
Before you start, a warning: the workshop slides were adapted from a general template (the Nepal model). Some slides still say "MKD = Nepal", show provincial/local government, oil revenue, tourism matrix for Nepal or SOE investment. None of these exist in the MKD code you have. In each tab below, the box "In your MKD code" tells you what the model really does, checked against equations.prg.

The two roles (from 02_InterfaceOptions)

The technicianThe driver
Builds the model: collects data, estimates equations, programs EViews (files 05, 07, 12, INT)Uses the model: sets assumptions, runs forecasts and policy scenarios in Excel, without programming (files 02, 09, 11)

The Excel interface serves both: the technician uses it to check inconsistencies, the driver to run simulations.

01_WhatIsMFMod.pdf: the philosophy (Charl Jooste)

IdeaIn plain words
Combine theory with dataEach equation has a theoretical shape (e.g. consumption depends on lifetime income); the coefficients are estimated from MKD data.
Conditional forecastThe model does not "predict the future" by itself; it says "if these assumptions hold, then this is the result". The economist provides the judgement (add factors, assumptions).
Flexible, encompassing, tractableEasy to extend (only data limits it), large information set, all assumptions are visible and can be criticised.
Short run vs long runIn the long run GDP converges to potential GDP, which grows with population and TFP (balanced growth path). In the short run, prices and wages adjust slowly (nominal rigidities), so demand matters.
Potential GDPNot the maximum GDP, but the GDP when employment is at its natural rate and prices are in equilibrium. Actual ÷ potential − 1 = output gap, which drives inflation, interest and fiscal reactions.
Micro-foundationsFirms minimise cost → demand for labour and capital and a marginal-cost price P*; prices are reset with inertia (a Phillips curve); households follow the permanent-income hypothesis; investment equates required and expected return (user cost of capital).
ExpectationsMostly backward-looking (simple, robust); the model can be made forward-looking but this is not the default.

All these theory points are explained in detail, with the MKD equations, in 📘 Theory behind MFMod and the ⚙ Supply side section.

04_ModelLayout_MKD.pptx: the map of the model

This is the most important presentation. It says, for every block, which variables are behavioural, which are quasi-identities and which are identities, and what drives each one. The colour code on the slides is the same everywhere:

Colour on slideTypeMeaningIn EViews
RedBehavioural (ECM)Estimated equation: long-run target + short-run dynamicsequation _X.LS DLOG(X) = …, has an add factor
GreenQuasi-identity (DUMH)Close to an accounting rule, with a history-only residual… + C(1)*DUMH, add factor = 0 in forecast
PurpleIdentityPure accountingMKD.APPEND @IDENTITY …
OrangeHistorical share / trendFixed ratio to GDP or another baseX/BASE = C(1)

Every variable comes in three units: KN real (constant prices), XN deflator (price), CN nominal, linked by the identity CN = KN × XN. Usually two of the three have an equation and the third is the identity.

Slide by slide, with what the MKD code really does

SlideWhat the slide saysIn your MKD code (equations.prg)
3–4 FeaturesFour accounts (NIA, fiscal, external, monetary) + international links; ECM equations; theory: firm optimisation, permanent income, CES trade, New-Keynesian Phillips curve, UIP+PPP if floating, Taylor ruleSame structure. MKD is pegged to the euro, so UIP/PPP is not used: @PC(MKDPANUSATLS) = @PC(DEUPANUSATLS).
5 Economic mapSupply (participation, labour force, productivity) → potential; demand from domestic and external drivers and policies; GDP ↔ prices loopSame logic: the output gap (GDP vs potential) feeds the GDP deflator (0.2 × gap) and the labour market. Tourism is not a separate channel in MKD.
6 SoftwareExcel interface + EViews back end + central database (national sources, WDI/WEO, COMTRADE/ILO/GTAP)Your raw file MKDrawOctober2026.xlsx + ExogVarsOctober2026.xlsx; MfMod+ is your own Excel layer on top.
7 Potential outputY* = A · L^α · K(−1)^(1−α), α = 0.4 (compensation of employees 2011–2022), K by perpetual inventorySame formula (MKDNYGDPPOTLKN identity), but the labour exponent is 0.59 (series MKDNYYWBTOTLCN_ = 0.59 in readdat.prg). The slide and the code disagree; check which is intended (see Modeller's notes).
8 ConsumptionKN: + real disposable income (wages, PIT, subsidies, transfers, remittances), − real interest rate. XN: GDP factor-cost and import deflators, VAT & exciseKN: income = wage bill × (1 − PIT) + transfers + remittances × denar/USD; −0.2 × Δ(policy rate − inflation). XN: factor-cost deflator, import deflator and VAT only (excise is not in the price equation).
8 Gov. consumptionCN from public wages + goods & services; XN follows consumption deflatorSame: @PC(MKDNECONGOVTCN) = @PC(GNFS + WAGE) + C(1)*DUMH (quasi-identity).
8 Public investmentFederal + SOE investmentNo SOE split: NA public investment follows fiscal capital spending (quasi-identity).
8 Private investment+ operating surplus (GDP), − rental rate vs investment costSame idea: ECM to (1 − labour share) × potential ÷ (user cost / deflator), + growth of potential, −0.15 × change in user cost.
9 ExportsMerchandise and services separately: + world demand, − relative priceOne equation for goods & services: ECM to the export market MKDXMKT (12 partners) and relative price.
9 Imports+ domestic demand, − relative import priceLong run: domestic demand; short run: 0.8 × growth of potential (not of demand), −0.4 × relative price.
9 Inventories, discrepancyFully exogenousInventories = total investment − public − private in history; statistical discrepancy a ratio to GDP.
10 Consumption theoryEuler equation, Mankiw–Ball; ECM with income, transfers, wealth and real rateNo wealth term in MKD; long-run elasticity to income = 1 (−0.2 adjustment).
11–12 ProductionAgriculture and industry: lagged value and demand; services = residual; net taxes exogenousSame: MKDNVAGRTOTLKN, MKDNVINDTOTLKN behavioural; services is the residual. No industry sub-sectors.
13–14 RevenueRevenue = base × effective rate; VAT/excise on C+G, PIT/SSC on wage bill, CIT on operating surplus, trade taxes on M, others share of GDP; oil revenueVAT on (C+G) nominal, excise on C, PIT on wage bill, CIT on GDP × (1 − labour share), customs on imports; SSC, grants, other, property: ratio to GDP. No oil.
15 ExpenditureCurrent spending linked to GDP / wage bill; interest split domestic (policy rate) and external (US rate); capex to GDPWith !current = 1 each spending item is a share of (revenue − last year's interest). A debt-target rule exists in the code but is switched off.
16 FinancingBalance → financing requirement → external/domestic split → debt stocksDebt = debt(−1) − balance + valuation (quasi-identity); external share exogenous (MKDEXTLSHAREXN).
17–19 BOPExports/imports from NIA and exchange rate; remittances from partner GDP; other flows GDP trends; FDI, portfolio, other = GDP shares; reserves = residualSame, but remittances are a fixed % of GDP (not linked to partner GDP), and BOP flows mix EUR and USD conversions (see the remittance warning in Findings).
20 WagesNominal wage ECM to marginal product of labour × prices; short run: lag, prices, productivity, unemployment gapSame structure: −0.3 adjustment, lag weight C(8), −0.2 × (unemployment − NAIRU).
21 EmploymentECM to structural employment; real wage vs productivity; change in output gapSame: −0.3 to L*, −0.2 × (real wage − productivity), +0.1 × gap change.
22 MoneyTaylor rule; money supply, reserve money, NFA, NDAPolicy rate: MKDFMLBLPOLYXN = C(1)·rate(−1) + (1−C(1))·(C(2) + 1.2 × (inflation − expectations) + 0 × gap). No money block in the MKD equations.
23 InternationalTrade (top partners, 2015–19 weights), commodities (WB Pink Sheet), tourism, remittances (top-10 senders)Trade: 12 partners in MKDXMKT; commodities in MKDPXKEY/MKDPMKEY; no tourism or remittance matrix in the equations.
🧪 Test it in EViews · Check each block of the layout

What it checks: The defining identity of the expenditure, supply, fiscal, interest and exchange-rate blocks, plus one output per block.

What you should see: All five checks PASS (the peg check only in the forecast); four panels showing the main output of each block.

Paste into a new EViews program (File → New → Program) in the MKD workfile and press Run. Results open as a dashboard and a spool (all tables and graphs). Objects start with C2_; remove them with delete C2_*.

' ==============================================================================
'  MFMod MKD  |  TEST C2: Model layout: block checks
'  Purpose : Checks the main identity of each block and shows each block's output
'  Needs   : Baseline solved (actual series = baseline, *_0 series exist).
'  Output  : spool C2_SPOOL (tables + graphs) and dashboard C2_DASH
'  Clean up: delete C2_*
' ==============================================================================
%hs = "2005"      ' first year shown
%fs = "2026"      ' first forecast year (shaded area)
%fe = "2035"      ' last year shown
spool C2_SPOOL
smpl @all

' ---- Automatic checks (PASS if max |error| below threshold) ----------------

05_ReadingMFMSA.pptx: translating MFMod names and equations

Names follow the World Bank WDI system: country (3) + account (2) + main category (3) + sub-category (4) + unit (1) + currency (1).

PartCodes
CountryMKD (the slide says "MKD = Nepal": a template leftover), DEU, USA, WLD …
AccountNY national income · NE expenditure · NV value added · GG general government (GP provincial and GL local do not exist in MKD) · LM labour · FM financial · BX/BM/BN BOP exports/imports/net · BF capital & financial account
Main categoryCON consumption · GDI investment · GDP · EMP employment · EXP exports or expenditure · IMP imports · REV revenue · BAL balance · DBT debt · FIN financing · IND industry
Sub-categoryPRVT private · GOVT government · GNFS goods & non-factor services · TOTL total · MKTP market prices · FCST factor cost · OVRL overall …
UnitK constant prices (real) · C current prices (nominal) · X deflator / rate
CurrencyN national currency · D US dollars · R / no letter for ratios
ExampleMeaning
MKDNEEXPGNFSKNMKD · expenditure · exports · goods & services · constant prices · denars
USAGGBALOVRLCDUSA · general government · balance · overall · current prices · US dollars
MKDGPREVTAXTCN (quiz 3)Provincial government tax revenue, current denars. Does not exist in MKD (no provincial level).
MKDNEEXPMRCHXN (quiz 4)Deflator of merchandise exports. MKD has the total-exports deflator MKDNEEXPGNFSXN.

EViews equation cheat-sheet

WrittenMeans
@PC(X)% change of X
LOG(X), DLOG(X)natural log; change in log ≈ growth rate
X(-1)last year's X
@DURING("2020")dummy = 1 in 2020
-C(2)*(LOG(Y(-1)) - … - C(1))ECM term: C(2) = speed of adjustment, C(1) = long-run constant
C(10) and highershort-run coefficients
DUMHhistory dummy (1 in history, 0 in forecast) → quasi-identity
T_LRtrend (rises in history, flat in forecast)

The slide's example (government consumption deflator) is the same form as MKD's _MKDNECONGOVTXN: long-run tied to the consumption deflator, short-run homogeneity (coefficient 1). More in 2. Reading variable names; use the search box (press /) to decode any name.

🧪 Test it in EViews · Count and list series by account

07_LinksBetweenSheets.pptx: the accounting that holds the model together

Every number in the model must be consistent across accounts. This file explains the accounting identities; in MKD they are the purple identities.

ConceptFormulaMKD variables
GDP, expenditure sideY = C + G + I + X − M + DS (+ discrepancy)MKDNYGDPMKTPKN = …NECONPRVTKN + …NECONGOVTKN + …NEGDIFTOTKN + …NEEXPGNFSKN − …NEIMPGNFSKN + discrepancy
GDP, production sideY = agriculture + industry + services + net taxes on products…NVAGRTOTLKN, …NVINDTOTLKN, …NVSRVTOTLKN, …NYTAXNINDKN
GDP, income sideY = wage bill (W × N) + gross operating surplus (rk × K) + net taxesMKDNYYWBTOTLCN = wage × employment; operating surplus = the rest
GNP, GNDI, savingsGNP = GDP + net factor income; GNDI = GNP + transfers; S = GNDI − CPrimary and secondary income in the BOP (MKDBXFSTREMTCD, MKDBMFSTINTECD …)
BOP (BPM6)CA − KA + FA + E&O = change in reservesMKDBFBOPTOTLCD = capital + financial + current account + E&O
Fiscal (GFS)Overall balance = revenue − expense − net investment; financing = − balance (foreign + domestic)MKDGGBALOVRLCN = MKDGGREVTOTLCN − MKDGGEXPTOTLCN; debt accumulates the deficit
Central bankReserve money = NFA + NDANot modelled in MKD
Contribution to growthΔY/Y(−1) = ΔC/Y(−1) + ΔG/Y(−1) + ΔI/Y(−1) + ΔX/Y(−1) − ΔM/Y(−1)e.g. d(MKDNECONPRVTKN)/MKDNYGDPMKTPKN(-1)*100
GDP deflatorWeighted average of sector deflators, weights = real sharesMKDNYGDPFCSTXN = MKDNYGDPFCSTCN / MKDNYGDPFCSTKN
Why it matters: when you shock one account the others must follow. For example, higher exports raise GDP (NIA) and the current account (BOP); the extra revenue changes the fiscal balance. If an identity does not hold in history, run !check_id = 1 in master.prg.
🧪 Test it in EViews · Check the accounting identities

What it checks: Six identities across national accounts, BOP and fiscal accounts (PASS/CHECK), and the contributions to growth.

What you should see: All checks PASS; stacked bars that add up to GDP growth each year.

09_AddFactors.pptx: judgement in a forecast

A regression gives fitted values; the residual = actual − fitted. In the forecast there is no actual value, so the residual is replaced by the add factor: the amount by which your forecast differs from the pure model forecast. In the front end: Model suggestion + Add factor = User value (e.g. growth 2.0% + 0.3 pp judgement = 2.3%).

The four judgements, and how to write them in EViews

Suppose the last historical year (2025) has a large error in an equation, e.g. investment. What you assume about that error decides the add-factor path:

JudgementExampleAdd factor from 2026EViews (forecast sample)
1 · One-off errorA one-time event0X_A = 0
2 · Permanent level shiftA factory closedstays at the last errorX_A = @elem(X_A,"2025")
3 · Permanent growth shiftNo new investment in the sectormore and more negativeX_A = @elem(X_A,"2025")*(@year-2024)
4 · Temporary, fadingRecovery after a floodshrinks toward 0X_A = X_A(-1)*0.85
In your MKD code: solve.prg uses judgement 4 for every behavioural equation: the add factors decay by 15% a year (×0.85). Judgement 2 vs 3 depends on the equation form: in an error-correction equation (most MKD DLOG equations) a one-year add factor fades away, while a constant add factor gives a permanent level shift of add factor ÷ λ (e.g. 0.01 with λ = 0.2 → +5%). Only in a DLOG equation without an ECM term is a constant add factor a permanent growth shift. See 🔁 Error-correction models.

' Four add-factor judgements for private investment (run after the baseline)
' Pick ONE block; result in scenario _9
MKD.scenario(n, a=9, i="baseline", c) "AF judgement"
MKD.scenario "AF judgement"
MKD.override MKDNEGDIFPRVKN_A
smpl @all
series MKDNEGDIFPRVKN_A_9 = MKDNEGDIFPRVKN_A
smpl 2026 @last
' 1 one-off:            MKDNEGDIFPRVKN_A_9 = 0
' 2 level shift:        MKDNEGDIFPRVKN_A_9 = @elem(MKDNEGDIFPRVKN_A,"2025")
' 3 growth shift:       MKDNEGDIFPRVKN_A_9 = @elem(MKDNEGDIFPRVKN_A,"2025")*(@year-2024)
' 4 fading (default):   MKDNEGDIFPRVKN_A_9 = MKDNEGDIFPRVKN_A_9(-1)*0.85
MKDNEGDIFPRVKN_A_9 = 0
MKD.solve(s=d,d=d,o=g,i=a,c=1e-6)
smpl 2020 2035
show MKDNEGDIFPRVKN_A MKDNEGDIFPRVKN_A_9 (MKDNEGDIFPRVKN_9/MKDNEGDIFPRVKN_0-1)*100
smpl @all
🧪 Test it in EViews · Compare the four add-factor judgements

What it checks: The four judgement paths built from the 2025 add factor of private investment, and the path used in the baseline (no solve needed).

What you should see: Four diverging lines after 2025; the baseline path should match judgement 4 (×0.85 decay).

Paste into a new EViews program (File → New → Program) in the MKD workfile and press Run. Results open as a dashboard and a spool (all tables and graphs). Objects start with C5_; remove them with delete C5_*.

' ==============================================================================
'  MFMod MKD  |  TEST C5: Add-factor judgements, compared
'  Purpose : The four add-factor judgements for private investment, from its 2025 value, and the path the model actually uses
'  Needs   : Baseline solved (actual series = baseline, *_0 series exist).

%hs = "2018"      ' first year shown

C5_SPOOL.append C5_GR1
smpl {%hs} {%fe}

02_InterfaceOptions.pptx: the Excel front end

The World Bank front end is an Excel workbook with a ribbon tab "MFMod StandAlone". EViews runs in the background; you change numbers in Excel and press Solve.

Folders first. Create C:\WBG_MFMOD\ (or under your user folder) with Data, Programs and Baseline. Every solve saves a solution (.wf1) in Data and the EViews program that produced it in Programs, so you can recreate any old solution.

#ButtonWhat it does
1Load SolutionOpens an EViews workfile (.wf1) and fills the sheets
2Save SolutionSaves the workfile
3SolveSends your changes to EViews and solves the model
4RevertGoes back to another workfile
5Col BC visibilityShows/hides column B (mode triggers) and C (variable names)
6Exog/Endog sheetMakes a whole sheet exogenous (user in charge) or endogenous (model decides)
7Change Display ModeLevels, growth rates, % of GDP or contributions to growth
8Compare SolutionsCompares a policy shock or alternative forecast with the baseline
9OptionsDirectories, sheet options (which tabs, custom sheets), control strings (e.g. the list of quasi-identities), quarterly sheets
10–11About / HelpVersion updates and help

How to read a sheet

RowColourMeaning
Variable (e.g. Household consumption)redThe value used in the solution. If you type here, it becomes the user value.
Fitted value (_M)blackWhat the equation alone would give
Add factor (_A)blueThe judgement: user − model

Mode letters next to each row: x exogenous (you set it), e endogenous (model sets it), i identity. Right-click → View Equation shows the estimated equation and statistics.

Link with your add-in: MfMod+ does the same job in your own way: it creates EViews scenarios (overrides, excludes, shocks) from Excel and brings the comparison tables back. The World Bank front end works sheet-by-sheet with user/model/add-factor triplets.
🧪 Test it in EViews · See the user / model / add-factor triplet

What it checks: For private consumption: the value used, the equation's own suggestion and the add factor that separates them.

What you should see: The two lines differ exactly where the add factor is non-zero; in the forecast the gap shrinks as the add factor decays.

11_MakingChangesFrontEnd.pptx: how the Excel sheets are wired

Each sheet row is linked to EViews by a few hidden columns. Unhide columns B and C (button 5) to see them.

ColumnContainsExample
BTriggers: if this row changes mode, what else changesx:NECONPRVTKN_A=e;e:NECONPRVTKN_A=x: if consumption is made exogenous (x), its add factor becomes endogenous (e), and vice versa
CVariable code (without country prefix): which series EViews loads into the rowNECONPRVTKN, NECONPRVTKN_M (model suggestion), NECONPRVTKN_A (add factor)
EMode: x exogenous, e endogenous, i identitydrop-down list
FDisplay: g growth, l level, cont contribution, %gdp share of GDP, r report formuladrop-down list

Changing a drop-down: select the cell → Data → Data Validation → Allow: List → type the options separated by commas (e.g. g,l,%gdp,contr).

The trigger logic is the same as "exogenise via add factor": when you type a consumption value (x), the model keeps the equation but computes the add factor (e) that reproduces your number. This is exactly method B in 🎯 How to shock.

The Reports page

A free sheet for a preset list of indicators. Column C can contain any EViews expression, with display mode r:

@pcy(MKDNECONPRVTKN)/@pcy(MKDNYGDPMKTPKN)              ' income elasticity of consumption
MKDGGBALOVRLCN/MKDNYGDPMKTPCN*100                     ' fiscal balance % of GDP
(MKDNEGDIFGOVCN+MKDNEGDIFPRVCN)/MKDNYGDPMKTPCN*100    ' investment % of GDP

Adding sheets: either directly in the workbook, or in EViews by adding the sheet to the string MFMSAOptions (in interface.prg).

12_ModelBuild_MKD.pptx: the back end, step by step

Building the model is iterative: prepare data → build (estimate, assume, solve) → debug (consistency, sensible coefficients, long-run and simulation properties) → back to the start if needed.

Workshop programWhat it doesYour file
00_master.prgGlobal settings (samples, solver, checks) and runs everything in ordermaster.prg
01_read_data.prgReads country and global data from the Excel data filereaddat.prg (+ datafromserver.prg)
02_create_data / 02a_create_potlTransforms data, balances accounts; builds capital stock, TFP, potentialinside readdat.prg (see ⚙ Supply side)
03_equations.prgEstimates behavioural equations, adds identities and quasi-identitiesequations.prg
04_extend_exog.prgForecasts global and exogenous variables, structural parametersreadexovars.prg (ExogVars file)
05_solve_model.prgSolves over history, creates add factors, extends them, solves the forecastsolve.prg
06_interface.prgSets up the Excel interface pagesinterface.prg
07_convergence / 08_IRFChecks long-run convergence and impulse responsesconvergence.prg, convergence_check.prg

Data file (workshop name MKDdataforupdate.xlsx; yours: MKDrawOctober2026.xlsx + ExogVarsOctober2026.xlsx): national data (history), global data (partners' imports, FX, inflation, GDP: history + forecast), commodity prices (WB), population projections, and weight matrices (trade partners, remittance senders).

The four update exercises, answered for MKD

For every change the slides ask: history or forecast? Which account and file? Correct unit and scale? Which equations use the variable, and what should change?

ExerciseHow to do it in your files
1 · Move the end of history one yearAdd the new year to the raw data file; change %end_dat in master.prg; re-run. Equations whose sample uses %end_dat are re-estimated; check add factors in the last year (should be small).
2 · Remove provincial revenue sharingTemplate exercise (Nepal). MKD has no provincial level, so it does not apply.
3 · CIT as a fixed share of GDP at factor costIn equations.prg replace the CIT equation (see code below). The rate MKDGGREVCITTXN then no longer affects revenue, but it still enters the user cost of capital.
4 · Report contributions of TFP, K and L to potential growthContribution of TFP = Δlog TFP; of L = α × Δlog L*; of K = (1 − α) × Δlog K(−1). Add as Reports rows (display r) or run the code below. The same series are in ⚙ Supply side → EViews code B.

' Exercise 3: CIT as a fixed share of GDP at factor cost (replace in equations.prg)
' old:
' equation _MKDGGREVCITTCN.LS(OPTMETHOD=LEGACY) MKDGGREVCITTCN = (MKDGGREVCITTXN/100 * (MKDNYGDPMKTPCN * (1-MKDNYYWBTOTLCN_))) + C(1)
' new:
equation _MKDGGREVCITTCN.LS(OPTMETHOD=LEGACY) MKDGGREVCITTCN/MKDNYGDPFCSTCN = C(1)

' Exercise 4: contributions to potential growth (pp)
series CONT_TFP = dlog(MKDNYGDPTFP)*100
series CONT_LAB = MKDNYYWBTOTLCN_*dlog(MKDLMEMPSTRLCN)*100
series CONT_CAP = (1-MKDNYYWBTOTLCN_)*dlog(MKDNEGDIKSTKKN(-1))*100
series POT_GR   = dlog(MKDNYGDPPOTLKN)*100
smpl 2010 2035
show POT_GR CONT_TFP CONT_LAB CONT_CAP POT_GR-(CONT_TFP+CONT_LAB+CONT_CAP)
smpl @all

INT.docx: how interest payments are calculated, and how to target them

The two formulas in the note:

(1)  Interest_t = r_t / 100 × Debt_(t−1)
(2)  r_t        = anchor_t + premium_t

The anchor is the policy rate for domestic debt and the US average rate for external debt; the premium is computed in history as actual rate − anchor.

To hit a target interest bill in the forecast, reverse both: r = 100 × target ÷ debt(−1), then premium = r − anchor. The note's example: debt 100, target interest 2 → r = 2%; anchor 0.5% → premium 1.5%. Check: (0.5 + 1.5)/100 × 100 = 2.

External debtDomestic debt
Formula (1) in MKDMKDGGEXPINTECN = MKDINTREXN/100 * MKDGGDBTEXTLCN(-1)MKDGGEXPINTDCN = MKDINTRDXN/100 * MKDGGDBTDOMTCN(-1)
Formula (2) in MKDidentity MKDINTREXN = MKDINTREDIFF + USAINTRXN (as in the note)behavioural: MKDINTRDXN = C(1) + C(2)·policy rate + 5 × (debt/GDP − 0.6). Different from the note: there is a debt-risk premium.
To target itoverride the spread MKDINTREDIFFshift the add factor of MKDINTRDXN (level equation → add factor in percentage points)

' Target the interest bill in 2027: external 6,000 and domestic 5,000 (million denars)
MKD.scenario(n, a=8, i="baseline", c) "Interest target"
MKD.scenario "Interest target"
MKD.override MKDINTREDIFF MKDINTRDXN_A
smpl @all
series MKDINTREDIFF_8 = MKDINTREDIFF
series MKDINTRDXN_A_8 = MKDINTRDXN_A
smpl 2027 2027
' external: r = 100*target/debt(-1); spread = r - US rate
MKDINTREDIFF_8 = 100*6000/MKDGGDBTEXTLCN_0(-1) - USAINTRXN
' domestic: shift the equation by (target rate - baseline rate)
MKDINTRDXN_A_8 = MKDINTRDXN_A + (100*5000/MKDGGDBTDOMTCN_0(-1) - MKDINTRDXN_0)
smpl 2026 @last
MKD.solve(s=d,d=d,o=g,i=a,c=1e-6)
smpl 2026 2028
show MKDGGEXPINTECN_8 MKDGGEXPINTDCN_8 MKDINTREXN_8 MKDINTRDXN_8
smpl @all

The 2027 interest uses the debt at the end of 2026, which the shock does not change, so the targets are hit exactly in 2027. In later years debt changes with the deficit, so the bill moves.

🧪 Test it in EViews · Check the interest formulas

🔁 Error-correction models (ECM) and the other models in MFMod

Most behavioural equations in the MKD model are error-correction models: they say where a variable wants to be in the long run and how fast it gets there. This section explains the idea once, goes through all 14 ECMs and the 3 partial-adjustment equations, then covers the related econometric methods (ARDL, VECM, DOLS, NARDL, threshold, Markov switching, panel, PAC…) and the other equation types in the MKD model.

The idea in one picture

Think of a dog on a long leash. The owner (the long-run target) walks a predictable path; the dog (the actual variable) runs around, but the leash always pulls it back. The ECM describes both: where the owner goes, and how strongly the leash pulls.

Δlog Yt = − λ × [ log Yt−1 − log Y*t−1 ]  +  short-run terms  +  constant  +  add factor
                ╰──────── error-correction term ────────╯
PieceNameMeaning
log Y* Long-run target (cointegrating relation)Where theory says Y should be, given its drivers (income for consumption, foreign demand for exports, productivity for wages…)
log Yt−1 − log Y*t−1Equilibrium error (the "gap")How far Y was from its target last year, in % (log points)
λSpeed of adjustmentShare of the gap closed each year (0.2 = 20%). Written with a minus sign, so a positive gap pulls growth down.
Short-run termsDynamicsImmediate reactions to changes in the drivers (Δlog income, Δ relative prices…), inertia, dummies

How to read an MFMod ECM

In EViewsMeans
DLOG(Y)growth rate of Y (the left side is always growth)
-0.2*(LOG(Y(-1)) - LOG(X(-1)))ECM term: λ = 0.2 imposed, long-run elasticity of Y to X = 1
-C(2)*( … ) or C(1)*( … )λ estimated from data (if written with +, the estimate must be negative)
+ 1*DLOG(X)short-run elasticity 1 (= "dynamic homogeneity": when X grows, Y grows the same, no new gap)
@LOGIT(C(1))an estimated weight forced between 0 and 1
@DURING("2020")dummy for one-off events (only history)

Why MFMod uses ECMs

  • Theory in the long run, data in the short run. The target comes from economics (budget constraints, profit maximisation); the dynamics come from MKD history.
  • Stable forecasts. Whatever the shock, variables return to sensible ratios (consumption/income, imports/demand, wages/productivity): the model has a balanced growth path.
  • Interpretation. λ tells you how persistent a shock is; the long-run elasticities tell you where you end up.

Imposed vs estimated coefficients

Many MKD coefficients are imposed (0.2, 0.3, 1, 0.4…) rather than estimated. With only ~20 annual observations, estimated speeds are imprecise and can have the wrong sign; the modellers fixed them at values that give sensible simulation properties (see 🎓 12 · Model build: "coefficients make sense: trade-off between data fitting and simulation properties"). Estimated coefficients are C(n); open the equation (EViews button) to see their values.

Rules of thumb for λ

λGap closed per yearHalf-life (years)90% closed after (years)Used in MKD for
0.022%34114NAIRU
0.220%3.110.3consumption, exports, sector deflators
0.330%1.96.5wages, employment, consumption/export/import deflators
0.550%1.03.3–

Half-life = ln(0.5) ÷ ln(1 − λ). These are the pure ECM speeds; in the full model the target itself moves, so actual adjustment can be faster or slower.

All 14 ECMs at a glance

EquationVariableBlockLong-run targetλHalf-life (yrs)
Private consumption (real)MKDNECONPRVTKNDemandlog C* = log(real disposable income YD/Pc) + constant0.23.1
Private investment (real)MKDNEGDIFPRVKNDemandlog I* = log[(1−α) × potential GDP ÷ real user cost of capital] + constantC(2)estimated
Exports of goods and services (real)MKDNEEXPGNFSKNTradelog X* = log(export market XMKT) + 00.23.1
Imports of goods and services (real)MKDNEIMPGNFSKNTradelog M* = log(domestic demand) − 0C(2)estimated
Average gross wage (nominal)MKDNEWRTTOTLCNLabourlog W* = log(α × potential output per structural worker) + log(consumer prices)0.31.9
Total employmentMKDLMEMPTOTLCNLabourlog L* = log(structural employment) — employment returns to (1 − NAIRU) × participation × working-age population0.31.9
Private consumption deflatorMKDNECONPRVTXNPriceslog Pc* = C(2) × log(domestic price) + (1 − C(2)) × log(import price) + log(1 + VAT)0.31.9
Export deflatorMKDNEEXPGNFSXNPriceslog PX* = 00.31.9
Import deflatorMKDNEIMPGNFSXNPriceslog PM* = 00.31.9
Public investment deflatorMKDNEGDIFGOVXNPriceslog PIG* = log Pc + constant−C(1)estimated
Private investment deflatorMKDNEGDIFPRVXNPriceslog PIP* = log Pc + constant−C(1)estimated
Government consumption deflatorMKDNECONGOVTXNPriceslog PG* = log Pc + constant−C(1)estimated
Agriculture value-added deflatorMKDNVAGRTOTLXNPriceslog PAGR* = log Pc + constant0.23.1
Industry value-added deflatorMKDNVINDTOTLXNPriceslog PIND* = log Pc + constant0.23.1

Long-run anchors: what everything converges to

AnchorVariables that follow it
Real disposable incomeconsumption
Potential GDP and the user cost of capitalprivate investment (→ capital stock → potential again)
Partner imports (XMKT)exports
Domestic demandimports
Productivity × priceswages
Structural employmentemployment
Consumer pricesinvestment, government and sector deflators
World prices × denar/USD (+ domestic prices)export and import deflators → consumer prices

Together with potential GDP (TFP, labour, capital) these anchors define the model's long-run growth path. See also 🧭 Modeller's notes → Long-run anchors.

Speed simulator: how fast does a gap close?

Start with Y 10% above its long-run target. Choose λ and see the gap year by year (pure ECM, everything else unchanged).

Presets:

The 14 ECMs, one by one

Click a row to open it. Each card has the equation as written in equations.prg, the long-run target, the speed, every short-run term, what drives the long run, cautions, an EViews button and a small program to plot the equilibrium error.

E01 Private consumption (real) MKDNECONPRVTKN λ = 0.2

Sample: 2007–2025

DLOG(MKDNECONPRVTKN) = -0.2*(LOG(MKDNECONPRVTKN(-1)) - 1*LOG(YD(-1)/MKDNECONPRVTXN(-1)))
   + C(3)*DLOG(YD/MKDNECONPRVTXN) - 0.2*D(MKDFMLBLPOLYXN/100 - DLOG(MKDNECONPRVTXN))
   + C(4) + C(12)*(@DURING("2020")-@DURING("2021")) + C(13)*@DURING("2007 2008")

YD = MKDNYYWBTOTLCN*(1-MKDGGREVPITTXN/100) + MKDGGEXPTRNSCN + MKDBXFSTREMTCD*MKDPANUSATLS
PartExplanation
Long run (target)log C* = log(real disposable income YD/Pc) + constant. Elasticity 1: in the long run households spend a constant share of their real disposable income (wages after PIT + social transfers + remittances).
Speed of adjustment λ0.2 imposed → 20% of the gap closed each year; half-life 3.1 years; 90% closed after 10.3 years
Short run
C(3) × Δlog real incomepart of an income change is spent in the same year (estimated marginal propensity)
−0.2 × Δ(policy rate − inflation)a higher real interest rate this year → save more, consume less (intertemporal substitution)
C(4)constant: together with C(3) and λ it fixes the long-run consumption/income ratio
C(12), C(13)dummies: COVID 2020 (and rebound 2021), crisis 2007–2008
What moves the long runwages and employment (wage bill), PIT rate, pensions and social transfers, remittances, the policy rate
CautionRemittances (EUR data) are multiplied by the denar/USD rate, so income moves with EUR/USD and is about 10% too low. No wealth or credit term.

Check the equilibrium error 

' ==============================================================================
'  MFMod MKD  |  TEST EC: ECM Private consumption (real)
'  Purpose : Equilibrium error, actual vs fitted, unit-root test on the gap
'  Needs   : Model equations estimated; baseline solved.
'  Output  : spool EC_SPOOL (tables + graphs) and dashboard EC_DASH
'  Clean up: delete EC_*
' ==============================================================================
%hs = "2000"      ' first year shown
%fs = "2026"      ' first forecast year (shaded area)
%fe = "2035"      ' last year shown
spool EC_SPOOL
smpl @all
series ECMGAP_C = log(MKDNECONPRVTKN) - log((MKDNYYWBTOTLCN*(1-MKDGGREVPITTXN/100)+MKDGGEXPTRNSCN+MKDBXFSTREMTCD*MKDPANUSATLS)/MKDNECONPRVTXN)
ECMGAP_C.displayname Equilibrium error, log points (0 = on the long-run target)
smpl {%hs} 2025
_MKDNECONPRVTKN.fit EC_FIT
EC_FIT.displayname Fitted (static, equation only)
smpl @all
series EC_ACT = MKDNECONPRVTKN
EC_ACT.displayname Actual / baseline
smpl {%hs} {%fe}
group EC_G1 ECMGAP_C
freeze(EC_GR1) EC_G1.line
EC_GR1.addtext(t) "Private consumption (real): equilibrium error (stationary? settles in forecast?)"
EC_GR1.draw(shade, bottom) {%fs} {%fe}
EC_GR1.draw(line, left) 0
EC_SPOOL.append EC_GR1
smpl {%hs} 2025
group EC_G2 EC_ACT EC_FIT
freeze(EC_GR2) EC_G2.line
EC_GR2.addtext(t) "Private consumption (real): actual vs fitted"
EC_SPOOL.append EC_GR2
smpl {%hs} 2025
freeze(EC_UR) ECMGAP_C.uroot(adf)

E02 Private investment (real) MKDNEGDIFPRVKN λ = C(2)

Sample: 2000–2025

DLOG(MKDNEGDIFPRVKN) = C(1) - C(2)*(LOG(MKDNEGDIFPRVKN(-1))
   - LOG((1-MKDNYYWBTOTLCN_(-1))*MKDNYGDPPOTLKN(-1)/(MKDNEKRTTOTLXN(-1)/MKDNYGDPFCSTXN(-1))))
   + 1*DLOG(MKDNYGDPPOTLKN) - 0.15*DLOG(MKDNEKRTTOTLXN/MKDNEGDIFTOTXN)
PartExplanation
Long run (target)log I* = log[(1−α) × potential GDP ÷ real user cost of capital] + constant. This is the firm's first-order condition (desired capital = capital share × output ÷ rental price), so investment rises 1:1 with potential GDP and falls 1:1 with the real cost of capital.
Speed of adjustment λC(2) (estimated: open the equation to see the value)
Short run
+1 × Δlog potential GDPinvestment grows with capacity (dynamic homogeneity: no growth-related gap)
−0.15 × Δlog(user cost / investment deflator)a jump in the cost of capital cuts investment at once
C(1)constant
What moves the long runpotential GDP (TFP, labour, capital), the labour share α, the user cost: policy rate, risk premium MKDNEKRTPREMFR, depreciation, expected inflation, CIT rate
CautionUses α = 0.59 (the training slides say 0.4); a different α changes the investment level the model aims for.

E03 Exports of goods and services (real) MKDNEEXPGNFSKN λ = 0.2

Sample: start–2025

DLOG(MKDNEEXPGNFSKN) = -0.2*(LOG(MKDNEEXPGNFSKN(-1)) - LOG(MKDXMKT(-1)) - 0.3*LOG(MKDNEEXPGNFSXN(-1)/MKDNYGDPFCSTXN(-1)))
   + C(5)*DLOG(MKDXMKT) + 0.5*DLOG(MKDNEEXPGNFSXN/MKDNYGDPFCSTXN)
   + C(4) + C(10)*T_LR + C(11)*@DURING("2008")
PartExplanation
Long run (target)log X* = log(export market XMKT) + 0.3 × log(export price ÷ domestic price) + constant. Elasticity 1 to foreign demand: in the long run MKD keeps a constant share of its partners' imports.
Speed of adjustment λ0.2 imposed → 20% of the gap closed each year; half-life 3.1 years; 90% closed after 10.3 years
Short run
C(5) × Δlog XMKTshort-run response to partner demand (estimated)
+0.5 × Δlog(PX/P)relative price term
C(10) × T_LRtrend: market-share gains in history (free zones); the trend is flat in the forecast
C(4), C(11)constant; 2008 dummy
What moves the long runpartner imports (12 countries in MKDXMKT), world prices via the export deflator
CautionThe relative-price sign is positive (exports rise when export prices rise relative to domestic prices). This can be read as export profitability, but standard theory expects a negative competitiveness effect. Check the intention.

E04 Imports of goods and services (real) MKDNEIMPGNFSKN λ = C(2)

Sample: 2004–2025

DLOG(MKDNEIMPGNFSKN) = -C(2)*(LOG(MKDNEIMPGNFSKN(-1)) - LOG(MKDNEGDETTOTKN(-1)) + 0.3*LOG(MKDNEIMPGNFSXN(-1)/MKDNYGDPFCSTXN(-1)))
   - 0.4*DLOG(MKDNEIMPGNFSXN/MKDNYGDPFCSTXN) + C(5) + 0.8*DLOG(MKDNYGDPPOTLKN)
   + C(10)*@DURING("2009") + C(12)*(@DURING("2020")-@DURING("2021 2022"))
PartExplanation
Long run (target)log M* = log(domestic demand) − 0.3 × log(import price ÷ domestic price) + constant. Elasticity 1 to domestic demand, −0.3 to relative prices.
Speed of adjustment λC(2) (estimated: open the equation to see the value)
Short run
−0.4 × Δlog relative import pricemore expensive imports → fewer imports at once
+0.8 × Δlog potential GDPshort-run growth follows capacity, not demand
C(5), C(10), C(12)constant; 2009 and COVID dummies
What moves the long rundomestic demand (C, G, I), import and domestic prices
CautionExports do not enter, although MKD exports (free zones) have high import content. In the short run imports follow potential, not demand, so demand shocks show a large impact multiplier.

E05 Average gross wage (nominal) MKDNEWRTTOTLCN λ = 0.3

Sample: start–2025

DLOG(MKDNEWRTTOTLCN) = C(1) - 0.3*(LOG(MKDNEWRTTOTLCN(-1)) - LOG(MKDNYYWBTOTLCN_(-1)*MKDNYGDPPOTLKN(-1)/MKDLMEMPSTRLCN(-1)) - LOG(MKDNECONPRVTXN(-1)))
   + C(8)*DLOG(MKDNEWRTTOTLCN(-1)) + (1-C(8))*DLOG(MKDNYGDPPOTLKN/MKDLMEMPSTRLCN)
   + (0.9*DLOG(MKDNECONPRVTXN(-1)) + 0.1*MKDINFLEXPT/100)
   - 0.2*(MKDLMUNRTOTLCN - MKDLMUNRSTRLCN)/100 + dummies 2007, 2012, 2018, 2019
PartExplanation
Long run (target)log W* = log(α × potential output per structural worker) + log(consumer prices). The real wage equals the marginal product of labour (labour share × productivity), so in the long run wages grow with productivity plus inflation.
Speed of adjustment λ0.3 imposed → 30% of the gap closed each year; half-life 1.9 years; 90% closed after 6.5 years
Short run
C(8) × last year's wage growthwage inertia (contracts, indexation)
(1−C(8)) × productivity growththe rest follows trend productivity
0.9 × last year's inflation + 0.1 × expected inflationprice compensation
−0.2 × (unemployment − NAIRU)Phillips curve: unemployment above NAIRU slows wages
What moves the long runTFP and capital (productivity), structural employment, consumer prices, unemployment gap
CautionLabour share fixed at 0.59 (measured share ≈ 0.5); minimum-wage decisions are not modelled (use the add factor).

E06 Total employment MKDLMEMPTOTLCN λ = 0.3

Sample: start–2025

DLOG(MKDLMEMPTOTLCN) = -0.3*(LOG(MKDLMEMPTOTLCN(-1)) - LOG(MKDLMEMPSTRLCN(-1))) + DLOG(MKDLMEMPSTRLCN)
   - 0.2*(DLOG(MKDNEWRTTOTLCN/MKDNYGDPFCSTXN) - DLOG(MKDNYGDPTFP)/MKDNYYWBTOTLCN_)
   + 0.1*(DLOG(MKDNYGDPMKTPKN) - DLOG(MKDNYGDPPOTLKN)) + C(1) + C(11)*@DURING("2019") + C(12)*@DURING("2009")
PartExplanation
Long run (target)log L* = log(structural employment) — employment returns to (1 − NAIRU) × participation × working-age population.
Speed of adjustment λ0.3 imposed → 30% of the gap closed each year; half-life 1.9 years; 90% closed after 6.5 years
Short run
+1 × Δlog structural employmentjobs grow with the labour supply
−0.2 × (real product wage growth − TFP growth/α)wages rising faster than productivity cost jobs
+0.1 × change in the output gapOkun-type cyclical response
C(1), C(11), C(12)constant; 2019 and 2009 dummies
What moves the long runworking-age population, participation, NAIRU, wages vs productivity, the business cycle
CautionThe unemployment rate is the identity 1 − employment ÷ labour force, so every error here moves unemployment one-for-one.

E07 Private consumption deflator MKDNECONPRVTXN λ = 0.3

Sample: 2003–2025

DLOG(MKDNECONPRVTXN) = -0.3*(LOG(MKDNECONPRVTXN(-1)) - C(2)*LOG(MKDNYGDPFCSTXN(-1)) - LOG(1+MKDGGREVGNFSXN(-1)/100) - (1-C(2))*LOG(MKDNEIMPGNFSXN(-1)))
   + C(3) + 0.3*DLOG(MKDNEIMPGNFSXN) + (1-0.3)*DLOG(MKDNYGDPFCSTXN) + DLOG(1+MKDGGREVGNFSXN/100)
PartExplanation
Long run (target)log Pc* = C(2) × log(domestic price) + (1 − C(2)) × log(import price) + log(1 + VAT). Consumer prices are a weighted average of domestic and import prices (weights sum to 1 = homogeneity) plus VAT.
Speed of adjustment λ0.3 imposed → 30% of the gap closed each year; half-life 1.9 years; 90% closed after 6.5 years
Short run
0.3 × Δlog import deflator30% immediate pass-through of import prices
0.7 × Δlog domestic (factor-cost) deflator70% from domestic costs
1 × Δlog(1 + VAT)a VAT change passes through fully in the same year
C(3)constant
What moves the long runGDP deflator (wages, marginal cost, gap), import prices (world commodities, EUR/USD), VAT rate
CautionExcise duties are not in this equation, so excise changes do not raise prices in the model.

Short run
C(5) × Δlog domestic deflatorlocal cost share in the short run
(1−C(5)) × Δlog(PMKEY × denar/USD)world prices in denars
C(4)constant
What moves the long runworld commodity prices (MKDPMKEY), EUR/USD, domestic prices
