Partial-adjustment equations: ECM cousins

These three equations also pull a variable toward a target, but in a simpler way: Y = ρ × Y(−1) + (1 − ρ) × target. Adjustment per year = 1 − ρ. They are not written as DLOG ECMs, but the logic (and the half-life formula) is the same.

P1 GDP deflator at factor cost (Phillips curve) MKDNYGDPFCSTXN 

DLOG(MKDNYGDPFCSTXN) = C(3)*DLOG(MKDNYGDPFCSTXN(-1)) + (1-C(3))*(0.5*DLOG(MKDPSTAR) + 0.5*MKDINFLEXPT/100)
   + 0.2*MKDNYGDPGAP_/100 + C(11)*@DURING("2022")

A Phillips curve in growth rates: inflation = C(3) × last year's inflation (inertia) + the rest split between marginal-cost growth (P*) and expected inflation, + 0.2 × output gap. There is no level ECM term: the price level is not pulled back to P*, only inflation is anchored. The theory slides (01_WhatIsMFMod) show the level version; MKD uses the Phillips-curve version derived from it.

Speed: C(3) = inertia; adjustment of inflation = 1 − C(3) per year

P2 Policy interest rate (smoothed Taylor rule) MKDFMLBLPOLYXN 

MKDFMLBLPOLYXN = C(1)*MKDFMLBLPOLYXN(-1) + (1-C(1))*(C(2) + 1.2*(@PC(MKDNECONPRVTXN) - MKDINFLEXPT) + 0.0*MKDNYGDPGAP_)

Partial adjustment: each year the rate moves (1 − C(1)) of the way toward its target (neutral rate C(2) + 1.2 × inflation gap). Output-gap weight is 0. Under the euro peg, NBRM in practice follows the ECB.

Speed: 1 − C(1) per year (estimated)

P3 NAIRU (structural unemployment) MKDLMUNRSTRLCN 

MKDLMUNRSTRLCN = 0.98*MKDLMUNRSTRLCN(-1) + (1-0.98)*MKDLMUNRTARGT + C(10)*@DURING("2009")

Partial adjustment toward the target (7.2%): only 2% of the gap closes each year.

Speed: 0.02 imposed → half-life 34 years, 90% after 114 years

Add factors in an ECM

The add factor is added to the right-hand side, so it changes growth in that year. Because the ECM pulls back, its long-run effect depends on how long you keep it:

Add factor pathEffect on the level of YExample (λ = 0.2, AF = 0.01)
One year onlytemporary: jumps, then fades as the ECM closes the gap+1% in year 1, ≈ +0.8% year 2, +0.64% year 3 …
Constant every yearpermanent level shift = AF ÷ λ (growth back to normal)+0.01 ÷ 0.2 = +5% in the long run
Decaying ×0.85 (MKD default in solve.prg)temporary, longer-lasting than one yearfades over ~10 years
Rising linearlypermanent growth shiftjudgement 3 in 09 · Add factors

So in an ECM a constant add factor is the same as moving the long-run target by AF ÷ λ. That is why large add factors at the end of history matter: with ×0.85 decay they still shift the forecast for years.

Checks every modeller should run

CheckWhat good looks likeHow
Speeds have the right signλ between 0 and 1 (C(n) negative where written with +)open each equation (spool program below)
Equilibrium errors are stationary in historyfluctuate around a constant, no trendgap program below
Equilibrium errors settle in the forecastflat by 2030–2035same plot, forecast years
Add factors at the end of historysmall (|AF| < 0.02)show *_A for the last historical year
Long-run ratios sensibleC/income, M/demand, X/XMKT stable in the forecastModeller's notes → Forecast checklist

1. All ECM estimation outputs in one spool

' Collect the estimation output of all ECM equations in one spool (EViews 7+)
spool ECM_ALL
for %e MKDNECONPRVTKN MKDNEGDIFPRVKN MKDNEEXPGNFSKN MKDNEIMPGNFSKN MKDNEWRTTOTLCN MKDLMEMPTOTLCN MKDNECONPRVTXN MKDNEEXPGNFSXN MKDNEIMPGNFSXN MKDNEGDIFGOVXN MKDNEGDIFPRVXN MKDNECONGOVTXN MKDNVAGRTOTLXN MKDNVINDTOTLXN
  freeze(tmp_out) _{%e}.output
  ECM_ALL.append tmp_out
  delete tmp_out
next
show ECM_ALL

2. All equilibrium errors in one chart (history + forecast)

' Equilibrium errors of all ECMs, history + forecast
series ECMGAP_C = log(MKDNECONPRVTKN) - log((MKDNYYWBTOTLCN*(1-MKDGGREVPITTXN/100)+MKDGGEXPTRNSCN+MKDBXFSTREMTCD*MKDPANUSATLS)/MKDNECONPRVTXN)
series ECMGAP_IP = log(MKDNEGDIFPRVKN) - log((1-MKDNYYWBTOTLCN_)*MKDNYGDPPOTLKN/(MKDNEKRTTOTLXN/MKDNYGDPFCSTXN))
series ECMGAP_X = log(MKDNEEXPGNFSKN) - log(MKDXMKT) - 0.3*log(MKDNEEXPGNFSXN/MKDNYGDPFCSTXN)
series ECMGAP_M = log(MKDNEIMPGNFSKN) - log(MKDNEGDETTOTKN) + 0.3*log(MKDNEIMPGNFSXN/MKDNYGDPFCSTXN)
series ECMGAP_W = log(MKDNEWRTTOTLCN) - log(MKDNYYWBTOTLCN_*MKDNYGDPPOTLKN/MKDLMEMPSTRLCN) - log(MKDNECONPRVTXN)
series ECMGAP_EMP = log(MKDLMEMPTOTLCN) - log(MKDLMEMPSTRLCN)
series ECMGAP_PC = log(MKDNECONPRVTXN) - _MKDNECONPRVTXN.@coefs(1)*log(MKDNYGDPFCSTXN) - log(1+MKDGGREVGNFSXN/100) - (1-_MKDNECONPRVTXN.@coefs(1))*log(MKDNEIMPGNFSXN)
series ECMGAP_PX = log(MKDNEEXPGNFSXN) - 0.4*log(MKDNYGDPFCSTXN) - 0.6*log(MKDPXKEY*MKDPANUSATLS)
series ECMGAP_PM = log(MKDNEIMPGNFSXN) - 0.2*log(MKDNYGDPFCSTXN) - 0.8*log(MKDPMKEY*MKDPANUSATLS)
series ECMGAP_IGX = log(MKDNEGDIFGOVXN) - log(MKDNECONPRVTXN)
series ECMGAP_IPX = log(MKDNEGDIFPRVXN) - log(MKDNECONPRVTXN)
series ECMGAP_GX = log(MKDNECONGOVTXN) - log(MKDNECONPRVTXN)
series ECMGAP_AGX = log(MKDNVAGRTOTLXN) - log(MKDNECONPRVTXN)
series ECMGAP_INX = log(MKDNVINDTOTLXN) - log(MKDNECONPRVTXN)
group G_ECMGAP ECMGAP_C ECMGAP_IP ECMGAP_X ECMGAP_M ECMGAP_W ECMGAP_EMP ECMGAP_PC ECMGAP_PX ECMGAP_PM ECMGAP_IGX ECMGAP_IPX ECMGAP_GX ECMGAP_AGX ECMGAP_INX
smpl 2000 2035
show G_ECMGAP.line(m)
smpl @all

These programs have not been run on your workfile. _MKDNECONPRVTXN.@coefs(1) assumes C(2) is the first coefficient listed in that equation's output; check it once. The gaps use current-year values (the equations use last year's), which is fine for a visual check.

Methods related to the ECM

The ECM belongs to a family. Some methods are the same model written differently, some are systems of ECMs, some estimate the long run better, and some extend the ECM (asymmetry, regimes, time variation, panels, expectations).

GroupMethodsUse for MKD
Same familyARDL, partial adjustment, KoyckARDL bounds test: best first check with short annual data
System / testsEngle–Granger, Johansen VECM, Bayesian VECMEngle–Granger to test each long run; VECM only for research (data too short)
Long-run estimationDOLS, FMOLS, CCRTest the imposed elasticities (1, 0.3, 0.4…)
ExtensionsNARDL, threshold, Markov switching, time-varying, panel PMG, PACNARDL for price pass-through; PMG with regional peers for short samples

Calculator: from ARDL to ECM

Type the coefficients of an ARDL(1,1) in logs, Y = a + b·Y(−1) + c0·X + c1·X(−1), and see the ECM form.

a   b   c0   c1 



The methods, one by one




R01 ARDL: autoregressive distributed lag Same family

Yt = a + b·Yt−1 + c0·Xt + c1·Xt−1 + εt


Relation to the ECMAn ECM is an ARDL model rearranged. Subtract Yt−1 from both sides and you get: ΔY = −(1−b)·[Yt−1 − θ·Xt−1] + c0·ΔX, with speed λ = 1 − b and long-run elasticity θ = (c0+c1)/(1−b). Use the calculator below.


When it is usedThe standard tool for short samples. The Pesaran–Shin–Smith bounds test tells you whether a long-run relationship exists even if you are not sure whether the series are I(0) or I(1). Lags are chosen automatically (AIC/SIC).


MKD exampleCheck the consumption equation: does the MKD data support a long-run income elasticity of 1 and λ ≈ 0.2?


StrengthRobust in small samples; directly gives the ECM form.
WeaknessMany lags eat degrees of freedom with ~25 annual observations: keep max lags at 1–2.


EViews 
' real disposable income, as in the MKD consumption equation
series YDREAL = (MKDNYYWBTOTLCN*(1-MKDGGREVPITTXN/100) + MKDGGEXPTRNSCN + MKDBXFSTREMTCD*MKDPANUSATLS)/MKDNECONPRVTXN
smpl 2000 2025
equation EQ_C_ARDL.ardl(deplags=2, reglags=2) log(MKDNECONPRVTKN) log(YDREAL)
show EQ_C_ARDL
' In the equation window: View > Coefficient Diagnostics > Long Run Form and Bounds Test
' Compare: long-run coefficient on log(YDREAL) (MFMod imposes 1) and the CointEq(-1) coefficient (MFMod imposes -0.2)
smpl @all
R02 Partial adjustment (and Koyck lags) Same family

Yt = ρ·Yt−1 + (1−ρ)·Y*t


Relation to the ECMAn ECM with no separate short-run terms: the short-run effect of X is forced to be (1−ρ) times the long-run effect. The Koyck distributed lag (effect of X declining geometrically) is the same model.


When it is usedWhen there is no good theory for the short-run dynamics, or for policy rules.


MKD exampleAlready in MKD: policy rate (ρ = C(1)), NAIRU (ρ = 0.98). See tab 5.


StrengthVery simple, stable.
WeaknessShort-run and long-run effects cannot differ independently.


EViews 
' Example: estimate the NAIRU persistence instead of imposing 0.98
smpl 2000 2025
equation EQ_NAIRU_PA.ls MKDLMUNRSTRLCN c MKDLMUNRSTRLCN(-1)
' rho = coefficient on the lag; implied target = c/(1-rho)
show EQ_NAIRU_PA
smpl @all
R03 Engle–Granger two-step System / tests

Step 1: Y = α + θX + u (long run, OLS) · Step 2: ΔY = −λ·ut−1 + γΔX + e


Relation to the ECMThis is exactly how MFMod-type equations are built, one equation at a time: the long run is fixed first, then the dynamics are estimated around it. The test checks that u is stationary (otherwise there is no long-run relation).


When it is usedQuick check of each long-run relation in the model.


MKD exampleTest whether imports, domestic demand and relative prices are cointegrated.


StrengthSimple, transparent.
WeaknessLow power in short samples; only one relation; normalisation matters.


EViews 
smpl 2000 2025
group G_M log(MKDNEIMPGNFSKN) log(MKDNEGDETTOTKN) log(MKDNEIMPGNFSXN/MKDNYGDPFCSTXN)
G_M.coint(method=eg)      ' Engle-Granger test (single-equation cointegration)
smpl @all
R04 Johansen VECM (vector error correction) System / tests

ΔZt = α·β′Zt−1 + Γ·ΔZt−1 + εt


Relation to the ECMThe multi-equation ECM. All variables in Z can adjust (α = speeds for each variable), and the test finds how many long-run relations β exist. MFMod instead assumes which variable adjusts and imposes one relation per equation.


When it is usedResearch questions such as: does the trade balance adjust through imports, exports, or prices?


MKD exampleJoint system of exports, imports, relative prices and partner demand.


StrengthRigorous; tells you which variables do the adjusting.
WeaknessNeeds many observations; with ~25 years and 4 variables results are fragile. Bayesian VECM (priors) helps.


EViews 
smpl 2000 2025
group G_T log(MKDNEEXPGNFSKN) log(MKDXMKT) log(MKDNEIMPGNFSKN) log(MKDNEGDETTOTKN)
G_T.coint(s)              ' Johansen summary over all trend assumptions
' if rank = 1: estimate a VECM
var V_T.ec(c,1) 1 1 G_T
show V_T
smpl @all
R05 DOLS / FMOLS / CCR Long-run estimation

Y = α + θX + Σj=−p..p δjΔXt+j + u  (DOLS)


Relation to the ECMNot a different model, but better estimators of the long-run part θ of the ECM. Leads and lags of ΔX (DOLS) or a nonparametric correction (FMOLS, CCR) remove small-sample bias and endogeneity.


When it is usedChecking the long-run elasticities that MFMod imposes (1, 0.3, 0.4…).


MKD exampleIs the import elasticity to domestic demand really 1, and to relative prices −0.3?


StrengthValid t-tests on long-run coefficients.
WeaknessOnly the long run; dynamics still need an ECM.


EViews 
smpl 2000 2025
equation EQ_M_DOLS.cointreg(method=dols, lag=1, lead=1) log(MKDNEIMPGNFSKN) log(MKDNEGDETTOTKN) log(MKDNEIMPGNFSXN/MKDNYGDPFCSTXN)
equation EQ_M_FMOLS.cointreg(method=fmols) log(MKDNEIMPGNFSKN) log(MKDNEGDETTOTKN) log(MKDNEIMPGNFSXN/MKDNYGDPFCSTXN)
show EQ_M_DOLS
' MFMod imposes: demand = 1, relative price = -0.3
EQ_M_DOLS.wald c(1)=1      ' test elasticity 1 (check which c() is the demand coefficient in the output)
smpl @all
R06 NARDL: asymmetric ECM (Shin, Yu, Greenwood-Nimmo) Extensions

ΔY = −λ[Yt−1 − θ+X+t−1 − θ−X−t−1] + γ+ΔX+ + γ−ΔX−


Relation to the ECMX is split into the cumulative sum of its increases (X+) and decreases (X−), each with its own coefficients. Tests whether up and down movements pass through differently ("rockets and feathers").


When it is usedPrices that rise fast and fall slowly.


MKD examplePass-through of import prices to the consumption deflator: does it differ when world prices rise vs fall?


StrengthCaptures real asymmetries.
WeaknessDoubles the number of coefficients; needs enough ups and downs in the sample.


EViews 
' partial sums of increases and decreases in log import prices
series DPM  = dlog(MKDNEIMPGNFSXN)
series PMUP = @cumsum(@recode(DPM>0, DPM, 0))
series PMDN = @cumsum(@recode(DPM<0, DPM, 0))
smpl 2003 2025
equation EQ_PC_NARDL.ls dlog(MKDNECONPRVTXN) c log(MKDNECONPRVTXN(-1)) PMUP(-1) PMDN(-1) log(MKDNYGDPFCSTXN(-1)) d(PMUP) d(PMDN)
' asymmetry test (long run): -c(3)/c(2) = -c(4)/c(2)  ->  c(3)=c(4)
EQ_PC_NARDL.wald c(3)=c(4)
smpl @all
R07 Threshold ECM (TAR / M-TAR) Extensions

ΔY = −λ1·ut−1·I(|u|>τ) − λ2·ut−1·I(|u|≤τ) + …


Relation to the ECMThe speed of adjustment changes when the gap is larger than a threshold τ: small deviations are tolerated, large ones are corrected fast (menu costs, transaction costs).


When it is usedPrices or rates that react only to big deviations.


MKD exampleWages: does the correction toward productivity speed up when the gap is large?


StrengthNonlinear behaviour with a simple story.
WeaknessFew observations per regime in annual data.


EViews 
' gap of the wage ECM (see card E05), then estimate with a threshold on its lag
series WGAP = log(MKDNEWRTTOTLCN) - log(MKDNYYWBTOTLCN_*MKDNYGDPPOTLKN/MKDLMEMPSTRLCN) - log(MKDNECONPRVTXN)
smpl 2000 2025
equation EQ_W_TAR.threshold dlog(MKDNEWRTTOTLCN) c WGAP(-1) dlog(MKDNECONPRVTXN(-1)) @thresh WGAP(-1)
' or: Quick > Estimate Equation > Method: THRESHOLD
smpl @all
R08 Markov-switching ECM Extensions

ΔY = −λs·ut−1 + γsΔX + …,  s = regime (normal / crisis)


Relation to the ECMCoefficients differ between unobserved regimes, and the model estimates the probability of being in each regime every year.


When it is usedEconomies with crises and calm periods.


MKD exampleConsumption or investment behaviour in crisis years (2008–09, 2020) vs normal years, instead of dummies.


StrengthReplaces ad-hoc dummies with an estimated regime.
WeaknessVery data-hungry; with annual data the regimes are hard to identify.


EViews 
' Quick > Estimate Equation > Method: SWITCHREG (Markov switching), regime-specific: c and the ECM term
smpl 2000 2025
equation EQ_IP_MS.switchreg(type=markov) dlog(MKDNEGDIFPRVKN) c ECMGAP_IP(-1) @nv dlog(MKDNYGDPPOTLKN)
smpl @all
' (run the ECM-gap program from tab 6 first to create ECMGAP_IP)
R09 Time-varying ECM (state space / Kalman filter) Extensions

ΔY = −λt·ut−1 + …,  λt = λt−1 + ηt


Relation to the ECMThe speed (or the long-run coefficients) is allowed to drift slowly over time and is estimated with the Kalman filter.


When it is usedStructural change: the economy is not the same in 2005 and 2025.


MKD exampleExports: did the response to partner demand change after the free zones opened (≈ 2010)?


StrengthShows how behaviour changed.
WeaknessHard to use for forecasting: you must assume the future path of the coefficient.


EViews 
' EViews sspace object (sketch)
sspace SS_X
SS_X.append @signal dlog(MKDNEEXPGNFSKN) = c(1) + sv1*dlog(MKDXMKT) + [var = exp(c(2))]
SS_X.append @state sv1 = sv1(-1) + [var = exp(c(3))]
smpl 2000 2025
SS_X.ml
SS_X.makestates(t=smooth) *_sm     ' sv1_sm = time-varying elasticity
show sv1_sm.line
smpl @all
R10 Panel ECM: pooled mean group (Pesaran, Shin, Smith 1999) Extensions

ΔYit = −λi[Yi,t−1 − θ·Xi,t−1] + γiΔXit + …


Relation to the ECMEstimates the ECM for several countries together: the long run θ is common, the speeds and short-run terms are country-specific.


When it is usedShort national samples: borrow information from similar economies.


MKD exampleEstimate consumption or export elasticities for MKD together with ALB, SRB, BIH, MNE, KOS and new EU members.


StrengthMuch more data for the long run.
WeaknessAssumes the same long run across countries.


EViews 
' Needs a panel workfile (country x year). In EViews: Quick > Estimate Equation
' Method: ARDL, with a panel workfile -> Pooled Mean Group (PMG) is the default panel ARDL estimator
' equation EQ_PMG.ardl(deplags=1, reglags=1) log(C) log(YD)
R11 PAC: polynomial adjustment costs (FRB/US, ECB, Banque de France) Extensions

ΔYt = −λ·ut−1 + Σ ajΔYt−j + Σ bi·EtΔY*t+i


Relation to the ECMA forward-looking ECM: agents adjust toward where the target is expected to be, not only where it was. Mentioned in 01_WhatIsMFMod (history slide) as the modern successor of ECMs.


When it is usedPolicy models where announced future policies (tax changes, EU funds) should affect behaviour before they happen.


MKD exampleInvestment reacting in advance to an announced CIT change or to the EU accession date.


StrengthExpectations without full rational-expectations solving.
WeaknessComplex; needs an expectations block.


EViews 
' Not built into EViews; implemented by projecting the expected target path
' with an auxiliary VAR (FRB/US approach). Main idea in EViews terms:
'   1) estimate a small VAR for the target drivers
'   2) compute the discounted sum of expected future changes in the target
'   3) add that sum as a regressor to the ECM


Before running: these programs have not been run on your workfile. The ardl, cointreg, coint, var commands are standard EViews (version 9 or later); for threshold, switchreg and sspace the menu path is given in case the command options differ in your version. Annual MKD samples are short (≈ 25 observations): treat these as checks of the model's assumptions, not as replacements for its equations.






The other equation types in MFMod MKD


ECMs are only one of seven kinds of equations in the model. Altogether there are 161 equations: 58 behavioural (14 ECM, 31 ratio, 5 tax, 2 logit-share, 6 rules), 10 quasi-identities and 93 identities. The full list, filterable by type, is in the equation catalogue.


TypeNumberGeneral formUsed for
ECM (error correction)14DLOG(Y) = −λ·[LOG(Y(−1)) − long-run target] + short-run termsconsumption, investment, exports, imports, wages, employment, 8 deflators
Ratio (share) equation31Y / BASE = C(1)fiscal spending items (base: revenue − last year's interest), SSC, grants, other revenue; remittances, FDI, portfolio, other investment, capital account (base: GDP); merchandise share of BOP trade; statistical discrepancy; net indirect taxes
Tax equation (base × rate)5TAX = RATE/100 × BASE + C(1)VAT (base C + G nominal), excise (C), customs (imports), PIT (wage bill), CIT (GDP × (1 − labour share))
Logit-share growth equation2@PC(VA) = @LOGIT(C(1)) × @PCY(final demand)agriculture and industry value added (real)
Rule / partial adjustment6Y = ρ·Y(−1) + (1−ρ)·target, or a Phillips curve in growth ratespolicy rate (Taylor rule), NAIRU, GDP deflator (Phillips curve), domestic interest rate (debt premium), CPI (follows the consumption deflator), participation
Quasi-identity (DUMH)10@PC(Y) = @PC(source) + C(1)·DUMHNA public investment and government consumption (follow fiscal data), BOP exports/imports (follow national accounts), debt stocks, unemployment copy, denar/USD (peg)
Identity93Y = A + B − C …, CN = KN × XN, stocks = stocks(−1) + flowsGDP and demand totals, nominal = real × price, capital stock, potential GDP, P*, revenue and spending totals, balances, interest payments, BOP balances, REER/NEER, PXKEY/PMKEY


How they work together


The ECMs carry the economics (behaviour of households, firms, prices, labour). The tax and ratio equations make the fiscal and external accounts follow the economy. Rules describe policy (interest rate) and slow structural variables (NAIRU). Quasi-identities tie different data sources together. Identities make every account add up. When you shock the model, the shock enters through one type and spreads through the others.


2 Ratio (share) equation 31 equations


The simplest behavioural equation: Y keeps its historical share of a base. C(1) is the average share in the estimation sample. In the forecast Y grows exactly with the base, plus the add factor (in ratio units: 0.01 = 1 pp of the base).
Example from equations.prg 
(MKDBFCAFFFDICD/MKDNYGDPMKTPCD) = C(1)
Where: fiscal spending items (base: revenue − last year's interest), SSC, grants, other revenue; remittances, FDI, portfolio, other investment, capital account (base: GDP); merchandise share of BOP trade; statistical discrepancy; net indirect taxes


How to shock it: {
"Ratio (share) equation":"add factor in ratio units (method A), or exclude it and set the level (method C).",
"Tax equation (base × rate)":"change the exogenous rate in pp (method D); keep spending fixed if you want the revenue saved.",
"Logit-share growth equation":"DLOG-type add factor on growth (log points).",
"Rule / partial adjustment":"exclude the variable and set its path (method C), or shift the add factor (level units, e.g. pp for rates).",
"Quasi-identity (DUMH)":"shock the source variable (e.g. fiscal capex), or exclude the quasi-identity.",
"Identity":"cannot be shocked; shock a component."}[a]} 🎯 How to shock
3 Tax equation (base × rate) 5 equations


Revenue = effective rate × tax base. The rate (…XN) is exogenous, so tax policy is shocked by changing the rate in percentage points. C(1) is a constant (collection gap). Revenue follows the economy automatically through the base: these are the model's automatic stabilisers.
Example from equations.prg 
MKDGGREVGNFSCN = (MKDGGREVGNFSXN/100 * (MKDNECONPRVTCN+MKDNECONGOVTCN)) + C(1)
Where: VAT (base C + G nominal), excise (C), customs (imports), PIT (wage bill), CIT (GDP × (1 − labour share))


How to shock it: {
"Ratio (share) equation":"add factor in ratio units (method A), or exclude it and set the level (method C).",
"Tax equation (base × rate)":"change the exogenous rate in pp (method D); keep spending fixed if you want the revenue saved.",
"Logit-share growth equation":"DLOG-type add factor on growth (log points).",
"Rule / partial adjustment":"exclude the variable and set its path (method C), or shift the add factor (level units, e.g. pp for rates).",
"Quasi-identity (DUMH)":"shock the source variable (e.g. fiscal capex), or exclude the quasi-identity.",
"Identity":"cannot be shocked; shock a component."}[a]} 🎯 How to shock
4 Logit-share growth equation 2 equations


Sector growth is a fraction (between 0 and 1, forced by @LOGIT) of the growth of final demand. Services is the residual (GDP − agriculture − industry − net taxes), so the three sectors always add up.
Example from equations.prg 
@PC(MKDNVINDTOTLKN) = @LOGIT(C(1))*@PCY(MKDNECONPRVTKN+MKDNECONGOVTKN+MKDNEGDIFTOTKN+MKDNEEXPGNFSKN)
Where: agriculture and industry value added (real)


How to shock it: {
"Ratio (share) equation":"add factor in ratio units (method A), or exclude it and set the level (method C).",
"Tax equation (base × rate)":"change the exogenous rate in pp (method D); keep spending fixed if you want the revenue saved.",
"Logit-share growth equation":"DLOG-type add factor on growth (log points).",
"Rule / partial adjustment":"exclude the variable and set its path (method C), or shift the add factor (level units, e.g. pp for rates).",
"Quasi-identity (DUMH)":"shock the source variable (e.g. fiscal capex), or exclude the quasi-identity.",
"Identity":"cannot be shocked; shock a component."}[a]} 🎯 How to shock
5 Rule / partial adjustment 6 equations


Behavioural, but written as a policy or adjustment rule rather than an ECM. Several coefficients are imposed (1.2 inflation response, 0.98 NAIRU persistence, 5 × debt above 60% of GDP). See tab 5.
Example from equations.prg 
MKDINTRDXN = C(1) + C(2)*MKDFMLBLPOLYXN + 5*(MKDGGDBTTOTLCN/MKDNYGDPMKTPCN - 0.6)
Where: policy rate (Taylor rule), NAIRU, GDP deflator (Phillips curve), domestic interest rate (debt premium), CPI (follows the consumption deflator), participation


How to shock it: {
"Ratio (share) equation":"add factor in ratio units (method A), or exclude it and set the level (method C).",
"Tax equation (base × rate)":"change the exogenous rate in pp (method D); keep spending fixed if you want the revenue saved.",
"Logit-share growth equation":"DLOG-type add factor on growth (log points).",
"Rule / partial adjustment":"exclude the variable and set its path (method C), or shift the add factor (level units, e.g. pp for rates).",
"Quasi-identity (DUMH)":"shock the source variable (e.g. fiscal capex), or exclude the quasi-identity.",
"Identity":"cannot be shocked; shock a component."}[a]} 🎯 How to shock
6 Quasi-identity (DUMH) 10 equations


An accounting link between two sources that measure almost the same thing but differ in the data (fiscal vs national accounts, BOP vs NA). DUMH = 1 in history, so C(1) absorbs the average difference; DUMH = 0 in the forecast, so the link becomes exact and the add factor is set to 0.
Example from equations.prg 
@PC(MKDNECONGOVTCN) = @PC(MKDGGEXPGNFSCN+MKDGGEXPWAGECN) + C(1)*DUMH
Where: NA public investment and government consumption (follow fiscal data), BOP exports/imports (follow national accounts), debt stocks, unemployment copy, denar/USD (peg)


How to shock it: {
"Ratio (share) equation":"add factor in ratio units (method A), or exclude it and set the level (method C).",
"Tax equation (base × rate)":"change the exogenous rate in pp (method D); keep spending fixed if you want the revenue saved.",
"Logit-share growth equation":"DLOG-type add factor on growth (log points).",
"Rule / partial adjustment":"exclude the variable and set its path (method C), or shift the add factor (level units, e.g. pp for rates).",
"Quasi-identity (DUMH)":"shock the source variable (e.g. fiscal capex), or exclude the quasi-identity.",
"Identity":"cannot be shocked; shock a component."}[a]} 🎯 How to shock
7 Identity 93 equations


Pure accounting or definitions: always hold exactly, have no coefficients and no add factor (MKD.APPEND @IDENTITY). They cannot be shocked directly: shock a component.
Example from equations.prg 
MKDNEGDIKSTKKN = MKDNEGDIKSTKKN(-1)*(1-MKDDEPR) + MKDNEGDIFTOTKN - MKDNEGDISTKBKN
Where: GDP and demand totals, nominal = real × price, capital stock, potential GDP, P*, revenue and spending totals, balances, interest payments, BOP balances, REER/NEER, PXKEY/PMKEY


How to shock it: {
"Ratio (share) equation":"add factor in ratio units (method A), or exclude it and set the level (method C).",
"Tax equation (base × rate)":"change the exogenous rate in pp (method D); keep spending fixed if you want the revenue saved.",
"Logit-share growth equation":"DLOG-type add factor on growth (log points).",
"Rule / partial adjustment":"exclude the variable and set its path (method C), or shift the add factor (level units, e.g. pp for rates).",
"Quasi-identity (DUMH)":"shock the source variable (e.g. fiscal capex), or exclude the quasi-identity.",
"Identity":"cannot be shocked; shock a component."}[a]} 🎯 How to shock










📐 Econometrics & statistics for MFMod


All the econometric and statistical knowledge needed to understand, judge and use the MKD model, in plain language: the maths behind the equations, regression and EViews output, diagnostic tests, stationarity and cointegration, filters, how the model is solved, and how forecasts are evaluated. Every topic has an MKD example and the EViews command.






What you need to know, and where it is used in the model


You do not need a PhD to understand MFMod. You need about ten ideas. This table tells you which idea is used where, so you can learn them in the order the model needs them.


#TopicWhy you need it in MFModTabLevel


1Logs, growth rates, elasticities, %, ppEvery equation is in logs (DLOG); every result is a % or pp deviation2Essential


2Real, nominal, deflators, contributionsCN = KN × XN; GDP growth decomposition2Essential


3OLS regression and reading EViews outputEvery behavioural equation is estimated with .LS3Essential


4Dummies, trends, samples, imposed coefficients@DURING, T_LR, DUMH, numbers fixed by the modeller3Essential


5Diagnostic testsJudging whether an equation is acceptable4Important


6Stationarity, unit roots, cointegrationWhy equations are written as ECMs5Important


7Error-correction models14 core equations🔁 ECM sectionEssential


8HP filter, Solow residual, Cobb-Douglas, perpetual inventoryPotential GDP, TFP, capital, NAIRU, output gap6Important


9Model solution: Gauss-Seidel, add factors, scenarios, multipliersEvery forecast and every shock7Essential


10Forecast evaluationChecking how good the model is8Useful


Suggested route for a beginner: tab 2 → tab 3 → ECM tab 1 → tab 7 → 🎯 How to shock. Then tabs 4, 5, 6 when you want to judge or change equations. Test yourself in tab 10.


The basic maths behind every equation
Click a topic to open it.
Natural logarithm and why the model uses logs


LOG(X) in EViews is the natural logarithm (base e ≈ 2.718).


PropertyUse in MFMod


log(A × B) = log A + log Blog(nominal) = log(real) + log(price), so CN = KN × XN becomes additive


log(A / B) = log A − log Brelative prices, ratios (C/income) in the ECM long run


log(Aα) = α·log ACobb-Douglas: log Y* = log TFP + α·log L + (1−α)·log K


Coefficient in a log-log equation = elasticity"income elasticity of consumption = 1"
Growth rates: @PC, DLOG and the approximation


MeasureFormulaEViewsExample: 100 → 110


Percentage change(Xt/Xt−1 − 1) × 100@PC(X) (or @PCY = year-on-year)10.0%


Log differencelog Xt − log Xt−1DLOG(X)0.0953 (≈ 9.5%)


For small changes DLOG ≈ growth rate (0.02 ≈ 2%). For large changes they differ: convert with growth = eDLOG − 1. That is why a +10% shock needs an add factor of LOG(1.10), not 0.10 (see 🎯 How to shock).


Compounding: 2% a year for 10 years = 1.0210 − 1 = 21.9%, not 20%. Average annual growth (CAGR) = (Xend/Xstart)1/n − 1.
Elasticity, semi-elasticity, multiplier


ConceptMeaningMKD example


Elasticity% change in Y for a 1% change in X (log-log)imports to domestic demand = 1 in the long run


Semi-elasticity% change in Y for a 1-unit (pp) change in Xconsumption −0.2 × Δ real interest rate: +1 pp → C growth −0.2 pp


Short-run vs long-run elasticityImmediate effect vs effect after full adjustmentexports: short-run C(5) to XMKT, long-run 1


MultiplierΔ GDP ÷ Δ spending (both in money units or % of GDP)public investment +1% of GDP → GDP +x% in year 1 (see scenario S22)
Percent (%) vs percentage points (pp)


% is a relative change; pp is a difference between two rates.


Unemployment 15% → 14% is −1 pp but −6.7%. VAT 18% → 19% is +1 pp. In MFMod results: levels (GDP, consumption) are reported as % deviation from baseline; rates and ratios (unemployment, balance % GDP, inflation) as pp deviation.
Real, nominal, deflators, base years


SuffixMeaningExample


KNReal = constant prices (volume)MKDNECONPRVTKN


CNNominal = current prices (value)MKDNECONPRVTCN


XNDeflator = CN ÷ KN (price index, base year = 1 or 100)MKDNECONPRVTXN


Growth of nominal ≈ growth of real + growth of the deflator (exactly in logs). The GDP deflator covers everything produced; the CPI covers what households buy (in MKD the CPI follows the consumption deflator). Chain-linked real series are not additive: real GDP may differ slightly from the sum of real components, which is why there is a statistical discrepancy.
Contributions to growth and to deflator growth


Contribution of component C to GDP growth = ΔCt ÷ GDPt−1 × 100. The contributions add up to GDP growth (imports with a minus sign).


Deflator growth is a weighted average of component deflator growth, weights = real shares (see 🎓 07 · Accounting links).
smpl 2010 2035
series CONT_C = d(MKDNECONPRVTKN)/MKDNYGDPMKTPKN(-1)*100
series CONT_G = d(MKDNECONGOVTKN)/MKDNYGDPMKTPKN(-1)*100
series CONT_I = d(MKDNEGDIFTOTKN)/MKDNYGDPMKTPKN(-1)*100
series CONT_X = d(MKDNEEXPGNFSKN)/MKDNYGDPMKTPKN(-1)*100
series CONT_M = -d(MKDNEIMPGNFSKN)/MKDNYGDPMKTPKN(-1)*100
show @pc(MKDNYGDPMKTPKN) CONT_C CONT_G CONT_I CONT_X CONT_M
smpl @all
Index numbers and weights


An index sets a base year = 100 (or 1): Xt/Xbase × 100. MKD uses @elem(X,2010) to rebase (REER, NEER) and fixed weights for the export market (XMKT) and the commodity price indices (PXKEY, PMKEY). A weighted index = Σ weighti × indexi, with weights summing to 1 (or 100).
🧪 Test it in EViews · See the maths on real data


What it checks: @PC vs DLOG on real GDP (the approximation error), and nominal = real + deflator in log growth.
What you should see: @PC and DLOG almost identical except in big years (2020); the nominal/real/deflator check PASS.

OLS regression: what EViews does with .LS


Ordinary least squares chooses the coefficients that make the sum of squared residuals (actual − fitted)² as small as possible. In MFMod every behavioural equation is estimated this way: equation _NAME.LS(OPTMETHOD=LEGACY) ….


Residual = actual − fitted value in history. In the forecast the residual becomes the add factor (your judgement).


Reading an EViews output, line by line


The numbers below are illustrative (made up to show the layout), not your MKD estimates. Open a real equation with its EViews button.


Dependent Variable: DLOG(MKDNEIMPGNFSKN)
Method: Least Squares
Sample (adjusted): 2004 2025
Included observations: 22 after adjustments
DLOG(MKDNEIMPGNFSKN) = -C(2)*(LOG(MKDNEIMPGNFSKN(-1)) - ...) + C(5) + ...

             Coefficient   Std. Error   t-Statistic   Prob.
C(2)          0.350        0.110         3.18         0.0055     <- (1)(2)(3)(4)
C(5)          0.012        0.008         1.50         0.1510
C(10)        -0.150        0.040        -3.75         0.0016

R-squared            0.82    Mean dependent var     0.051       <- (5)
Adjusted R-squared   0.79    S.D. dependent var     0.072
S.E. of regression   0.033   Akaike info criterion -3.85        <- (6)(8)
Sum squared resid    0.019   Schwarz criterion     -3.61
Log likelihood       44.3    Hannan-Quinn criter.  -3.79
Durbin-Watson stat   1.92                                       <- (7)


#ItemMeaningRule of thumb


1CoefficientEstimated effect. Here C(2) = λ, the ECM speedSign and size must make economic sense


2Std. ErrorUncertainty of the estimateSmall relative to the coefficient = precise


3t-StatisticCoefficient ÷ std. error|t| > 2 ≈ significant at 5%


4Prob. (p-value)Probability of a coefficient this large if the true value were 0< 0.05 = significant; < 0.10 = weakly


5R² / adjusted R²Share of the variation of the left-hand side explainedFor growth (DLOG) equations 0.4–0.8 is normal; a high R² alone means little


6S.E. of regressionTypical size of the residual0.033 in a DLOG equation ≈ 3.3% typical error per year


7Durbin–WatsonFirst-order autocorrelation of residuals≈ 2 good; < 1.5 suspicious (use the LM test, tab 4)


8Akaike / SchwarzFit penalised for the number of coefficientsLower = better when comparing specifications


Things you will see in MKD equations


ElementEViewsMeaning


Estimated coefficientC(n)Value chosen by OLS


Imposed (calibrated) coefficienta number, e.g. -0.2*, 0.3*Fixed by the modeller; not estimated, no standard error. Used when data are too short or give nonsense signs.


Restriction(1-C(3)), @LOGIT(C(1))Forces weights to sum to 1 or lie between 0 and 1


Dummy@DURING("2020")1 in that year, 0 otherwise: removes a one-off event from the estimate


History dummyDUMH1 in history, 0 in forecast (quasi-identities)


TrendT_LRRises in history, flat in the forecast


Samplesmpl 2004 2025 before .LSYears used for estimation; many MKD equations stop in 2019 (before COVID)


Wald test: is a coefficient equal to a value?


Use it to test an imposed value against the data, e.g. "is the ECM speed of imports 0.3?" or "do two weights sum to 1?"


' Is the estimated import ECM speed C(2) different from 0.3?
_MKDNEIMPGNFSKN.wald c(2)=0.3
' p-value > 0.05 -> the data do not reject 0.3

Diagnostic tests: is the equation acceptable?


Every test has a null hypothesis (H0), the "nothing wrong" case. A small p-value (< 0.05) rejects H0, i.e. signals a problem. With ~20–25 annual observations tests have low power: use them as warnings, together with economic sense and simulation properties.


TestH0 (no problem)Problem if p < 0.05EViews (on an equation)What to do


Breusch–Godfrey LMNo autocorrelation of residualsResiduals are correlated: dynamics missingeq.auto(2)Add lags or ECM term; check dummies


Breusch–Pagan–Godfrey / WhiteConstant residual varianceHeteroskedasticity: standard errors wrongeq.hettest(type=bpg)Robust (HAC) standard errors: .LS(cov=hac)


Jarque–BeraResiduals are normalOutliers / skewnesseq.histLook for one-off years → dummy


Ramsey RESETFunctional form is correctMissing nonlinearity or variableeq.reset(1)Logs, ratios, extra variable


Chow breakpointSame coefficients before and after a dateStructural breakeq.chow 2009Split sample, dummy, or trend


CUSUM / CUSUM of squaresStable coefficientsLine leaves the 5% bandseq.rls(c) / eq.rls(q)Same as Chow


Recursive coefficients–Coefficient drifts as years are addedeq.rls(r)Consider imposing a value


WaldCoefficient = a valueData reject the imposed valueeq.wald c(2)=0.3Re-think calibration


Problems specific to macro models


ProblemMeaningIn MKD


Small sampleFew observations → imprecise estimates, low test power~20–25 annual points; that is why many coefficients are imposed


MulticollinearityRegressors move together → individual coefficients unstableincome and GDP, domestic and import prices


Endogeneity / simultaneityA regressor is itself caused by Y → OLS biasedconsumption and income (C is part of GDP). Solutions: lags, instruments (TSLS), imposing theory


Spurious regressionTwo trending series look related when they are nottab 5


Overfitting with dummiesToo many dummies make the fit perfect but the forecast poorcheck how many @DURING terms an equation has


Lucas critiqueBehaviour changes when policy changeslarge reforms (EU accession) may change coefficients


' Full diagnostic set for one equation (example: imports)
_MKDNEIMPGNFSKN.auto(2)
_MKDNEIMPGNFSKN.hettest(type=bpg)
_MKDNEIMPGNFSKN.hist
_MKDNEIMPGNFSKN.reset(1)
_MKDNEIMPGNFSKN.rls(c)
_MKDNEIMPGNFSKN.chow 2009
These are equation views. In the equation window the same tests are under View → Residual Diagnostics / Stability Diagnostics / Coefficient Diagnostics.

What it checks: Serial correlation, heteroskedasticity, normality, functional form, stability (CUSUM, recursive coefficients, Chow 2009) for one equation.
What you should see: p-values above 0.05 for LM, BPG, JB, RESET and Chow; CUSUM lines inside the 5% bands; recursive coefficients roughly flat.

Stationarity: the key idea of time-series econometrics


ConceptMeaningMKD example


Stationary, I(0)Fluctuates around a constant mean; shocks fadegrowth rates, inflation, output gap, unemployment gap


Non-stationary, I(1) (unit root)Wanders without returning; shocks are permanent; its difference is stationarylog GDP, log consumption, log prices


Trend-stationaryStationary around a deterministic trendsometimes log TFP


Random walkXt = Xt−1 + shock: the simplest I(1)– 


Unit-root tests


TestH0ReadEViews


ADF (augmented Dickey–Fuller)Unit root (non-stationary)p < 0.05 → stationaryX.uroot(adf)


Phillips–PerronUnit rootp < 0.05 → stationaryX.uroot(pp)


KPSSStationary (opposite H0!)statistic above critical value → non-stationaryX.uroot(kpss)


Run them in levels and in differences: if the level has a unit root and the difference does not, the series is I(1).


Spurious regression


Regressing one I(1) series on another unrelated I(1) series often gives a high R² and "significant" t-statistics by pure chance (Granger–Newbold). A very high R² with a very low Durbin–Watson is the classic warning sign. That is why MFMod does not regress levels on levels with OLS.


Cointegration: the solution


Two I(1) series are cointegrated if a combination of them is stationary: they wander, but together. Example: log consumption and log income both trend up, but log(C/income) is stable. The stationary combination is the long-run relation; its deviation is the equilibrium error.


Granger representation theorem: if series are cointegrated, there is an error-correction model linking them. This is the theoretical reason every important MKD equation is an ECM: DLOG on the left (stationary), the lagged equilibrium error on the right (stationary), so the regression is valid. Details in 🔁 ECMs & other models.


Cointegration testEViews


Engle–Granger (residual-based)group.coint(method=eg)


Johansen (system, number of relations)group.coint(s)


ARDL bounds testARDL equation → View → Long Run Form and Bounds Test


' Unit-root tests on log real consumption: level and first difference
smpl 2000 2025
series LC = log(MKDNECONPRVTKN)
LC.uroot(adf, trend)        ' level, with trend: expect a unit root (p > 0.05)
LC.uroot(adf, dif=1)        ' first difference: expect stationary (p < 0.05)
LC.uroot(kpss)              ' KPSS: H0 = stationary
' Is the consumption equilibrium error stationary? (needs ECMGAP_C from the ECM section)
ECMGAP_C.uroot(adf)
smpl @all
Other time-series ideas you will meet


IdeaMeaning


Lag operator, ARDLX(−1), X(−2): past values; models with lags of Y and X


Autocorrelation (ACF)Correlation of a series with its own past: X.correl(5)


Persistence / half-lifeHow long shocks last: ln 0.5 / ln ρ


Granger causalityDoes X help predict Y beyond Y's own past? group.cause(2) (predictive, not true causality)


VAREvery variable regressed on lags of all variables; MFMod is a theory-restricted version
🧪 Test it in EViews · Test stationarity and cointegration


What it checks: ADF (level with trend, first difference), KPSS, ADF on the consumption gap, and an Engle–Granger test of consumption vs income.
What you should see: Unit root not rejected in the level, rejected in the difference; the gap closer to stationary than the levels. With ≈ 25 observations, treat results as indicative.

Statistics behind the supply side


Hodrick–Prescott (HP) filter


Splits a series into a smooth trend and a cycle by minimising: Σ(X − trend)² + λ × Σ(Δ²trend)². A large λ gives a smoother trend.


Data frequencyUsual λ
Annual100 (MKD) or 6.25
Quarterly1600
Monthly14400


Used in MKD for: smoothing TFP, participation and NAIRU in readdat.prg (λ = 100), after extending the series into the forecast so the end of the sample is not distorted.


Weakness: end-point problem. The last years of the trend move a lot when new data arrive. That is why the series are extended before filtering.
smpl 2000 2025
hpf(lambda=100) log(MKDNYGDPMKTPKN) LGDP_HP     ' trend of log GDP
series GAP_HP = (log(MKDNYGDPMKTPKN) - LGDP_HP)*100
show GAP_HP MKDNYGDPGAP_                          ' compare with the model's production-function gap
smpl @all
Cobb-Douglas production function and the Solow residual


Y = A · Lα · K1−α. In logs: log Y = log A + α·log L + (1−α)·log K. With constant returns, α = labour share of income (MKD: 0.59).


Solow residual = TFP = what is left of output growth after labour and capital: Δlog A = Δlog Y − α·Δlog L − (1−α)·Δlog K. It is measured, not estimated, so it absorbs measurement errors and the business cycle; that is why it is then HP-filtered.


Details and MKD numbers in ⚙ Supply side.
Perpetual inventory method (capital stock)


Kt = (1 − δ)·Kt−1 + It, with δ = 5% in MKD. The unknown starting stock is set so that the capital/output ratio is stable after ~15 years (initial K ≈ 2.23 × GDP in 2000). See ⚙ Supply side → Capital.
Steady state and balanced growth


In the steady state all real variables grow at the same rate and all ratios (C/Y, I/Y, K/Y, M/demand) are constant. With Cobb-Douglas, long-run growth ≈ TFP growth ÷ α + growth of employment (MKD ≈ 2.4%). ECM long-run relations are exactly these constant ratios.
Marginal cost, markups and the Phillips curve


Firms set prices as a markup over marginal cost; with Cobb-Douglas, marginal cost P* depends on wages, TFP and the capital/output ratio (identity MKDPSTAR). The Phillips curve links inflation to its own past, expected inflation, marginal-cost growth and the output gap.
🧪 Test it in EViews · Compare filters and gaps


What it checks: HP trends (λ = 100 and 6.25), the HP gap vs the model's production-function gap, and raw vs filtered TFP.
What you should see: λ = 6.25 follows GDP more closely; both gaps share the cycle but differ at the end of the sample (end-point problem); filtered TFP smooth through the raw residual.

From equations to a forecast: how a model is solved


A model is a system of simultaneous equations


GDP depends on consumption, consumption depends on income, income depends on GDP… The model must find values for all 161 variables that satisfy all equations at the same time, year by year.
Solution algorithms: Gauss–Seidel and Newton


MethodHow it worksEViews option


Gauss–SeidelSolve each equation in turn using the latest values of the others; repeat until nothing changes more than the toleranceo=g (MKD default)


NewtonSolve all equations together with derivatives; faster near the solution, more robust for strongly linked blockso=n


BroydenNewton with approximate derivativeso=b


Convergence: the solution is accepted when changes are smaller than the tolerance (c=1e-6). If it fails: check for missing data, impossible values (log of a negative number), or an explosive equation.
Dynamic vs static, deterministic vs stochastic


OptionMeaning


Dynamic (s=d)Uses the model's own solution for lagged variables: what a real forecast does


Static (s=s)Uses actual data for lags: a one-step-ahead check in history


Deterministic (d=d)No random shocks: one path


Stochastic (d=s)Draws random residuals many times: gives confidence bands (fan charts)
Add factors, baseline, scenarios


History: solving with add factors = residuals reproduces the data exactly. Forecast: add factors carry the judgement (MKD: decay ×0.85). A scenario changes inputs (overrides, excludes, add factors) and is compared with the baseline. Details: 15. Solve, 🎯 How to shock, 🔁 ECM → Add factors.
Measuring results: deviations, multipliers, impulse responses


MeasureFormula


% deviation (levels)(scenario ÷ baseline − 1) × 100


pp deviation (rates, ratios)scenario − baseline


Fiscal multiplierΔ GDP ÷ Δ spending (both in denars or % of GDP)


Impulse response (IRF)Path of deviations after a one-time shock


Cumulative multiplierΣ Δ GDP ÷ Σ Δ spending over n years
Model properties to check (simulation diagnostics)


A model can have good equations and still behave badly as a system. Check: does it converge back to baseline after a temporary shock? Are long-run ratios stable? Are multipliers plausible (fiscal 0.3–1.0 in a small open economy)? Does a permanent price shock leave real variables unchanged in the long run (neutrality)? MKD programs: convergence.prg, convergence_check.prg.
🧪 Test it in EViews · Impulse response and fiscal multiplier


What it checks: A one-year public-investment shock: impulse responses of the main variables and the impact and cumulative multipliers.
What you should see: GDP jumps in 2027 and returns towards baseline; the cumulative multiplier rises and then levels off; a permanently slightly higher capital stock.


 Paste into a new EViews program (File → New → Program) in the MKD workfile and press Run. Results open as a dashboard and a spool (all tables and graphs). Objects start with K7_; remove them with delete K7_*.


' ==============================================================================
'  MFMod MKD  |  TEST K7: Impulse response and multiplier
'  Purpose : Temporary public-investment shock (+1% of GDP in 2027): impulse responses and fiscal multipliers
'  Needs   : Baseline solved (actual series = baseline, *_0 series exist).
'  Output  : spool K7_SPOOL (tables + graphs) and dashboard K7_DASH
'  Clean up: delete K7_*
' ==============================================================================
%hs = "2010"      ' first year shown
%fs = "2026"      ' first forecast year (shaded area)
%fe = "2035"      ' last year shown
spool K7_SPOOL
smpl @all

' ---- Scenario --------------------------------------------------------------
MKD.scenario(n, a=51, i="baseline", c) "K7 capex 2027"
MKD.scenario "K7 capex 2027"
MKD.exclude MKDGGEXPCAPTCN
MKD.override MKDGGEXPCAPTCN
smpl @all
series MKDGGEXPCAPTCN_51 = MKDGGEXPCAPTCN_0
smpl 2027 2027
MKDGGEXPCAPTCN_51 = MKDGGEXPCAPTCN_0 + 0.01*MKDNYGDPMKTPCN_0
smpl 2026 @last
MKD.solve(s=d,d=d,o=g,i=a,c=1e-6)
smpl @all
series K7_MULT = (MKDNYGDPMKTPCN_51-MKDNYGDPMKTPCN_0)/(MKDGGEXPCAPTCN_51-MKDGGEXPCAPTCN_0)
K7_MULT.displayname Impact multiplier (nominal)
smpl 2027 2035
series K7_CUM = @cumsum(MKDNYGDPMKTPCN_51-MKDNYGDPMKTPCN_0)/@elem(MKDGGEXPCAPTCN_51-MKDGGEXPCAPTCN_0,"2027")
K7_CUM.displayname Cumulative multiplier
smpl @all

' ---- Graphs: scenario vs baseline (deviations) -----------------------------
spool K7_SPOOL
smpl @all
series K7_GDP = (MKDNYGDPMKTPKN_51/MKDNYGDPMKTPKN_0-1)*100
K7_GDP.displayname Real GDP, % dev.
series K7_C = (MKDNECONPRVTKN_51/MKDNECONPRVTKN_0-1)*100
K7_C.displayname Private consumption, % dev.
series K7_I = (MKDNEGDIFPRVKN_51/MKDNEGDIFPRVKN_0-1)*100
K7_I.displayname Private investment, % dev.
series K7_X = (MKDNEEXPGNFSKN_51/MKDNEEXPGNFSKN_0-1)*100
K7_X.displayname Exports, % dev.
series K7_M = (MKDNEIMPGNFSKN_51/MKDNEIMPGNFSKN_0-1)*100
K7_M.displayname Imports, % dev.
series K7_CPI = (MKDFPCPITOTLXN_51/MKDFPCPITOTLXN_0-1)*100
K7_CPI.displayname CPI level, % dev.
series K7_UNR = MKDLMUNRTOTLCN_51-MKDLMUNRTOTLCN_0
K7_UNR.displayname Unemployment rate, pp dev.
series K7_BAL = (MKDGGBALOVRLCN_51/MKDNYGDPMKTPCN_51-MKDGGBALOVRLCN_0/MKDNYGDPMKTPCN_0)*100
K7_BAL.displayname Fiscal balance % GDP, pp dev.
series K7_DEBT = (MKDGGDBTTOTLCN_51/MKDNYGDPMKTPCN_51-MKDGGDBTTOTLCN_0/MKDNYGDPMKTPCN_0)*100
K7_DEBT.displayname Public debt % GDP, pp dev.
series K7_CA = (MKDBNCABFUNDCD_51/MKDNYGDPMKTPCD_51-MKDBNCABFUNDCD_0/MKDNYGDPMKTPCD_0)*100
K7_CA.displayname Current account % GDP, pp dev.
series K7_LV0 = MKDNYGDPMKTPKN_0
K7_LV0.displayname Real GDP, baseline
series K7_LV1 = MKDNYGDPMKTPKN_51
K7_LV1.displayname Real GDP, scenario
smpl 2024 2035
group K7_G1 K7_GDP K7_C K7_I K7_X K7_M
freeze(K7_GR1) K7_G1.line
K7_GR1.addtext(t) "Public investment +1% GDP (2027 only): demand, % deviation from baseline"
K7_GR1.draw(shade, bottom) 2026 2035
K7_GR1.draw(line, left) 0
K7_SPOOL.append K7_GR1
smpl 2024 2035
group K7_G2 K7_CPI K7_UNR
freeze(K7_GR2) K7_G2.line
K7_GR2.addtext(t) "Public investment +1% GDP (2027 only): prices (%) and unemployment (pp)"
K7_GR2.draw(shade, bottom) 2026 2035
K7_GR2.draw(line, left) 0
K7_SPOOL.append K7_GR2
smpl 2024 2035
group K7_G3 K7_BAL K7_DEBT K7_CA
freeze(K7_GR3) K7_G3.line
K7_GR3.addtext(t) "Public investment +1% GDP (2027 only): public finance and external, pp of GDP"
K7_GR3.draw(shade, bottom) 2026 2035

K7_SPOOL.append K7_GR3
smpl 2024 2035
group K7_G4 K7_LV0 K7_LV1
freeze(K7_GR4) K7_G4.line

K7_GR4.draw(shade, bottom) 2026 2035

How good is the forecast?


MeasureFormulaRead


Bias (mean error)mean(actual − forecast)≠ 0 → systematic over- or under-forecasting


MAEmean |actual − forecast|typical error, same units


RMSE√ mean (actual − forecast)²like MAE but punishes large errors


MAPEmean |error ÷ actual| × 100% error (avoid when values near 0)


Theil URMSE of model ÷ RMSE of a naive forecast< 1 → better than "no change"


Type of testMeaning


In-sample fitHow well equations explain the data they were estimated on (always looks good)


Out-of-sample / pseudo real-timeEstimate up to year T, forecast T+1…T+h, compare with actual data. The honest test.


Historical (dynamic) simulationSolve the whole model over history without add factors: does it track GDP, inflation, the CA?


' Dynamic historical simulation of the whole model, add factors set to zero
MKD.scenario(n, a=h) "History no AF"
MKD.scenario "History no AF"
smpl 2012 2025
MKD.addinit(v=z) @stochastic     ' zero add factors in this scenario
MKD.solve(s=d,d=d,o=g,c=1e-6)
series ERR_GDP = (MKDNYGDPMKTPKN - MKDNYGDPMKTPKN_h)/MKDNYGDPMKTPKN*100
scalar RMSE_GDP = @sqrt(@mean(ERR_GDP^2))
show ERR_GDP
smpl @all
Check first that addinit writes into the scenario's add factors and not the baseline ones; if unsure, run it on a copy of the workfile.


Uncertainty


Every forecast is uncertain: equation errors, coefficient uncertainty, wrong assumptions (world demand, prices), data revisions. Show it with scenarios (upside/downside), stochastic simulation (fan charts), or historical forecast errors (± RMSE bands).
🧪 Test it in EViews · Test the forecast out of sample


What it checks: Estimates the import equation only to 2018, forecasts 2019–2025 dynamically, and compares with the actual data and with a naive forecast.
What you should see: Bias, MAE, RMSE and Theil U in a table; Theil U below 1 means the equation beats the naive forecast. 2020–2022 (COVID) will dominate the errors.


 Paste into a new EViews program (File → New → Program) in the MKD workfile and press Run. Results open as a dashboard and a spool (all tables and graphs). Objects start with K8_; remove them with delete K8_*.


' ==============================================================================
'  MFMod MKD  |  TEST K8: Out-of-sample forecast test
'  Purpose : Re-estimates the import equation to 2018 and forecasts 2019-2025 dynamically
'  Needs   : Data loaded.
'  Output  : spool K8_SPOOL (tables + graphs) and dashboard K8_DASH
'  Clean up: delete K8_*
' ==============================================================================
%hs = "2010"      ' first year shown
%fs = "2019"      ' first forecast year (shaded area)
%fe = "2025"      ' last year shown
spool K8_SPOOL
smpl @all
smpl 2004 2018
equation K8_EQ.ls DLOG(MKDNEIMPGNFSKN) = -C(2)*(LOG(MKDNEIMPGNFSKN(-1))-LOG(MKDNEGDETTOTKN(-1))+0.3*LOG(MKDNEIMPGNFSXN(-1)/(MKDNYGDPFCSTXN(-1))))-0.4*DLOG(MKDNEIMPGNFSXN/MKDNYGDPFCSTXN)+C(5)+0.8*DLOG(MKDNYGDPPOTLKN)+C(10)*@DURING("2009")
freeze(K8_OUT) K8_EQ.output
K8_SPOOL.append K8_OUT
smpl 2019 2025
K8_EQ.forecast(d) K8_F
K8_F.displayname Forecast (dynamic, estimated to 2018)
smpl @all
series K8_A = MKDNEIMPGNFSKN
K8_A.displayname Actual imports
series K8_N = @recode(@year>2018, @elem(MKDNEIMPGNFSKN,"2018"), MKDNEIMPGNFSKN)
K8_N.displayname Naive: no change from 2018
smpl 2019 2025
series K8_E = (K8_A-K8_F)/K8_A*100
series K8_EN = (K8_A-K8_N)/K8_A*100
table(6,3) K8_ACC
K8_ACC(1,1) = "Measure (% error)"
K8_ACC(1,2) = "Model"
K8_ACC(1,3) = "Naive"
K8_ACC(2,1) = "Bias (mean error)"
K8_ACC(2,2) = @mean(K8_E)
K8_ACC(2,3) = @mean(K8_EN)
K8_ACC(3,1) = "MAE"
K8_ACC(3,2) = @mean(@abs(K8_E))
K8_ACC(3,3) = @mean(@abs(K8_EN))
K8_ACC(4,1) = "RMSE"
K8_ACC(4,2) = @sqrt(@mean(K8_E^2))
K8_ACC(4,3) = @sqrt(@mean(K8_EN^2))
K8_ACC(5,1) = "Theil U (model RMSE / naive RMSE)"
K8_ACC(5,2) = @sqrt(@mean(K8_E^2))/@sqrt(@mean(K8_EN^2))
K8_ACC.setwidth(1) 34
K8_SPOOL.append K8_ACC
smpl @all
smpl {%hs} {%fe}
group K8_G1 K8_A K8_F K8_N
freeze(K8_GR1) K8_G1.line
K8_GR1.addtext(t) "Imports: actual vs out-of-sample forecast vs naive (shaded = test period)"
K8_GR1.draw(shade, bottom) {%fs} {%fe}
K8_SPOOL.append K8_GR1

graph K8_DASH.merge K8_GR1
K8_DASH.align(2,1,1)
K8_DASH.addtext(t) "MFMod MKD | Test K8"
smpl @all
show K8_DASH
show K8_SPOOL


Glossary of econometric and statistical terms
TermMeaning
Add factorResidual used as judgement in the forecast; _A series
ADF testUnit-root test, H0 = non-stationary
AIC / SICInformation criteria for choosing models; lower = better
ARDLAutoregressive distributed lag model; an ECM in another form
CalibrationSetting a coefficient by judgement instead of estimating it
CointegrationNon-stationary series that move together in the long run
Confidence intervalRange that contains the true value with a given probability (≈ coefficient ± 2 s.e.)
DeflatorNominal ÷ real; a price index
Dummy variable0/1 variable for a special period
Durbin–WatsonAutocorrelation statistic; ≈ 2 is good
Dynamic forecastUses the model's own lagged forecasts
ECMError-correction model: long run + adjustment speed + short run
Elasticity% change in Y per 1% change in X
EndogenousDetermined inside the model
ExogenousSet outside the model (assumption)
Fitted valueValue predicted by the equation
Gauss–SeidelIterative algorithm that solves the model equation by equation
Half-lifeYears until half of a gap has closed
HeteroskedasticityResidual variance not constant
HP filterTrend–cycle decomposition; λ = 100 for annual data
I(0), I(1)Stationary; stationary after differencing once
IdentityAccounting equation that always holds
Impulse responsePath of variables after a shock
Long runEquilibrium the ECM converges to
MultiplierΔ output per unit of Δ spending
NAIRUUnemployment rate consistent with stable inflation
OLSOrdinary least squares: minimises squared residuals
Output gap(GDP ÷ potential − 1) × 100
p-valueProbability of the result if H0 were true; < 0.05 → reject H0
Percentage pointDifference between two rates
Potential GDPOutput at normal use of labour and capital
Quasi-identityAccounting link with a history-only residual (DUMH)
R²Share of variation explained
ResidualActual − fitted
RMSERoot mean squared error
ScenarioAlternative solution compared with the baseline
Serial correlationResiduals correlated over time
Solow residualTFP measured as output growth not explained by inputs
Spurious regressionFalse relation between trending series
Standard errorUncertainty of an estimate
StationaryConstant mean and variance; shocks fade
Steady statePath where ratios are constant
t-statisticCoefficient ÷ standard error; |t| > 2 ≈ significant
TFPTotal factor productivity
Unit rootProperty of a non-stationary series: shocks are permanent
Wald testTests restrictions on coefficients
Model-specific terms are in the main Glossary.
Self-test: 12 questions
Click an answer. The explanation appears immediately; your score is at the bottom.








Theory behind MFMod


The economics behind the equations, summarised from the World Bank's Macro-Fiscal Model: Technical Description (Burns, Campagne, Jooste, Stephan and Bui, PRWP 8965, 2019), Charl Jooste's MKD/Western Balkans Theory and Application notes (2023), the MFMod: An Exposition slides, and the Garín–Lester–Sims Intermediate Macroeconomics textbook. Each block ends with how your MKD code implements it.



T1. What kind of model is MFMod?




A macro-structural econometric model
It belongs to the Klein / Cowles Commission family, like the Fed's FRB/US, the ECB's ECB-MC, the OECD's Interlink and the Banque de France model. It maps all the identities of the national accounts, balance of payments, labour market and fiscal accounts (like financial programming), but also estimates behaviour. The World Bank runs it for about 180 countries, linked through trade (export markets), remittances and commodity prices.


Theory in the long run, data in the short run
Each equation is an error-correction model. The long-run (steady-state) part comes from optimisation theory: firms minimise cost, households smooth consumption, prices are a markup over marginal cost. The short-run dynamics are estimated from the data, so the speed of return to equilibrium is the one observed in North Macedonia. In a DSGE model, by contrast, the steady state comes from calibrated micro-founded parameters.


Keynesian short run, neoclassical long run
Because of nominal rigidities (sticky prices and wages), demand moves GDP in the short run and fiscal multipliers can exceed 1. In the long run, GDP returns to potential, which only TFP, labour and capital can move. The output gap is the main equilibrating force: a positive gap raises inflation (Phillips curve), which cuts real incomes and raises the cost of capital until the gap closes.


Expectations and estimation
The standard version is backward-looking: expectations are adaptive, plus an exogenous anchor INFLEXPT. Model-consistent expectations are possible, but in most cases they give similar results except for anticipated shocks. Equations are estimated one by one (OLS), some as systems (LIML/FIML), and many coefficients are calibrated (imposed). That is why your code has fixed numbers like −0.2 or 0.3 next to C(n).





T2. Production structure


Capital and labour produce domestic value added (Cobb-Douglas). Combined with imports (CES aggregation), this gives total supply. Total supply is split (CET transformation) between domestic sales (GDE) and exports.




T3. The blocks: theory, then how MKD implements it



Supply side and marginal cost


Y* = A · N*α · Kt−11−α,   N* = (1 − U*) · PR* · WPOP


Cost minimisation (min WN + RK subject to the production function) gives the factor demands and the marginal cost:


W/P = α·Y/N (real wage = marginal product of labour)  ·  R = (1−α)·P·Y/K  ·  P* = (1/A)·(W/α)α·(R/(1−α))1−α


Long-run growth is g* ≈ population growth + TFP growth/α. Potential is not the maximum GDP: it is the GDP at the natural rate of unemployment with prices in equilibrium, so the gap is a measure of capacity utilisation. The capital stock starts from a K/Y ratio (perpetual inventory with an estimated K0), and TFP is the HP-filtered Solow residual.


In MKD: α = 0.59, δ = 5%, an HP filter with λ = 100 and series extended before filtering, as the paper describes. MKDPSTAR uses the equivalent form P* = (1/A)1/α·(W/α)·(Y/K)(1−α)/α, which eliminates R by using R = (1−α)PY/K. One difference: MKD subtracts inventories when it accumulates capital.





Household consumption


Two-period permanent-income model: maximise u(C1) + βu(C2) subject to C1 + C2/(1+r) = V1 + W1N1(1−τ) + W2N2(1−τ)/(1+r). With CRRA utility, the Euler equation C2 = ((1+r)/(1+ρ))σ·C1 gives


c* = ln( W·N·(1 − τN) + V ) + Δy* − μ·(r − π)   →  consumption is a fixed share of GDP in the long run


Consumption rises with expected (permanent) income and wealth V and falls with the real interest rate. In the theory notes, wealth is proxied as domestic capital minus external liabilities.


In MKD: long-run income = wage bill × (1 − PIT rate) + social transfers + remittances × FX, with elasticity 1 and no wealth term. The real rate enters as −0.2·Δ(i − π). This is the "liquidity-constrained household" version, which suits a country with large remittances.





Private investment


Tobin's Q: firms maximise market value V = qK with quadratic adjustment costs, which gives I = (q − 1)/a with q = marginal product of capital / cost of capital. On the balanced growth path K grows with potential, so I/K = g + δ. With the capital demand K = (1−α)PY*/R:


I* = (δ + g) · (1 − α) · P · Y* / R    (gross operating surplus × expected growth / cost of capital)


User cost (Hall-Jorgenson): R = PI · (i + premium + δ − π) / (1 − τCIT)


The premium is a catch-all: the equity premium, bank regulation and concentration, and the cost of recovering collateral. In history it is a residual so that the identity holds; in the forecast it is exogenous.


In MKD: exactly this. MKDNEKRTPREMFR is backed out in readdat.prg, and the ECM targets (1−α)·Ypot/(R/PY), with (δ+g) absorbed in the constant C(1). Total capital is one stock, so public investment raises potential exactly like private investment. The paper notes that a separate public capital stock would "crowd in" private investment instead.





Exports and imports




Imports (CES demand): minimising the cost of total supply gives

M = ω · ((1+τM)·PM / λ)−ε · YT

Imports keep a constant share of domestic demand (the homogeneity restriction) and fall when imports get dearer than domestic goods. A trend can capture rising import penetration.


Exports (CET supply): a price-taking small open economy chooses between selling at home and abroad:

X = ω · (PX / λ)−ε · Y*,   X grows with XMKT

A higher export price relative to domestic prices makes exporting more profitable, a movement along the export supply curve. Homogeneity: exports grow with world demand, plus a trend for market-share gains that is phased out in the forecast.




In MKD: the export long run is ln X = ln XMKT + 0.3·ln(PX/PY). The positive sign is the CET logic above, not a mistake. T_LR is the trend, and solve.prg freezes it (T_LR = T_LR(-1)), as the paper recommends. In imports, the short-run activity term uses potential GDP; the paper uses actual demand.





Prices: Phillips curve, consumer prices, trade prices


Producer prices follow a New Keynesian framework: firms set P = σ/(σ−1)·MC (a markup over marginal cost), prices are sticky, and the markup varies with the output gap.


πFCST = β1·πFCST−1 + (1−β1)·[β2·πe + (1−β2)·Δln P*] + β3·gap


Why there is no error-correction term: wages and prices are both I(1) and share one stochastic trend (the wage-price loop). Only one of the two equations needs the ECM, and in MFMod it is the wage equation. That is why MKDNYGDPFCSTXN is written in growth rates only.


Consumer prices are a weighted average of producer and import prices plus VAT. The markup μ = PC/PFCST can be recovered from the constant. Other domestic deflators are indexed to PC.


Import and export prices converge to world prices in denars (law of one price) with partial indexation. Each world price is a Keyfitz price: commodity prices weighted by the country's own trade structure. Weights sum to one, so if all prices rise 1%, trade prices rise 1%.


In MKD: β2 = 0.5 (half expectations, half marginal cost) and a gap coefficient of 0.2. MKDPXKEY and MKDPMKEY are the Keyfitz prices, with base year 2020 and MUV-dominated weights. The import deflator uses 0.8 world / 0.2 domestic; the export deflator 0.6 / 0.4. VAT passes 100% into consumer prices on impact.





Labour market, wages and the NAIRU


Employment converges to structural employment N*. In the short run it falls when the real producer wage grows faster than productivity (W/P − ΔlnA/α, i.e. above the marginal product) and rises with the change in the output gap.


Wages error-correct to the nominal marginal product of labour, ln W − ln P − ln(α·Y*/N*), with inertia and partial indexation, and fall when unemployment exceeds the NAIRU (the wage Phillips curve).


NAIRU from first principles: firms set a price markup mp = σ/(σ−1); a union that maximises (1−τ)(w−b)Nζ sets a wage markup mw over the outside option b. In equilibrium:


u* = 1 − ( (1−α)·A / (mp · mw · b) )1/α,    labour-demand elasticity ε = σ / (1 + α(σ−1))


The natural rate rises with taxes, markups, union power and the replacement income b, and falls with productivity.


In MKD: readdat.prg contains this formula with σ = 4.4, ζ = 2.12, α = 0.31, replacement ratio 0.45 and the PIT rate as τ. It is commented out, and the target is fixed at 7.2%. Re-activating it would make the NAIRU respond to PIT changes, a channel the current model lacks.





Monetary policy, exchange rate and interest rates


Taylor rule: i = ρ·i−1 + (1−ρ)·[ rⁿ + π* + β1(π − π*) + β2·gap ]


Natural rate: iⁿ = [ P(1−τCIT)·((1−α)Y*/K + π*) ] / PI − δ


Exchange rate (UIP): Δln FX = iworld − idomestic + premium. Under a peg, the central bank gives up independent policy: UIP becomes the policy rule, so i = iworld + target depreciation + risk premium, and reserves (not the exchange rate) absorb the adjustment.


Interest on public debt follows the policy rate plus a term premium that rises when debt passes a threshold: term = a·(eD−D* − 1).


In MKD: the denar follows the euro (@PC(MKDPANUSATLS) = @PC(DEUPANUSATLS)), and reserves balance the BOP, consistent with a peg. The policy rate, however, still follows a Taylor-type rule on domestic inflation (1.2, no gap term). Theory says it should track the ECB rate plus a premium. The debt premium is linear: 5·(D/Y − 0.6).





Fiscal block


Revenue: Rk = τe·TBk, where the effective rate = statutory rate × coverage θ. Coverage captures zero-rating, exemptions, collection efficiency and evasion. It can be made to vary with the output gap, giving automatic stabilisers. Bases: wage bill (PIT and social contributions), gross operating surplus (CIT), consumption (VAT), imports (customs).


Expenditure rule (theory notes):


Gi = β·Gi−1 + (1−β) · ḡri · (1 − B̄B) · (R − GINT) − ψA·IA + ψB·BI


Spending is a long-run share ḡr of revenue net of interest, with persistence β, a deficit target B̄B and climate-adaptation terms. A rule like this is important for model convergence.


Debt: D = D−1 − balance + revaluation. Interest = implicit rate × lagged debt, with the external rate = US rate + spread. GFS spending is mapped to national-accounts G and IG through quasi-identities with a dummy, so historical GFS/NA gaps are kept.


In MKD: the active rule is the special case β = 0, no deficit target: spending = C(1)·(R − INT−1). Effective tax rates are constant (no gap-dependent coverage), and other revenues are shares of GDP, as in the paper.





Balance of payments and sectors


BOP: BOP exports and imports grow with the NA values in foreign currency, keeping the last historical BOP/NA ratio. In the standard model, remittance inflows follow the income of the countries where emigrants live; outflows, other income, FDI and portfolio grow with GDP in USD. Reserves = −(overall BOP).


Sectors: without sectoral capital and labour data, value added is driven by demand. The theory notes use an input-output mapping, Yj = [(1+βj)·Σ αjd·Dd − αjM·M − αjT·T] / (1+γj), where the α are the shares of each demand component in each sector.


In MKD: the paper's BOP is in USD; MKD's is in EUR. That explains the mixed EUR/USD conversions flagged in "Things to watch". Remittances are a fixed % of GDP, not linked to host-country income. The input-output sector mapping appears only in the climate module (MKDNVAGRSMKN …); the core uses growth shares.





T4. Reading the speed of adjustment


In an ECM, Δy = −θ·[y−1 − y*−1] + …, a fraction θ of the gap closes each year. Stability needs 0 < θ < 1. The half-life is ln(0.5)/ln(1−θ).


θHalf of gap closed90% closedUsed in MKD for


0.2≈ 3.1 years≈ 10 yearsConsumption, exports, sector deflators


0.3≈ 1.9 years≈ 6.5 yearsConsumption deflator, import and export deflators, wages, employment


C(2)estimated: see the EViews output (EViews button)Private investment, imports


0.02≈ 34 years≈ 114 yearsNAIRU toward its target (0.98 persistence)


For the whole system: written as A(L)·y = B·x, the model is stable if the roots of A(z) lie outside the unit circle; the long-run multiplier is A(1)−1B. In practice, convergence_check.prg checks this by plotting growth rates out to 2100.



T5. Where MKD differs from the standard MFMod theory


BlockStandard MFMod (papers)Your MKD codeWhat it means


ConsumptionIncome + wealth (sum to 1), real rateIncome incl. transfers and remittances, no wealthNo wealth/asset-price channel


Investment(δ+g)(1−α)PY*/R(1−α)Ypot/(R/P), (δ+g) in the constantSame dynamics if g is stable


ImportsShort run on demand growthShort run on potential growthDemand shocks reach imports more slowly


NAIRUStructural (taxes, markups, b)Fixed target 7.2% (formula commented out)PIT does not affect the NAIRU


Monetary policyPeg: UIP rulePeg on FX, but a Taylor rule on the policy rateRate responds to inflation, not to the ECB


FiscalRule with persistence and deficit targetShare of revenue net of interest (β=0)Debt not stabilised automatically


Tax coverageCan vary with the gapConstant effective ratesWeaker automatic stabilisers


BOP currencyUSDEUR (with some USD conversions)Check interest and gov. financing lines


RemittancesLinked to host-country income% of GDPNo link to the German/EU cycle



T6. Installing MFMod StandAlone (MFMSA)


    

  1. Requirements: 64-bit Windows, 64-bit Excel 2010+, 64-bit EViews 9+.
    2. 

  2. In EViews, type REGCOMPONENTS at the command line, answer Yes (All) and accept the admin prompt. This registers the COM components that Excel uses, and that MfMod+ also uses.
    3. 

  3. Download and run the MFMSA middleware setup.exe from isimulate.worldbank.org/mfm_admin/mfmsav1/. On Bank computers, install it in C:\WBG\LocalITUtilities.
    4. 

  4. Open the country Excel front end (MFMSA_MKD…xlsx), accept the dialog and set the default directories for programs and data (they must exist). The solve dates are model-specific.
    5. 

  5. Troubleshooting: if the publisher is not trusted, add https://isimulate.worldbank.org to Internet Options → Security → Trusted sites and rerun setup. If Excel warns about custom code, the file came from email or a network drive: use File → Save as to save it locally.
    6.

🧪 Test it in EViews · See the theory in the data


What it checks: Marginal-cost price vs the deflator, the consumption/income ratio (permanent income) and the user cost vs the investment rate.
What you should see: P* and the deflator moving together in the long run; a stable consumption/income ratio in the forecast; investment rate falling when the user cost rises.


 Paste into a new EViews program (File → New → Program) in the MKD workfile and press Run. Results open as a dashboard and a spool (all tables and graphs). Objects start with TH_; remove them with delete TH_*.


' ==============================================================================
'  MFMod MKD  |  TEST TH: Theory in the data
'  Purpose : Marginal-cost price P* vs the GDP deflator, consumption/income, user cost vs investment
'  Needs   : Baseline solved (actual series = baseline, *_0 series exist).
'  Output  : spool TH_SPOOL (tables + graphs) and dashboard TH_DASH
'  Clean up: delete TH_*
' ==============================================================================
%hs = "2005"      ' first year shown
%fs = "2026"      ' first forecast year (shaded area)
%fe = "2035"      ' last year shown
spool TH_SPOOL
smpl @all
smpl @all
series TH_PS = MKDPSTAR/@elem(MKDPSTAR,"2015")*100
TH_PS.displayname Marginal-cost price P* (2015 = 100)
series TH_PY = MKDNYGDPFCSTXN/@elem(MKDNYGDPFCSTXN,"2015")*100
TH_PY.displayname GDP deflator, factor cost (2015 = 100)
series TH_CY = MKDNECONPRVTKN/((MKDNYYWBTOTLCN*(1-MKDGGREVPITTXN/100)+MKDGGEXPTRNSCN+MKDBXFSTREMTCD*MKDPANUSATLS)/MKDNECONPRVTXN)
TH_CY.displayname Consumption / real disposable income
series TH_UC = MKDNEKRTTOTLXN/MKDNYGDPFCSTXN
TH_UC.displayname Real user cost of capital
series TH_IY = MKDNEGDIFPRVKN/MKDNYGDPPOTLKN*100
TH_IY.displayname Private investment / potential GDP, %
smpl {%hs} {%fe}
group TH_G1 TH_PS TH_PY
freeze(TH_GR1) TH_G1.line
TH_GR1.addtext(t) "Prices follow marginal cost"
TH_GR1.draw(shade, bottom) {%fs} {%fe}
TH_SPOOL.append TH_GR1
smpl {%hs} {%fe}
group TH_G2 TH_CY
freeze(TH_GR2) TH_G2.line
TH_GR2.addtext(t) "Consumption / disposable income (permanent income)"
TH_GR2.draw(shade, bottom) {%fs} {%fe}
TH_SPOOL.append TH_GR2
smpl {%hs} {%fe}
group TH_G3 TH_UC TH_IY
freeze(TH_GR3) TH_G3.line(m)
TH_GR3.addtext(t) "User cost vs investment rate"
TH_GR3.draw(shade, bottom) {%fs} {%fe}
TH_SPOOL.append TH_GR3

graph TH_DASH.merge TH_GR1 TH_GR2 TH_GR3
TH_DASH.align(2,1,1)
TH_DASH.addtext(t) "MFMod MKD | Test TH"
smpl @all
show TH_DASH
show TH_SPOOL








2. Reading variable names


MFMod uses the World Bank WDI-style mnemonic: Country (3) + Concept (8) + Unit suffix (2).


MKD · NE CON PRVT · KN   =   North Macedonia · National-accounts Expenditure · CONsumption · PRiVaTe · constant prices (Kostant, National currency)




SuffixMeaningExample


KNReal, constant prices, millions of denarsMKDNYGDPMKTPKN real GDP


CNNominal, current prices, millions of denarsMKDNYGDPMKTPCN nominal GDP


XNPrice index / deflator = CN / KN (1 in the base year)MKDNECONPRVTXN consumption deflator


CDCurrent foreign currency (BOP in EUR here, see section 16)MKDBXGSRGNFSCD BOP exports


KDReal, foreign currency (partner imports)DEUNEIMPGNFSKD


_ or FRRatio / rate / %MKDNYGDPGAP_, MKDNEKRTPREMFR


_A, _0, _3Add factor; baseline solution; scenario 3 solutionMKDNECONPRVTKN_A





  
First letters (concept)
NY GDP/income · NE expenditure · NV value added · GG general government · B balance of payments · LM labour market · SP population · FM/FP financial market / prices · PA exchange rate

  
Fiscal
GGREV… revenue · GGEXP… expenditure · GGBAL… balance · GGDBT… debt · GGFIN… financing. Ending in XN inside fiscal means an effective tax rate (%), e.g. GGREVGNFSXN = VAT rate.

  
BOP
BX credit (exports/inflows) · BM debit (imports/outflows) · BN net · BF financial account. GSR goods and services · MRCH merchandise · NFSV services · FST factor services and transfers.

' ==============================================================================

3. Data sources and how they link


readdat.prg imports five ranges from MKDrawOctober2026-XL2.xlsx. Rows are series with the mnemonic in the 3rd column; years run across.




Excel sheetWhat it containsSource (from the URL column)


MAINGDP expenditure side KN/CN, production side (agri, industry, services and sub-sectors), net taxes, BOP (merchandise, services, primary and secondary income, financial account, reserves), fiscal revenue/expenditure/debt, FX rates, remittances, CPI and HICP, employment, wages, unemployment, participation, policy rate, creditMakStat national accounts (ESA 2010), NBRM BOP and exchange rates, Ministry of Finance debt stock, MakStat labour force survey, Eurostat HICP


YTotal population, working-age population (15–74 and 15+), Gini, poverty, hours, electricity, school yearsMakStat / UN / IEA / Barro-Lee


CMDYWorld commodity prices (WLDF…) and MUV indexWorld Bank Pink Sheet


external_Q2Partner real imports (…NEIMPGNFSKD), partner FX indices (…EXR05) and consumer prices (…PCEXN05) for 12 partnersMFMod global database / WEO


ExtraTransport and energy NIA splits, US and EU interest rates, velocity, fiscal financing items, carbon taxes, energy volumes and emissions, R&DVarious





Derived series created in readdat.prg


Before any equation is estimated, the program builds the variables the equations need:




WhatHow (code)Why it matters


All deflatorsXN = CN / KN for GDP, C, G, I, inventories, X, M, GDP fc, agri, services, energyPrices are implicit deflators, not separate surveys


Public/private investment deflatorsMKDNEGDIFGOVXN = MKDNEGDIFPRVXN = MKDNEGDIFTOTXNBoth use the total GFCF deflator


InventoriesNEGDISTKB = NEGDIFTOT − NEGDIFGOV − NEGDIFPRVResidual. Note that NEGDIFTOT includes inventories in this model


Statistical discrepancyNYGDPDISC = GDP − (C+G+I+X−M)Keeps GDP = sum of components in history


Industry VANVINDTOTL = NYGDPFCST − NVAGRTOTL − NVSRVTOTLIndustry is the residual in the data


WagesNEWRTTOTLCN = 12 × monthly gross wage; NYYWBTOTLCN = wage × employmentWage bill uses official average wage data


Effective tax ratesPIT/wage bill, CIT/(GDP×(1−0.59)), VAT/(C+G), excise/C, customs/M (all ×100)Tax revenue in the forecast = rate × base


Interest rates on debtINTREXN = ext. interest / ext. debt(−1), same for domesticImplicit rates paid on the debt stock


Capital stockPerpetual inventory, δ = 5% (see section 4)Feeds potential GDP


TFPSolow residual, HP-filteredFeeds potential GDP and marginal cost


Trade weights, XMKT, REER, NEER, PXKEY, PMKEYSee section 7External block




The older datafromserver.prg pulled the same mnemonics from the World Bank server database (S:\MFM\MFMOD\SM23\baseline.edb). It is a legacy path; the current build reads Excel.
