4. Starting assumptions (how the model "starts")


Hard-coded parameters (readdat.prg)




AssumptionValueWhere used


Labour share α (MKDNYYWBTOTLCN_)0.59 (constant)Cobb-Douglas exponent; capital share = 0.41; CIT base; investment target; marginal cost


Depreciation rate (MKDDEPR)5%Capital stock, rental cost


Inflation expectations (MKDINFLEXPT)1.35% in history (overridden from ExogVars "Prices" in the forecast)Phillips curve, wages, policy rate, rental cost


Unemployment target (MKDLMUNRTARGT)7.2%Long-run anchor for the NAIRU


Unemployment path after 2025 (data prep)ut = 0.9·ut−1 + 0.1·7.2Only to extend the series before HP filtering


Participation path after 2025 (data prep)pt = 0.7·pt−1 + 0.3·57Same: converges to 57%


NAIRU and structural participationHP filter (λ = 100) of the extended seriesLMUNRSTRLCN, LMPRTSTRLCN


TFP growth after 2025 (data prep)+1.6% per year, then HP filter (λ = 100)MKDNYGDPTFP


Trade and REER weightsDEU 0.43, SRB 0.05, GRC 0.037, HUN 0.035, ITA 0.029, BEL 0.025, TUR 0.022, ESP 0.02, ROU 0.017, BIH 0.014, HRV 0.014, ALB 0.013, rescaled to sum to 1 (÷0.706)XMKT, REER, NEER


Debt target / balance target60% of GDP (rolling); −3% of GDPDefined, but the fiscal rule is switched off (see section 11)





Capital stock and TFP: the supply-side starting point




Capital stock (perpetual inventory)


K0 = ratio × GDP0;   Kt = Kt−1(1 − δ) + It − Inventoriest

The initial K/Y ratio is taken from a trial accumulation 15 years after the first investment observation. Inventories are subtracted (change of 14 Oct 2025).


TFP (Solow residual)


TFPraw = GDP / ( L*0.59 · Kt−10.41 ),   TFP = HP(TFPraw)

L* is structural employment = (1 − NAIRU)·structural participation·working-age population. Potential GDP is then rebuilt from these pieces.





Forecast extension rules (solve.prg)


Before solving, every exogenous variable is extended from 2026 to 2100 with a "half-momentum" rule (ρ = 0.5):


xt = xt−1 · [ 1 + ρ·gt−1 + (1−ρ)·g* ],   gt−1 = last year's growth




GroupSteady-state growth g*


Generic exogenous (default)popgr + tfpgr = −0.2% + 1.5% = 1.3%


Population (SPPOPTOTL, SPPOPWORK)−0.2%


Foreign prices and commodity prices1.8% (inflrate)


Partner real imports (list "reals")1.3% straight (no momentum)


Rates and ratios in the "excl" list (tax rates, NAIRU, labour share, interest spread, inflation expectations, financing items …)held flat at last value


TFPconverges to 1.5% × 0.67 ≈ 1.0% per year




After this, readexovars.prg overrides these default paths with your own assumptions from ExogVarsOctober2026.xlsx. Variables you put in that file win; the rule above only covers the ones you leave out.

5. Exogenous variables (what you control)


These are the variables listed in readexovars.prg (the %varsToExog list), grouped by the ExogVars sheet they come from, plus a few others that are exogenous in the model code.




Sheet / groupVariablesRole in the model


Labor structural participation · MKDNYYWBTOTLCN_ labour share · , MKDSPPOPTOTL population ·  TFP ·  unemployment targetSupply side: potential GDP, structural employment


FiscalMKDGGREVCITTXN CIT · MKDGGREVCUSTXN customs · MKDGGREVEXCSXN excise · MKDGGREVGNFSXN VAT · MKDGGREVPITTXN PIT (effective rates, %)Tax revenue = rate × base; VAT also enters the consumer price; PIT enters disposable income; CIT enters the cost of capital


CmdyWLDF… 35 commodity prices (oil, gas, metals, food …), MUVBuild PXKEY and PMKEY, the foreign-currency export and import price indices


TradePALB/BEL/BIH/DEU/ESP/GRC/HRV/HUN/ITA/ROU/SRB/TUR NEIMPGNFSKDPartner real imports → export market 


NomFXidx…PCEXN05 partner consumer-price indicesREER


RealFXidx…EXR05 partner exchange-rate indices (vs USD)REER, NEER


Prices inflation expectations · DEUNECONPRVTXN EU prices ·  EUR/USD · MKDNEKRTPREMFR risk premium · MKDINTREDIFF spread to US · USAINTRXN US rate · USANECONPRVTXNNominal anchor, peg, cost of capital, external interest rate


FinancingMKDBFCAFNEOMCD errors and omissions · MKDEXTLSHAREXN external share of debt · MKDGGBALOTHRCN below-the-line · MKDGGFINDOMTCN, MKDGGFINDPRVCN, MKDGGFINEAMTCN, MKDGGFINEDSBCNDebt split, financing table, BOP


Other exogenous in codeMKDDEPR depreciation · MKDNEGDISTKBKN/CN inventories · MKDGGEXPRANDDCN R&D · T_LR trend · DUMHInventories are projected with the same growth rule; everything else is held flat




Quasi-identities: equations whose formula ends in + C(1)*DUMH (e.g. exchange rate, government consumption, BOP exports, debt) are listed by solve.prg as quasi_identity. Their add factors are set to 0 in the forecast, so they behave exactly like identities there.

6. National accounts: expenditure and production approach






Expenditure side (real, KN). This is what determines GDP


GDP =  +  +  +  −  + Disc


Itot =  +  + Inventories


Domestic demand  = C + G + Itot + Disc


MKDNYGDPMKTPKN = MKDNECONPRVTKN + MKDNECONGOVTKN + MKDNEGDIFTOTKN + MKDNEEXPGNFSKN - MKDNEIMPGNFSKN + MKDNYGDPDISCKN
MKDNEGDIFTOTKN = MKDNEGDIFGOVKN + MKDNEGDIFPRVKN + MKDNEGDISTKBKN


The same identity holds in nominal terms (CN). The GDP deflator is NYGDPMKTPXN = CN/KN, so it is a result, not an equation. The discrepancy is a fixed share of GDP (NYGDPDISC/NYGDPMKTP = C(1)).






Production side (value added). This is derived from demand


GDPfc = GDPmp − net indirect taxes


Services = GDPfc − Agriculture − Industry


Agriculture and industry (real) grow with final demand:


@PC(MKDNVAGRTOTLKN) = @LOGIT(C(1)) * @PCY(MKDNECONPRVTKN+MKDNECONGOVTKN+MKDNEGDIFTOTKN+MKDNEEXPGNFSKN)
@PC(MKDNVINDTOTLKN) = @LOGIT(C(1)) * @PCY(…same…)


Each sector's growth is a share (0–1) of the growth of C + G + I + X. Services is the residual, so the two sides always add up. Net taxes (KN) are a fixed share of real GDP.


Sector deflators (agri, industry) follow the consumption deflator through an ECM; the services deflator = services CN / KN, where services CN = GDPfc CN − agri CN − industry CN.






Key idea: this is a demand-driven model in the short run (GDP = sum of spending) and a supply-driven model in the long run. Spending equations are anchored to potential GDP (investment, imports) and to income (consumption), and prices adjust through the output gap until GDP returns to potential.


🧪 Test it in EViews · Expenditure and production side

What you should see: Checks PASS; consumption the largest contributor in most years; sector growth proportional to final-demand growth in the forecast (logit-share equations).

7. External sector: trade, exchange rate, REER



Export market (foreign demand) 


XMKT = Σi wi · Mireal, partner · FX2010


A weighted sum of the real imports of 12 partners (ALB, BEL, BIH, DEU, ESP, GRC, HRV, HUN, ITA, ROU, SRB, TUR), converted at the 2010 denar/USD rate. Germany carries about 61% of the weight after rescaling (0.43 / 0.706).



Exchange rate  (denar per USD)


@PC(MKDPANUSATLS) = @PC(DEUPANUSATLS) + C(1)*DUMH
MKDPANEUATLS = MKDPANUSATLS * (1 / DEUPANUSATLS)


This is the de facto euro peg. The denar/USD rate moves one-for-one with the euro/USD rate (DEUPANUSATLS, exogenous). The denar/EUR rate MKDPANEUATLS is therefore constant in the forecast (≈61.5). The C(1)*DUMH term only fits history; it is switched off in the forecast.



Real and nominal effective exchange rate


MKDEXR05  = MKDPANUSATLS / MKDPANUSATLS(2010)        ' nominal index, 2010 = 1
MKDPCEXN05 = MKDNECONPRVTXN / MKDNECONPRVTXN(2010)   ' domestic price index, 2010 = 1
MKDREER = 100 * Σ w_i / ( (MKDEXR05/MKDPCEXN05) / (iEXR05/iPCEXN05) )
MKDNEER = 100 * Σ w_i / ( MKDEXR05 / iEXR05 )


REER = 100 · Σ wi · (Ei / EMKD) · (PMKD / Pi)


E is each currency per USD (index 2010 = 1) and P is consumer prices. A rise in the REER is a real appreciation (denar stronger, or Macedonian prices rising faster than partners'). The weights are the same as for XMKT.


Important: REER and NEER are reporting indicators only. No behavioural equation uses them; the only reference is in a commented-out merchandise-export equation. Competitiveness enters trade instead through the relative price of exports or imports versus the domestic GDP deflator (below).



Export and import world prices: PXKEY and PMKEY


Two foreign-currency price indices are built from World Bank commodity prices (2020 = 1). The weights reflect North Macedonia's trade structure:




Largest weights


 (exports)MUV (manufactures) 77.9 · iron ore 7.2 · aluminium 3.3 · tobacco 3.1 · orange 2.9 · maize 1.4 · cotton 1.3 · crude oil 1.2


 (imports)MUV 61.1 · platinum 11.7 · crude oil 7.7 · iron ore 4.6 · cotton 4.0 · natural gas 2.3 · beef 1.9




The platinum weight reflects the catalytic-converter industry in the free zones (imported platinum-group metals). Cotton appears twice in both indices with different weights.



Trade volumes and prices


See the equation cards for exports, imports, export deflator and import deflator. In short:


    

  • Exports follow the export market one-for-one in the long run, and rise when the export price is high relative to domestic costs (profitability of exporting).
    • 

  • Imports follow domestic demand one-for-one in the long run and fall when imports become relatively expensive. In the short run they respond to potential GDP growth (0.8).
    • 

  • Export deflator = 40% domestic costs + 60% world export prices in denars (PXKEY × FX).
    • 

  • Import deflator = 20% domestic costs + 80% world import prices in denars (PMKEY × FX).
    • 

  • Terms of trade MKDTOT = PX / PM.
    • 



🧪 Test it in EViews · Exchange rates and competitiveness

What you should see: A flat denar/EUR line (peg), denar/USD following EUR/USD, exports growing with the export market in the forecast.

8. How the balance of payments is created


The BOP block is mostly bridging equations: it translates national-accounts trade into BOP concepts and sets other flows as shares of GDP. BOP data are in millions of EUR (the import ranges are named "…MILLIONS_OF_CURRENT_EUR").


Current account




ItemEquation / identityType


NA exports, imports in EURMKDNEEXPGNFSCD = MKDNEEXPGNFSCN / MKDPANEUATLS (same for imports, GDP)identity


BOP exports G&S BXGSRGNFSCD@PC(BXGSRGNFSCD) = @PC(NEEXPGNFSCD) + C(1)*DUMH: grows like NA exportsquasi-identity


BOP imports G&S BMGSRGNFSCD@PC(BMGSRGNFSCD) = @PC(NEIMPGNFSCD) + C(1)*DUMHquasi-identity


Merchandise exports, importsBXGSRMRCHCD / BXGSRGNFSCD = C(1): fixed share of G&Sshare


ServicesBXGSRNFSVCD = BXGSRGNFSCD − BXGSRMRCHCDidentity


Remittances in/outBXFSTREMTCD / NYGDPMKTPCD = C(1): % of GDPshare


Other factor income/transfers in/outBXFSTOTHRCD / NYGDPMKTPCD = C(1)share


Interest on external public debtBMFSTINTECD = GGEXPINTECN / PANUSATLSidentity, fiscal link


Primary + secondary creditsBXFSTCABTCD = REMT + OTHRidentity


Primary + secondary debitsBMFSTCABTCD = REMT + OTHR + INTEidentity


Current account = BNGSRGNFSCD (G&S balance) + BNFSTCABTCD (net income and transfers)identity




Capital and financial account, reserves




Capital account, FDI, portfolio, other privateeach / NYGDPMKTPCD = C(1) (% of GDP)


Government external financingBFFINTGOVCD = GGFINEXTLCN / PANUSATLS, added to "other investment"


Financial account excl. reservesBFCAFFINXCD = FDI + portfolio + other


Overall BOPBFBOPTOTLCD = capital + financial + current + errors


Change in reservesBFCAFRACGCD = −(capital + financial − errors − current account): the balancing item




How to read it: trade volumes and prices are determined in the national-accounts block, the BOP simply converts them to EUR, and reserves absorb whatever is left over. This matches a pegged exchange-rate regime: the central bank's reserves, not the exchange rate, take the adjustment.

9. Prices and deflators: the price chain


Prices are built in a chain from costs → GDP deflator → consumption deflator → everything else:



  
Wages, TFP, K/Yproduction costs
→
  
PSTARmarginal cost price
→
  
GDP fc deflatorPhillips curve + gap
→
  
Consumption deflator+ import prices + VAT
→
  
G, I, sector deflators, CPIfollow consumption






DeflatorDriven byCard


 marginal-cost priceWage, TFP, GDP/K, labour share (identity from the Cobb-Douglas cost function)→


 GDP at factor cost deflatorOwn lag, PSTAR, inflation expectations, output gap→


 private consumption deflatorGDP fc deflator, import deflator, VAT rate→


 import deflatorPMKEY × FX (80%), GDP fc deflator (20%)→


 export deflatorPXKEY × FX (60%), GDP fc deflator (40%)→


MKDNECONGOVTXN, MKDNEGDIFGOVXN, MKDNEGDIFPRVXNECM on the consumption deflator with unit short-run pass-through→


MKDNEGDIFTOTXN total investment deflatorIdentity: total I CN / total I KN


 CPIGrows exactly like the consumption deflator plus a constant drift C(9)→


MKDNYGDPMKTPXN GDP deflator (market prices)Identity: nominal GDP / real GDP


 rental cost of capitalInvestment deflator × (policy rate + premium + δ − expected inflation) / (1 − CIT)→

10. Labour market and supply side






Labour supply chain


Labour force = participation × working-age pop.


L* (structural employment) = (1 − NAIRU) · part*str · pop15+


Unemployment u = 1 − Employment / Labour force


Wage bill = average wage × employment


Participation moves toward its structural level: LMPRTTOTLCN = C(3)·LMPRTSTRLCN + (1−C(3))·LMPRTTOTLCN(−1).


The NAIRU drifts slowly toward the target: LMUNRSTRLCN = 0.98·LMUNRSTRLCN(−1) + 0.02·7.2.






Potential output (Cobb-Douglas)


Ypot = TFP · (L*)0.59 · Kt−10.41


Gap = (GDP / Ypot − 1) × 100


Kt = (1−0.05) Kt−1 + Itot − Inventories


Potential grows with TFP (exogenous), working-age population and NAIRU (exogenous), and capital (endogenous, via investment). This is where investment raises long-run growth.






The two behavioural labour equations, wages and employment, are in section 13.


🧪 Test it in EViews · Labour market in graphs

What you should see: Employment converging to L*; unemployment following the slow-moving NAIRU (far from 7.2% even in 2040); real wage growth ≈ productivity growth in the forecast.

11. Fiscal block




Revenue = effective rate × tax base




TaxBase


PIT GGREVPITTCNwage bill


CIT GGREVCITTCNnominal GDP × (1 − 0.59) (capital income)


VAT GGREVGNFSCNnominal C + G


Excise GGREVEXCSCNnominal C


Customs GGREVCUSTCNnominal imports


Social contributions, non-tax, resource, grants, other, property, SRA, other taxesfixed % of nominal GDP




MKDGGREVTAXTCN = VAT + EXCISE + CUSTOMS + PIT + CIT + (PROPERTY+SRA) + OTHER TAXES
MKDGGREVTOTLCN = TAX + NONTAX + SSOC + COMM + GRANTS + OTHER


Expenditure = share of (revenue − last year's interest)


MKDGGEXPCAPTCN / (MKDGGREVTOTLCN - MKDGGEXPINTPCN(-1)) = C(1)
(same form for WAGE, GNFS, SUBS, SRAT, TOTS, TPNS, TSOC)


Each spending item is a constant share of revenue net of lagged interest. Spending therefore rises automatically with revenue (a "spend what you collect" rule).


Transfers  = social assistance + pensions + other social + (subsidies + SRA)
Current    = wages + goods&services + transfers + interest
Total      = current + capital
Interest   = ext. rate/100 × ext. debt(-1) + dom. rate/100 × dom. debt(-1)
ext. rate  = US rate + spread (exogenous)
Balance    = revenue − total expenditure






Debt dynamics


MKDGGDBTTOTLCN = MKDGGDBTTOTLCN(-1) - MKDGGBALOVRLCN + MKDGGDBTVALTCN
MKDGGDBTVALTCN / MKDNYGDPMKTPCN = C(1)      ' valuation/other, % GDP
External debt = total × external share (exog.)
Domestic debt = total × (1 − external share)


Link from fiscal to the real economy


    

  • Nominal government consumption grows with wages + goods and services spending; real G = nominal / G deflator.
    • 

  • Nominal public investment grows with capital expenditure.
    • 

  • Transfers and the PIT rate enter household disposable income → consumption.
    • 

  • VAT rate enters the consumption deflator.
    • 

  • CIT rate enters the cost of capital → private investment.
    • 

  • Structural balance = revenue and expenditure scaled by potential/actual GDP.
    • 





The debt-targeting fiscal rule is off. In equations.prg, !current = 1, so the simple share rules are used. The rule with persistence 0.8, debt-target weight −0.2 and balance-target weight 0.1 (MKDrule1 vector) is defined, but its equations are commented out. Debt is therefore not stabilised automatically; it is driven by your revenue assumptions and the spending shares.

12. Interest rates


MKDFMLBLPOLYXN = C(1)*MKDFMLBLPOLYXN(-1) + (1-C(1))*(C(2) + 1.2*(@PC(MKDNECONPRVTXN) - MKDINFLEXPT) + 0.0*MKDNYGDPGAP_)
MKDINTRDXN    = C(1) + C(2)*MKDFMLBLPOLYXN + 5*(MKDGGDBTTOTLCN/MKDNYGDPMKTPCN - 0.6) + C(10)*@DURING("2012")




Policy rate (Taylor-type rule)
Smoothed (C(1) = persistence); raises the rate by 1.2 for each point of inflation above expectations. The output-gap weight is 0, consistent with a peg where policy follows inflation and the ECB rather than domestic activity. Estimated on 2000–2024.


Domestic interest rate on public debt
Follows the policy rate plus a debt premium: +5 bp per percentage point of debt/GDP above 60% (the coefficient is on the ratio, so +0.05 pp per pp). Feeds domestic interest spending.




The policy rate affects the economy through (1) the real interest rate in consumption, (2) the rental cost of capital → private investment, and (3) the interest bill on domestic debt.


🧪 Test it in EViews · Interest rates in graphs

What you should see: NBRM close to the ECB in history; Taylor pressure near 0 in the forecast (inflation = expectations), so the policy rate settles at its neutral level.

13b. All equations: behavioural, quasi-identities and identities


Every equation that is in model MKD when it is built with the switches off: 161 in total, taken from equations.prg in the order they appear. The inactive fiscal-rule branch is left out, and where a name is defined twice the last definition counts, as in EViews. Click any variable inside a formula to jump to the equation that defines it.




Behavioural 58 equations
Estimated with .LS, with an add factor that makes them fit history exactly. In the forecast the add factor decays by 15% a year. Sub-types: ECM (long run plus short run), ratio rule (X/Y = C(1): the variable stays a fixed share of its base), tax rate × base, share of demand growth (@LOGIT) and other rules (Phillips curve, NAIRU, Taylor rule, participation).


Quasi-identity 10 equations
Written like an identity plus + C(1)*DUMH. DUMH = 1 in history, so C(1) absorbs any data gap there; in the forecast DUMH = 0 and solve.prg sets their add factors to 0, so they hold exactly. Examples: the exchange rate (peg), public debt, BOP exports and imports, and government consumption and investment.


Identity 93 equations
Added with APPEND @IDENTITY. Pure accounting: they always hold, with nothing estimated and no add factor (GDP = C+G+I+X−M, nominal = real × deflator, balances, cross rates, REER…).




The equation you see in EViews (Equation → View → Representations) is this same specification. Press EViews on a row to open the series and the estimated equation with its coefficient values.

15. How the model is solved (add factors)


    

  1. Merge: every estimated equation object is merged into model MKD.
    2. 

  2. In-sample (2012–2025): addassign(i,c) @stochastic + addinit(v=n) create an add factor (_A) for each behavioural equation, equal to the residual. The model therefore reproduces history exactly.
    3. 

  3. Extend exogenous variables to 2100 (section 4).
    4. 

  4. Add factors in the forecast: each decays by 15% per year (_A = _A(−1) × 0.85), so the last historical "surprise" fades out. Quasi-identity add factors are set to 0.
    5. 

  5. Solve 2012–2100: deterministic, dynamic, Gauss-Seidel (s=d, d=d, o=g, c=1e-6). Results are written to _0 and copied into the base series.
    6. 

  6. The discrepancy and net-tax equations are dropped from the model after solving.
    7. 



Why the add-factor decay matters: if 2025 private consumption was 3% above what the equation predicts, the forecast starts 3% above too, and that gap shrinks to 3% × 0.85t. Editing _A paths is the standard way to impose judgement on the forecast.


convergence_check.prg then plots the % change of GDP, the main components (KN, XN, CN), wages, employment and PSTAR, the output gap, the budget balance against −3%, debt against 60%, and GDP against potential, shading the years where the output gap changes sign.


🧪 Test it in EViews · Check the solution


What it checks: Whether the baseline reproduces history, how the add factors decay in the forecast, and whether growth and the gap converge.
What you should see: Checks PASS; add factors shrinking geometrically after 2025 (×0.85); the gap closing towards 0.


 Paste into a new EViews program (File → New → Program) in the MKD workfile and press Run. Results open as a dashboard and a spool (all tables and graphs). Objects start with SO_; remove them with delete SO_*.


' ==============================================================================
'  MFMod MKD  |  TEST SO: Solution checks
'  Purpose : History replication, add-factor paths in the forecast, convergence
'  Needs   : Baseline solved (actual series = baseline, *_0 series exist).
'  Output  : spool SO_SPOOL (tables + graphs) and dashboard SO_DASH
'  Clean up: delete SO_*
' ==============================================================================
%hs = "2010"      ' first year shown
%fs = "2026"      ' first forecast year (shaded area)
%fe = "2040"      ' last year shown
spool SO_SPOOL
smpl @all

' ---- Automatic checks (PASS if max |error| below threshold) ----------------
table(3,4) SO_CHK
SO_CHK(1,1) = "Check"
SO_CHK(1,2) = "Max |error|"
SO_CHK(1,3) = "Threshold"
SO_CHK(1,4) = "Result"
smpl 2005 2025
series SO_E2 = (MKDNYGDPMKTPKN_0/MKDNYGDPMKTPKN-1)*100
!m = @max(@abs(SO_E2))
SO_CHK(2,1) = "Baseline reproduces history: real GDP, %"
SO_CHK(2,2) = !m
SO_CHK(2,3) = 0.01
if !m < 0.01 then
  SO_CHK(2,4) = "PASS"
else
  SO_CHK(2,4) = "CHECK"
endif
smpl 2005 2025
series SO_E3 = (MKDLMEMPTOTLCN_0/MKDLMEMPTOTLCN-1)*100
!m = @max(@abs(SO_E3))
SO_CHK(3,1) = "Baseline reproduces history: employment, %"
SO_CHK(3,2) = !m
SO_CHK(3,3) = 0.01
if !m < 0.01 then
  SO_CHK(3,4) = "PASS"
else
  SO_CHK(3,4) = "CHECK"
endif
SO_CHK.setwidth(1) 46
SO_SPOOL.append SO_CHK
smpl @all
series SO_AC = MKDNECONPRVTKN_A
SO_AC.displayname MKDNECONPRVTKN_A
series SO_AI = MKDNEGDIFPRVKN_A
SO_AI.displayname MKDNEGDIFPRVKN_A
series SO_AX = MKDNEEXPGNFSKN_A
SO_AX.displayname MKDNEEXPGNFSKN_A
series SO_AM = MKDNEIMPGNFSKN_A
SO_AM.displayname MKDNEIMPGNFSKN_A
series SO_AW = MKDNEWRTTOTLCN_A
SO_AW.displayname MKDNEWRTTOTLCN_A
series SO_AP = MKDNECONPRVTXN_A
SO_AP.displayname MKDNECONPRVTXN_A
series SO_G = @pc(MKDNYGDPMKTPKN)
SO_G.displayname Real GDP growth, %
series SO_GAP = MKDNYGDPGAP_
SO_GAP.displayname Output gap, %
smpl {%hs} {%fe}
group SO_G1 SO_AC SO_AI SO_AX SO_AM SO_AW SO_AP
freeze(SO_GR1) SO_G1.line
SO_GR1.addtext(t) "Add factors: history and decay in the forecast"
SO_GR1.draw(shade, bottom) {%fs} {%fe}
SO_GR1.draw(line, left) 0
SO_SPOOL.append SO_GR1
smpl {%hs} {%fe}
group SO_G2 SO_G SO_GAP
freeze(SO_GR2) SO_G2.line
SO_GR2.addtext(t) "Convergence: growth and gap, %"
SO_GR2.draw(shade, bottom) {%fs} {%fe}
SO_GR2.draw(line, left) 0
SO_SPOOL.append SO_GR2

graph SO_DASH.merge SO_GR1 SO_GR2
SO_DASH.align(2,1,1)
SO_DASH.addtext(t) "MFMod MKD | Test SO"
smpl @all
show SO_DASH
show SO_SPOOL








16. Things to watch (from reading the code)


Currency mixing in the BOP. NA trade and GDP are converted to "CD" with the EUR rate (/MKDPANEUATLS), but external interest (BMFSTINTECD), government external financing (BFFINTGOVCD) and BNCABFUNDCN use the USD rate (MKDPANUSATLS). If BOP data are in EUR, those three items are mis-scaled by the EUR/USD rate (about 8–10%). Check before you use the reserves change.


Remittances converted with the USD rate. In the consumption equation, remittances (MKDBXFSTREMTCD, in EUR) are multiplied by MKDPANUSATLS (denar per USD) instead of MKDPANEUATLS. Household income from remittances is therefore about 10–11% too low, and it moves whenever EUR/USD moves.


REER is not a driver. It is calculated but not used in any active equation. A real appreciation shock to the REER will not move exports unless you route it through export prices.


Fiscal rule disabled. Spending is a fixed share of (revenue − lagged interest). Debt can drift. Toggle !current in equations.prg if you want the debt-target rule.


Import short-run driver is potential, not actual, GDP (0.8·Δln Ypot). Demand shocks therefore pass to imports mostly via the long-run domestic-demand anchor, more slowly than in many models.


Labour share fixed at 0.59 as the Cobb-Douglas exponent, but the wage bill comes from actual wages × employment, so the actual wage share can differ from 0.59. The CIT base also uses 0.41 × GDP.


Duplicate definitions. _MKDGGEXPGNFSCN and _MKDGGREVGRNTCN are each estimated twice. The last definition wins, which is fine but easy to misread. MKDEXR05/PCEXN05 are normalised to 2010 despite the "05" in the name.


Trade-partner extension list. In solve.prg the "reals" list omits HUN, ROU and SRB partner imports; they fall back to the generic rule unless you override them in the TradeP sheet (you do).


🧪 Test it in EViews · See each finding in the data


What it checks: Remittance conversion (USD vs EUR), imports vs their drivers, measured vs model labour share, TFP history vs forecast, CPI vs deflator, NBRM vs ECB rate.
What you should see: A remittance gap that moves with EUR/USD (≈ −10%), imports tracking demand and exports more than potential, a measured share below 0.59, forecast TFP growth well above its history, and NBRM following the ECB.


 Paste into a new EViews program (File → New → Program) in the MKD workfile and press Run. Results open as a dashboard and a spool (all tables and graphs). Objects start with FD_; remove them with delete FD_*.


' ==============================================================================
'  MFMod MKD  |  TEST FD: Roadmap issues, tested
'  Purpose : Shows each known model issue in the data
'  Needs   : Baseline solved (actual series = baseline, *_0 series exist).
'  Output  : spool FD_SPOOL (tables + graphs) and dashboard FD_DASH
'  Clean up: delete FD_*
' ==============================================================================
%hs = "2005"      ' first year shown
%fs = "2026"      ' first forecast year (shaded area)
%fe = "2035"      ' last year shown
spool FD_SPOOL
smpl @all
series FD_REMU = MKDBXFSTREMTCD*MKDPANUSATLS
FD_REMU.displayname Remittances in income: x denar/USD (model)
series FD_REME = MKDBXFSTREMTCD*MKDPANEUATLS
FD_REME.displayname Remittances: x denar/EUR (data are EUR)
series FD_REMD = (MKDBXFSTREMTCD*MKDPANUSATLS/(MKDBXFSTREMTCD*MKDPANEUATLS)-1)*100
FD_REMD.displayname Model vs EUR conversion, %
series FD_DM = dlog(MKDNEIMPGNFSKN)*100
FD_DM.displayname Imports growth, %
series FD_DGDE = dlog(MKDNEGDETTOTKN)*100
FD_DGDE.displayname Domestic demand growth, %
series FD_DPOT = dlog(MKDNYGDPPOTLKN)*100
FD_DPOT.displayname Potential growth, %
series FD_DX = dlog(MKDNEEXPGNFSKN)*100
FD_DX.displayname Exports growth, %
series FD_LSH = MKDNYYWBTOTLCN/MKDNYGDPMKTPCN
FD_LSH.displayname Measured wage share of GDP
series FD_ALF = MKDNYYWBTOTLCN_
FD_ALF.displayname Labour share used in the model
series FD_TFP = @pc(MKDNYGDPTFP)
FD_TFP.displayname TFP growth, %
series FD_CPI = @pc(MKDFPCPITOTLXN)
FD_CPI.displayname CPI inflation, %
series FD_PCD = @pc(MKDNECONPRVTXN)
FD_PCD.displayname Consumption deflator inflation, %
series FD_POL = MKDFMLBLPOLYXN
FD_POL.displayname NBRM policy rate, %
series FD_ECB = DEUFMLBLPOLYXN
FD_ECB.displayname ECB policy rate, %
smpl {%hs} {%fe}
group FD_G1 FD_REMU FD_REME
freeze(FD_GR1) FD_G1.line
FD_GR1.addtext(t) "Remittances: USD vs EUR conversion (denars)"
FD_GR1.draw(shade, bottom) {%fs} {%fe}
FD_SPOOL.append FD_GR1
smpl {%hs} {%fe}
group FD_G2 FD_REMD
freeze(FD_GR2) FD_G2.line
FD_GR2.addtext(t) "Remittance conversion error, %"
FD_GR2.draw(shade, bottom) {%fs} {%fe}
FD_GR2.draw(line, left) 0
FD_SPOOL.append FD_GR2
smpl {%hs} {%fe}
group FD_G3 FD_DM FD_DGDE FD_DPOT FD_DX
freeze(FD_GR3) FD_G3.line
FD_GR3.addtext(t) "Imports vs drivers, growth %"
FD_GR3.draw(shade, bottom) {%fs} {%fe}
FD_GR3.draw(line, left) 0
FD_SPOOL.append FD_GR3
smpl {%hs} {%fe}
group FD_G4 FD_LSH FD_ALF
freeze(FD_GR4) FD_G4.line
FD_GR4.addtext(t) "Labour share: measured vs model"
FD_GR4.draw(shade, bottom) {%fs} {%fe}
FD_SPOOL.append FD_GR4
smpl {%hs} {%fe}
group FD_G5 FD_TFP
freeze(FD_GR5) FD_G5.line
FD_GR5.addtext(t) "TFP growth, % (history vs forecast assumption)"
FD_GR5.draw(shade, bottom) {%fs} {%fe}
FD_GR5.draw(line, left) 0
FD_SPOOL.append FD_GR5
smpl {%hs} {%fe}
group FD_G6 FD_CPI FD_PCD
freeze(FD_GR6) FD_G6.line
FD_GR6.addtext(t) "CPI vs consumption-deflator inflation, %"
FD_GR6.draw(shade, bottom) {%fs} {%fe}
FD_SPOOL.append FD_GR6
smpl {%hs} {%fe}
group FD_G7 FD_POL FD_ECB
freeze(FD_GR7) FD_G7.line
FD_GR7.addtext(t) "NBRM policy rate vs ECB rate, %"
FD_GR7.draw(shade, bottom) {%fs} {%fe}
FD_SPOOL.append FD_GR7

' ---- Average TFP growth: history vs forecast -------------------------------
table(3,2) FD_TFP
FD_TFP(1,1) = "Period"
FD_TFP(1,2) = "Average TFP growth, %"
smpl 2015 2025
FD_TFP(2,1) = "2015-2025 (history)"
FD_TFP(2,2) = @mean(FD_TFP)
smpl 2026 2050
FD_TFP(3,1) = "2026-2050 (forecast)"
FD_TFP(3,2) = @mean(FD_TFP)
FD_SPOOL.append FD_TFP
smpl @all

graph FD_DASH.merge FD_GR1 FD_GR2 FD_GR3 FD_GR4 FD_GR5 FD_GR6 FD_GR7
FD_DASH.align(2,1,1)
FD_DASH.addtext(t) "MFMod MKD | Test M7"
smpl @all
show FD_DASH
show FD_SPOOL








17. Optional modules (switched off by default)




Climate mitigation (climateeqs.prg)
Splits industry into energy and non-energy, builds coal/oil/gas/renewables volumes, prices (world price + carbon tax) and CES nests with substitution elasticity 2. Private consumption is split into energy and other, imports into energy and non-energy, plus emissions, PM2.5, working days lost and health costs. It re-specifies sector shares, the consumption deflator and imports.


Climate damages (climate_damages.prg)
Flood damage to the capital stock with adaptation capital (Hallegatte and Vogt-Schilb), heat, health and agriculture productivity losses in the production function, and scenarios: 1% of GDP flood in 2035, adaptation policies, heat shock, agri shock, and a 1995-size flood (USD 500 mn) in 2027.


BCA and transport
BCA splits exports into chemicals, iron, refined, fertiliser and other, each with its own market and an EU-carbon-adjusted price. Transport adds petrol and diesel pump prices with excise, fuel demand, car ownership, transport emissions and excise revenue.

EViews link: open any variable in EViews


Every  button in this manual copies a short text such as MFMOD>MKDNECONPRVTKN>… to the clipboard. The MfMod+ add-in picks it up and shows that series, plus its estimated equation _MKD… if it has one, in your EViews workfile.


    

  1. Install once: run Add_Manual_to_MfModPlus.bat from the setup folder (close Excel first).
    2. 

  2. In Excel, open the MfMod+ tab and use Load workfile to choose your MKDSoln…wf1 (if you have not already).
    3. 

  3. Press Open Manual in the Model manual group. This opens the page and switches Follow Manual on.
    4. 

  4. Click any EViews button here. Within about a second, EViews shows the series and its equation.
    5. 



Without Follow Manual: click an EViews button, go to Excel and press Ctrl+Shift+E (or Show copied variable). You can also copy a plain name such as MKDNEEXPGNFSKN and press Ctrl+Shift+E.


Identities have no _MKD… equation object, so only the series opens. The add-in checks the clipboard only while Follow Manual is on.
